title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($π_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $π_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $π_{0.5}$.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising route to achieve general-purpose robot manipulation. By adapting large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to action driess2023palm, beyer2024paligemma, deitke2025molmo , VLAs combine broad visual and semantic knowledge with continuous control and increasingly handle manipulation tasks across objects, environments, and robot embodiments brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . Architecturally, VLAs typically combine a pretrained VLM backbone chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05, bjorck2025groot, deshpande2026molmobot, fang2026molmoact2, wen2025dexvla, wen2025tinyvla with a separate diffusion or flow-matching action expert that produces continuous control. The two modules are typically joined through a dense, layer-wise interface that conditions the expert on the backbone at every layer. Despite their growing real-world efficacy and partially due to the multi-modal architecture design, these models remain black boxes. VLAs transform thousands of image, language, and proprioceptive tokens through billions of parameters before producing a small set of continuous action tokens, leaving the internal mapping from perception to action an open area of study. We study three frontier open-source VLAs: , MolmoBot, and MolmoAct2 intelligence2025pi05,deshpande2026molmobot,fang2026molmoact2 . Across all three models, we find that perception and action communicate through a surprisingly narrow channel (1-3 cross-attention layers). Causal influence concentrates in a middle-to-late band of VLM layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. This suggests that the action expert ingests representations which already encode task-relevant spatial information, rather than depending equally on every stage of backbone computation. We apply our findings of the narrow action-conditioning interface between the AE and VLM to improve VLA efficiency. Many prior works have attempted to reduce VLA computation, by skipping or exiting backbone layers yue2024deer,zhang2025mole,zhang2026a1 , pruning redundant layers or parameters yang2025efficientvla,nguyen2026fewerlayers,sun2026dropthenrecovery,zhang2026redundancy , or conditioning the action head on only a subset of backbone layers bjorck2025groot,shukor2025smolvla . These methods decide what to remove using heuristics such as representational similarity or benchmark success. We offer a more mechanistic account of why these designs work. Our results show that the representations necessary for action are stored sparsely across tokens and layers. In this work we show that by leveraging causal analysis we can choose exactly the relevant areas of the model to prune. Restricting conditioning to the causally important layers removes of MolmoBot's cross-attention parameters and reduces the estimated VLM--action-expert floating-point operation count by up to with a similar change in real world measured latency. The simplified architecture achieves task success comparable to the vanilla policy across 3,000 evaluation episodes. The same approach carries over to preliminary trials on a real robot, where sparse and dense policies achieve comparable success rates (67 and 64 of 100 trials). We view these results as a step toward intentional design mcgrath2026intentional of VLA models, where the internal mechanisms connecting perception to control directly inform how robot policies are built and trained. Beyond just leveraging the action-conditioning interface we seek to understand and explain it. There are many promising approachs to understanding VLA computation via mechanistic interpretability grant2026features, bhardwaj2026decoding, molinari2025emergent, khan2025controlling, goyal2026hitchhiker, yang2026interpretable . In particular, activation patching vig2020causal, geiger2021causal, zhang2023bestpractices, heimersheim2024patching approaches aim to measure the causal role of an internal representation by replacing the target representation from one rollout with a donor from another rollout, while measuring the resulting change in behavior. In language models, such interventions have localized the computations behind factual recall and uncovered computations underlying numerous tasks meng2022rome,wang2022ioi,geiger2024causalabstractiontheoreticalfoundation,mueller-etal-2026-quest , helping elucidate the causal relationships between internal model representations and behavior. Recent work has begun to apply such tools to VLAs, identifying internal directions that steer movement, recovering sparse features tied to semantic concepts, and manipulating observable features to control behavior haon2025steering,swann2026sae,buurmeijer2026observing . Closest to our work, grant2026features performed activation-injection experiments and showed that patching representations into a VLA can redirect movement toward the spatial location of a donor task. shi2026vlatrace used attention knockout geva2023dissecting , which blocks attention from selected token positions (such as all image or all language tokens) at chosen layers and measures how the output changes, to characterize which modalities and layers action generation depends on. Together, these results establish that individual VLA representations can be causally manipulated. However, they do not address how task-relevant information is composed across the depth of the backbone and how it reaches the action expert. We answer these questions with counterfactual comparisons that test visual, semantic, and geometric hypotheses at the interface and within the backbone. We trace how the representations read by the expert reveals a progression across depth, from transferable object selection to spatially grounded action information. The two kinds of information also reside on different tokens: semantic content is carried by the noun token of the instruction, while geometric content is spread across the other prompt tokens and, in , the image tokens. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt, parsep=0pt, topsep=3pt] Discovery of a narrow action-conditioning interface. Across , MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot, we identify a narrow middle-to-late region through which the backbone conditions action generation. We show that this interface mediates geometric information about the target object. Mechanistically informed architectural improvements. We use the identified interface to design substantially sparser VLM--action-expert connections, preserving observed closed-loop performance while reducing the estimated combined operation count by up to . We validate the simplified architecture through direct training and adaptation in simulation, and demonstrate real-robot deployment with . A causal account of the information supplied to the interface. We build a counterfactual dataset with over 156 counterfactual pairs across sets of household objects. We run over 775,000 activation patching interventions across , MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot specifically designed to differentiate representations within the backbone. Visual information influences behavior through early image tokens, semantic information through the early target noun, and geometric information through later text and readout positions. Discovering the Action-Conditioning Interface sec:methods Our goal is to study how task-relevant information within the vision-language backbone is passed to the action expert. We then use the identified causal interface to create policies that improve efficiency without costing performance. Models and Notation. Their attention masks also differ: in MolmoBot and MolmoAct2, image positions cannot attend to subsequent instruction tokens, whereas uses bidirectional attention within the prefix. title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
summary: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior. Introduction sec:intro A vision-language-action (VLA) model maps visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to actions in the physical world intelligence2025pi05, lee2026molmoact, fang2026molmoact2, black2024pi0, brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla, deshpande2026molmob0t . Although today's VLAs rarely perform consequential real-world tasks, fully learned robotics models may soon see widespread deployment. Yet little is known about the computations underlying their actions. Understanding these internal representations will be essential for safe deployment. One way to understand the internal representation of a learned model is through the perspective of features, which are recurring internal variables that encode concepts, states, relationships and ultimately underlie the process by which the model converts input to output. A promising line of work, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs), leverages the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) park2023linear,huben2024sparse,gao2025scaling, elhage2022toy and assume that activations are composed of a sparse set of vectors. These methods have been well studied in language and vision modalities huben2024sparse,templeton2024scaling,gao2025scaling . Examining models in the basis of the features that they express is useful for a plethora of problems, such as to study generalization gallifant2025sparse,olson2025probing , steer model behavior templeton2024scaling, prasad2026features, turner2023steering, rimsky2024steering , attribute behaviors to training data kowal2026concept, bergen2026anatomy, koh2017understanding , and identify safety-relevant computation templeton2024scaling,marks2025auditing . However, a featurizer is ultimately a hypothesis about the data-generating process of the activations fel2026bsf . The LRH is particularly questionable for visual domains involving perception, since continuous factors such as viewpoint, illumination, position, and motion naturally generate low-dimensional manifolds that are reflected in learned representations cohen2020separability,kvinge2024internal,fel2026bsf, engels2025not,michaud2025understanding . Despite this, the majority of work in VLA interpretability assumes the LRH, with varying degrees of success. Early studies showed that specific MLP directions can offer limited control of variables like speed and height haon2025mechanistic . Complementary studies use linear probes and activation interventions to characterize the contributions of visual, language, and action pathways and identify representations of environmental dynamics and task progress molinari2025emergent,grant2026not,bhardwaj2026decoding, buurmeijer2026observing . More recently, SAEs have been applied to recover semantic concepts, motion primitives, task structure, and episode-specific memorization, demonstrating that interventions on individual features can alter policy behavior swann2026sparse,khan2025controlling,jin2026event, grant2026not .Prior work has improved our understanding of VLA policies, but precise behavioral steering remains challenging, with interventions often producing inconsistent, off-target, or weak effects. Much of this work relies on pooled visual activations or small activation corpora, leaving open whether training SAEs on individual token activations at greater scale improves feature discovery and steering. In this work, we apply recent methods for multi-dimensional feature discovery---block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) fel2026bsf ---to frontier open-source VLA models, training BSFs and baseline SAEs on the largest corpora of unpooled VLA token activations to date. BSFs represent features as sparse low-dimensional blocks yuan2006model,eldar2009block,jenatton2010structured,bach2012structured rather than single directions, making them a natural fit for robotic representations. Across models and layers, we recover a broad vocabulary of task-relevant features spanning visual perception, language, proprioceptive state, task variables and episode progress. BSFs outperform matched SAEs on recovering and intervening on task-relevant structure, suggesting that the additional geometry is useful rather than simply excess representational capacity. We then causally validate them through fine-grained steering experiments across multiple layers, inducing targeted changes at several stages of the policy: what is perceived in the observation, which object is selected, where that object is localized. Finally, we perform feature-based attribution to connect interpretable behaviors directly to the episodes in the fine-tuning dataset that shaped them. Related robot data-curation methods select demonstrations with datamodels, influence estimates, or mutual information dass2026datamil,agia2025cupid,hejna2025robot . Using a `failure-recovery' feature as as case-study, we isolate fewer than 1.4 of fine-tuning tokens in DROID whose influence is disproportionately associated with this behavior. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt, parsep=0pt, topsep=3pt] Comparing block-sparse and linear featurizers for VLAs. We systematically compare BSFs and SAEs in VLAs. BSFs recover features spanning perception, language, proprioception, task state and episode progress, better capturing computational geometry qualitatively and quantitatively. We also strengthen VLA SAE baselines with substantially larger, unpooled activation corpora to better evaluate multidimensional features. Causal validation through fine-grained steering. Across multiple layers, and computational regimes, we causally validate recovered features by steering perception, semantics, target-object selection, geometric localization, and downstream robot behavior. Feature-based dataset attribution and shaping. We trace behaviors captured by BSF features to the data that caused them. For failure recovery, masking of fine-tuning tokens qualitatively transforms robot behavior, demonstrating precise control over robot datasets and learned policies. From Sparse Directions to Sparse Subspaces sec:preliminaries r 0.46 fig:bsf-helix The goal of a featurizer is to factorize model activations into a set of interpretable concepts~ huben2024sparse, bricken2023monosemanticity, gao2025scaling, bussmann2024batchtopk, rajamanoharan2024jumping, fel2025archetypal, hindupur2026projecting, bussmann2025learning . Moreover, each featurizer also implicitly encodes a hypothesis about how activations are generated~ hindupur2026projecting . Choosing a featurizer for a VLA therefore requires matching this geometry to the variables the policy represents and computes. In this section, we first describe the feature unit assumed by sparse autoencoders, generalize it to block-sparse subspaces, explain their selection, and define the reconstruction metric shared by both featurizers. title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Code, data and policy checkpoints: https://github.com/DmytroBabarytskyi/drone-training
summary: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.

Introduction sec:intro A fixed site is approached by an airborne object on a ballistic or near-ballistic course. A sensor tracks the object and predicts where it will cross a defensive plane standing off from the site, with an error that shrinks as the track lengthens. A mesh of small interceptors, each able to engage whatever comes within a radius of it, must spread itself across that predicted crossing point and be on station before the object arrives. Three questions decide whether the concept is viable at all, and none of them is about control: how many interceptors the prediction's uncertainty demands, how early the mesh must commit to a position, and whether any commit time satisfies both the sharpness of the prediction and the distance the vehicles must fly. All three can be answered from geometry, before a controller exists. We strip the application to that geometry. Consider a team of agents constrained to a plane, each able to cover a disc of radius centred on itself. A point of interest will arrive somewhere in that plane at a known future time; the agents hold a noisy prediction of where. The team must distribute itself so that the arriving point falls inside some agent's disc. This is a coverage problem in the sense of Cort\'es et al.~ cortes2004 , specialised in two ways that turn out to matter a great deal. The density is a prediction with a quantified and time-varying error rather than a static importance map. And success is binary and instantaneous --- a point either lands within of some agent or it does not --- rather than an integrated sensing cost. Tasks of this shape invite a multi-agent reinforcement-learning treatment, and the recipe is easy to follow: define an environment, shape a reward, train a policy, report a success rate. The difficulty is that a bare success rate on a hand-designed task carries almost no information. Whether is a failure or a near-optimal result depends on what the configuration permits, and that quantity is rarely computed. Henderson et al.~ henderson2018 , Colas et al.~ colas2018 and Agarwal et al.~ agarwal2021 have each documented how fragile deep reinforcement-learning comparisons are to precisely this kind of missing context --- unreported baselines, too few seeds, and point estimates quoted without dispersion. This paper supplies the missing context for the coverage task above, in closed form, and then validates the assumptions the closed form rests on. We contribute: the uncertainty of the predicted arrival point, propagated from per-fix sensor noise through a least-squares track fit, with a delta-method term that a common heuristic omits at a cost of up to (Section~ sec:prediction ); the coverage probability attainable by agents at given and , in the plane and in a volume, including a ceiling no mesh can exceed at any size (Section~ sec:coverage ); an empirical check that hexagonal packing is the right arrangement, and a quantification of how far the standard coverage-control answer falls short of it on this objective (Section~ sec:strategies ); a robustness study of the Gaussian assumption, separating departures that make the law conservative from the one that breaks it (Section~ sec:robustness ); the admissible window of commit times for a team that must physically reposition, which can be empty (Section~ sec:commit ). Section~ sec:learning reports what happened when a learned placement policy was trained on this task, across three trainer seeds, and argues that the outcome is better explained by these bounds than by any property of the learner. Section~ sec:limits states what the analysis omits. Each individual result applies standard material --- ordinary least squares, the delta method, densest packing of equal spheres. The claim is that computing them first, and reporting them alongside learned results, changes what those results mean, and that this is not current practice. Related Work sec:related Coverage control The canonical formulation distributes agents over a density to minimise an integrated sensing cost, and is solved by Lloyd-type descent to a centroidal Voronoi configuration~ cortes2004,du1999 . The framework has been extended to agents that learn the density online~ schwager2009 and developed into a general theory of distributed robotic networks~ bullo2009 . More recently, graph neural networks have been used to let agents exploit multi-hop information and beat the purely local classical controller~ gosrich2022 . The objective in all of this work is continuous: a weighted integral of the distance from each point to its nearest agent. Our objective is the probability that a single draw lands within a fixed radius of some agent. The two are not equivalent, and Section~ sec:strategies measures the gap: at small budgets, the centroidal Voronoi configuration attains barely half the coverage of a packed one, because minimising mean squared distance rewards spreading into the tails while binary containment does not. Packing bounds That the densest packing of equal circles in the plane has density is classical, due to Thue and developed by Fejes T\'oth~ fejestoth1953,conway1999 ; the volumetric analogue is the Kepler conjecture, proved by Hales~ hales2005 and later verified formally by machine~ hales2017 . We use these as the ceiling on what any non-overlapping arrangement of covering discs can achieve --- a qualification that matters, and which Section~ sec:regimes makes explicit by showing what happens when the non-overlap constraint is dropped. To our knowledge this ceiling is not usually stated in the multi-agent coverage literature, where it is natural to write down an area ratio that tacitly assumes perfect tiling and therefore permits coverage probabilities that are unattainable at any team size. Track prediction and manoeuvre models Propagating measurement noise through a least-squares trajectory fit is standard estimation practice~ barshalom2001 , as is the recursive alternative~ kalman1960 . We use the batch closed form rather than a filter because the quantity wanted is not a running state estimate but the error covariance of an extrapolation to a fixed plane, and because a closed form keeps the resulting sizing law analytic end to end. The delta method used for the uncertain arrival time is likewise textbook~ oehlert1992 . The straight-line assumption is the weak point, and the tracking literature has long known it. Singer~ singer1970 models target acceleration as a correlated random process precisely because constant-velocity fits degrade badly under manoeuvre, and Li and Jilkov~ li2003 survey several decades of successors. Section~ sec:commit uses a deliberately crude version of this idea --- an independent per-axis acceleration with fixed standard deviation --- and finds that it dominates the sensor term by two orders of magnitude at realistic lead times. A Singer-type correlated model would refine the constant; it would not change which term binds. Assignment Allocating agents to positions at minimum total travel is a linear assignment problem, solved exactly by the Hungarian method~ kuhn1955 in . Distributed alternatives exist where centralised computation is unavailable~ bertsekas1988,zavlanos2008,choi2009 . This matters below because assignment is one of two classical sub-problems that an end-to-end policy is implicitly asked to rediscover, and the only one with an exact polynomial solution. Interception and pursuit Coverage of a predicted arrival point is adjacent to pursuit-evasion, surveyed for mobile robotics by Chung et al.~ chung2011 . The distinction is that the team here does not pursue: it positions itself ahead of the arrival and lets the geometry do the rest, which converts a speed problem into a placement problem. That is also why packing, rather than pursuit strategy, is the governing mathematics. Multi-agent reinforcement learning and its evaluation PPO~ schulman2017 remains a common default for continuous multi-agent control, and is a strong baseline in cooperative settings when implemented carefully~ yu2022 ; we use the Stable-Baselines3 implementation~ raffin2021 . Permutation-equivariant architectures~ battaglia2018,liu2020,vanderpol2022 are the standard remedy for policies whose action space treats interchangeable agents as unrelated output dimensions. Our negative result in Section~ sec:learning concerns an unstructured centralised baseline, and we are explicit that it does not settle the structured case. Reward-specification pathologies are well understood in principle~ ng1999,skalse2022,sutton2018 ; what we add is a concrete instance in which two of them produced the same observable symptom as a genuine learning failure, and were diagnosed only after the fact. On evaluation, we follow the recommendations of henderson2018,colas2018,agarwal2021 in reporting multiple seeds with interval estimates rather than point estimates, using the percentile bootstrap~ efron1993 . title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 41 pages, 10 pages of main text, 8 main text figures
summary: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Introduction Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric. Robotic systems operate in three-dimensional space through articulated kinematic structures, while the objects they manipulate and the tasks they perform have their own geometric organization, including symmetries, constraints, and phases of interaction. Any general manipulation policy must contend with this structure, and vision-language-action (VLA) models have become the dominant paradigm for building such policies brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla, team2024octo, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, lee2025molmoact, fang2026molmoact2, deshpande2026molmob0t . VLAs inherit visual and semantic priors from backbones pretrained on internet-scale data, including vision encoders radford2021learning, oquab2023dinov2, zhai2023sigmoid , language models touvron2023llama, team2024gemma , and full vision-language models driess2023palm, beyer2024paligemma, deitke2025molmo, wang2024qwen2 . This data has grown by orders of magnitude in volume and diversity o2024open, walke2023bridgedata, bu2025agibot, deshpande2026molmob0t, bjorck2025gr00t , with generalization improving along power-law-like trends lin2025data . The resulting systems are increasingly capable, general, and even deployed in the real world intelligence2025pi_, intelligence2025pi, team2025gemini, figure2026helix02, gemini2026robotics2, figure2025helix, figure2025bmw . How such competence is reflected in the representations of these VLAs is the subject of a nascent literature~ qi2025control, qi2026action, swann2026sparse, buurmeijer2026observing, haon2025mechanistic, bhardwaj2026decoding, lu2025probing, molinari2025emergent, khan2025controlling, grant2026not, goyal2026hitchhiker, yang2026interpretable, shi2026vla . In particular, one line of work uses probes, testing whether a quantity of interest can be read out from the model's activations joseph2026interpreting, buurmeijer2026observing, bhardwaj2026decoding, lu2025probing, molinari2025emergent, grant2026not, yang2026interpretable . A second trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs)~ cunningham2023sparse, bussmann2024batchtopk, rajamanoharan2024jumping, fel2025archetypal, costa2025flat, hindupur2025projecting, gao2025scaling, bricken2023monosemanticity, lubana2026priors, bhalla2026temporal, templeton2024scaling, rajamanoharan2024improving, lieberum2024gemma, thasarathan2025universal, makhzani2013k to discover concepts without supervision swann2026sparse, khan2025controlling, grant2026not , and the discovered features even provide control over the policy via steering~ joseph2025steering . Both lines of work share a limitation. A probe can ensure that a variable is decodable, yet says nothing about the structure through which the model ``realizes'' it, and an SAE inherits the linear representation hypothesis (LRH)~ park2023linear, costa2025flat , which casts each concept as a single direction in activation space and therefore fixes that structure in advance. Interpretability for language and vision models, conscious of this limitation, has moved beyond the single direction to multi-dimensional features and curved geometry~ modell2025origins,feucht2026arithmetic,wurgaft2026manifold,bhalla2026sparse, fel2026into, fel2026structuring, engels2025not, lubana2026priors, karkada2026symmetry, dooms2025finding, kantamneni2025language, gurnee2026models, yocum2025neural, park2025iclr, sarfati2026shape, costa2025flat, pearce2025tree, diego2024polar, chung2018classification, cohen2020separability, hosseini2026context, dhimoila2026cross, fel2025archetypal, gorton2024missing, sun2025dense, tvetkova2025convex, park2025geometry, park2026information , a line of work now gathered under the name of Neural Geometry geiger2026world . Do VLAs realize their variables through similarly rich geometry? Two facts suggest they might. First, vision models, including the backbones VLAs inherit, already carry colors, shadows, and position as multi-dimensional features rather than single directions~ fel2026into, fel2026structuring, pach2026latent, uselis2026compositional . Second, representations tend to inherit the symmetries of their training data, so that cyclic concepts, for example, come to be arranged on circles~ karkada2026symmetry . The variables a manipulation policy must track, such as poses, distances, contacts, and task phase, are geometric objects with symmetries of their own before the network ever represents them. We take up this question and make the following contributions: [nosep,leftmargin=*] Realized geometry as a lens for VLA interpretability. We formalize the distinction between concept realization---the capacity to extract information about a concept under a given readout---and its realized geometry---the structure activations trace as the concept varies. Linear readability establishes only that a concept is present, while its realized geometry determines how its values are structured and whether they can be manipulated. A taxonomy of realized geometry in MolmoBot. Combining controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we chart the realized geometry of seven control concepts: gripper state, end-effector position, distance to the target, target object position, contact, task phase, and wrist orientation. We find this geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts: joint limits leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, while the numerical precision of the embedding splits distance into orthogonal coarse (meter-scale) and fine (centimeter-scale) rulers. Real-world transfer. We reproduce these geometries in intelligence2025pi_ and MolmoAct2 fang2026molmoact2 on the real-world DROID dataset khazatsky2024droid , indicating they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. In particular, our aim here is to distinguish two questions that are frequently conflated in the literature: whether a concept can be recovered from a policy's activations -- which we term realized -- and what geometric shape that recovered concept takes within activation space -- which we term realized geometry. title: EgoJEPA: Beyond Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Videos
summary: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstra- tions, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains chal- lenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand- crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recal- ibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from ego- centric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human- action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decou- ples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evalu- ation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
full_text: Experiments sec:exp Experimental Setup Pre-training Data. We use a commercially acquired egocentric human dataset for stages~1 and~2. The dataset contains 1,111,943 episodes from 62,518 recording sessions, amounting to approximately 20,106.6 hours and 2.17 billion video frames. It covers 64,686 task instructions and 608 scene labels across diverse household and industrial activities. Each episode consists of a monocular RGB video recorded at approximately 30Hz, together with camera calibration and motion annotations comprising wrist poses and 21 three-dimensional keypoints for each hand. Robot Post-training Tasks. We evaluate EgoJEPA on five real-world manipulation tasks spanning three robot embodiments including a Sharpa dexterous hand sharpa_wave , a Wuji dexterous hand wuji_hand , and a Xense Tac UMI gripper xense_xtac_umi . Each task is associated with a task-specific robot demonstration dataset for Stage~3 post-training: 1) Toy grasping uses the Sharpa hand to grasp a plush toy; 2) Cup stacking uses the Wuji hand to arrange cups into a target stack, requiring sequential manipulation and precise placement; 3) Zipper pulling uses the Wuji hand to pinch and slide a zipper pull; 4) Bottle cap unscrewing uses the Wuji hand to uncap a bottle through coordinated grasping; 5) Cardboard box folding uses the Xense Tac UMI gripper to fold a paper box into a target configuration, requiring multi-step manipulation. See Appendix~ app:datasets for detailed specifications on both human pre-training and robot post-training datasets. Details. In Stage~1, the context and target visual encoders are initialized from the pretrained Wan2.2 VAE encoder~ wan2025 , and the predictor is a 24-layer Transformer with frame-causal attention. In Stage~2, the video Transformer is initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B~ wan2025 , while the Stage~1 action embeddings are average-pooled along the feature dimension to obtain 128-dimensional latent action targets for stable training. In Stage~3, the input and output action adapters each comprise a two-layer MLP with a ReLU activation between the layers. Full training configurations are provided in Table~ tab:training_config . Protocol. We evaluate all policies under both in-domain and out-of-domain settings across five tasks and three robot embodiments. In-domain evaluation uses the same object instances and spatial layouts as Stage~3 training. Out-of-domain evaluation considers two forms of distribution shift: 1) object shifts, using unseen object instances with different shapes, sizes, or materials while preserving task requirements; 2) spatial shifts, placing objects at positions and orientations outside the Stage~3 training distribution but within the robot's reachable workspace. All policies are evaluated without additional fine-tuning under matched test configurations. We conduct 20 trials per task for each setting and define success as full task completion. Compared Methods. We evaluate against five competitive methods and architectural variants: 1) LAPA ye2025latent , an action-free method that learns discrete latent actions directly from inter-frame visual changes for policy pre-training; 2) DexWild tao2025dexwild , an egocentric human-video method that co-trains dexterous manipulation policies on in-the-wild videos and robot demonstrations; 3) Retargeting-based pipeline, which shares our architecture but replaces the learned latent actions with embodiment-specific robot targets derived via geometric retargeting, followed by fine-tuning on robot data; 4) EgoJEPA (Robot-only), an ablation that omits Stage~1--2 human-video pre-training and is trained strictly on robot demonstrations; and 5) EgoJEPA (VQ-VAE), a variant that replaces Stage~1 JEPA pre-training with a VQ-VAE reconstruction objective van2017neural over hand-motion annotations, while maintaining identical Stage~2--3 protocols. Refer to Appendix~ app:implementation for more implementation details. Real-World Performance We present in-domain and out-of-domain manipulation results in Figure~ fig:mainRes , highlighting three key findings: 1) State-of-the-art performance. EgoJEPA attains the highest success rate on all five tasks, with average success rates of 94 and 74 under in- and out-of-domain settings, respectively, surpassing the retargeting pipeline by 14 and 9 absolute margins. 2) Generalization gap. All methods exhibit lower average success rates under out-of-domain evaluation, highlighting the challenges posed by unseen object instances and spatial layouts. Nevertheless, EgoJEPA achieves the highest out-of-domain success rate of 74 , compared with 65 for retargeting and 40 for DexWild. 3) Task-level variation. Bottle cap unscrewing and cardboard box folding yield EgoJEPA's lowest out-of-domain success rates. The former requires coordinated bimanual control to stabilize and rotate the bottle, while the latter involves multi-step operations with strict geometric alignments. These constraints increase sensitivity to contact noise and error accumulation, making reliable completion challenging. Ablation Studies We conduct ablation studies to evaluate EgoJEPA's architectural design and data efficiency. All policy evaluations follow the out-of-domain setting. of Human Pre-training. To assess the contribution of human pre-training to downstream manipulation, we compare EgoJEPA with a robot-only variant, , EgoJEPA (Robot-only) in Figure~ fig:mainRes , which retains the same architecture but omits human-data training in Stages~1--2 and is trained directly on robot demonstrations. As shown, human pre-training increases the average out-of-domain success rate from 40 to 74 , with improvements across all five tasks. The largest gain occurs on bottle cap unscrewing, with success increasing from 30 to 70 . This task requires coordinated bimanual control to stabilize the bottle while rotating the cap, suggesting the value of human manipulation priors for learning coordinated actions. We further examine Stage~3 training dynamics on bottle cap unscrewing by comparing action loss over training steps between EgoJEPA and its robot-only variant. As shown in Figure~ fig:training_data_efficiency (left), EgoJEPA converges faster and achieves substantially lower training loss, suggesting that priors learned from egocentric human videos facilitate embodiment-specific adaptation under limited robot supervision. To assess the benefit of JEPA-based predictive learning, we compare EgoJEPA with EgoJEPA (VQ-VAE), which replaces Stage~1 predictive learning with VQ-VAE-based action reconstruction~ van2017neural , using the same data and downstream training protocol. As shown in Figure~ fig:mainRes , EgoJEPA increases the average out-of-domain success rate from 63 to 74 , with gains across all five tasks. These results suggest that learning the visual consequences of human motion yields more effective representations for downstream control than reconstructing motion alone. Refer to Appendix app:implementation for more details. Data Efficiency. We evaluate data efficiency on bottle cap unscrewing using 10 , 25 , 50 , and 100 of the robot demonstration dataset during adaptation. As shown in Figure~ fig:training_data_efficiency (right), EgoJEPA consistently outperforms both robot-only training ( , EgoJEPA (Robot-only)) and the retargeting baseline across all data budgets. Notably, with only 10 of the demonstrations, EgoJEPA achieves a 35 success rate, surpassing the 30 attained by the robot-only model trained on the full dataset (100 ). Similarly, using just 50 of the demonstrations, EgoJEPA reaches a 65 success rate, outperforming retargeting using all demonstrations (60 ). These results demonstrate that pre-trained effect-aware representations enable substantially more data-efficient policy adaptation, significantly reducing reliance on costly robot teleoperation data. to Human Annotation Errors. Hand-motion annotations in human videos are susceptible to localization errors, temporal misalignment, and tracking failures, which can propagate through retargeting into robot action supervision. To evaluate robustness against noisy human pre-training data, we independently introduce three types of perturbation to hand annotations during Stages~1--2: 1) Position noise: additive Gaussian noise with per-axis standard deviation ~mm; 2) Temporal jitter: random frame shifts relative to original video frames, sampled uniformly from with maximum temporal offset frames; and 3) Annotation dropout: masking contiguous annotation segments covering a fraction of total frames, with missing keypoints linearly interpolated. All variants are evaluated on bottle cap unscrewing, keeping Stage~3 robot demonstration data and training settings identical across experiments. See Appendix~ app:robustness for further implementation details. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:robustness , EgoJEPA demonstrates significantly higher resilience to all three annotation error types compared with the retargeting pipeline. Under the maximum position noise ( ~mm), EgoJEPA experiences a modest 10 success-rate drop (70 to 60 ), whereas retargeting suffers a drastic 30 decline (60 to 30 ). Among the evaluated perturbations, temporal jitter induces the most severe performance decay for both models, while annotation dropout exhibits the mildest impact. Specifically, at the highest perturbation levels, EgoJEPA's success rate degrades to 50 under temporal jitter ( ) but maintains 65 under annotation dropout ( ). -Embodiment Efficiency. To further evaluate the computational efficiency, we record the wall-clock adaptation costs across five tasks and three distinct robot embodiments. Wall-clock time is reported rather than GPU hours because the human-robot calibration step in the retargeting baseline is executed entirely on CPUs, making real-time wall-clock duration a more consistent and fair measure of end-to-end deployment cost. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:efficiencyLayout , EgoJEPA seamlessly reuses pre-trained human action representations (Stages~1--2) across all downstream embodiments. In contrast, the retargeting pipeline requires re-running expensive calibration and latent world modeling whenever a new robot embodiment is introduced. For instance, when adapting to the Xense Tac UMI gripper for cardboard box folding, EgoJEPA requires only 37.5 hours of Stage~3 tuning, compared with 193.4 hours for retargeting (including 46.7 hours of CPU-based calibration and 109.2 hours of GPU-based world modeling). Across all five tasks, EgoJEPA reduces cumulative wall-clock training time from 743.2 hours to 392.7 hours, achieving a 47.2 overall cost reduction. These results highlight EgoJEPA's substantial time and compute savings when transferring shared, embodiment-agnostic action priors to new robotic platforms.

title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
summary: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
full_text: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly. \ Website \ Code \ Video Introduction Robots operating in unstructured environments must act safely despite uncertainty in their dynamics and surroundings. Robust control is one approach to achieve this, providing worst-case guarantees by treating uncertainty as persistently adversarial, propagating reachable tubes over admissible uncertainty, and tightening constraints accordingly. While this is appropriate for irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, it can be overly conservative for epistemic uncertainty arising from unknown but learnable physical parameters such as mass, friction, wind, or motor damage. Because this structured uncertainty can be reduced through interaction, robust adaptive control can become less conservative as parameter estimates improve online. As data is collected and parameter uncertainty shrinks, controllers can safely exploit the reduced uncertainty to improve performance. Moreover, because the rate of learning depends on how informative the chosen trajectory is, control actions can directly influence future parameter uncertainty, creating a tradeoff between performance, robustness, and information gathering. However, designing robust adaptive controllers for robotics remains an open problem, with two central challenges. First, synthesizing adaptive controllers while jointly reasoning about estimation error, aleatoric uncertainty, and parametric uncertainty is computationally expensive for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems, yet practical robotic systems require real-time learning, verification, and controller adaptation. Second, many existing methods update parameter estimates online but plan using the current parameter uncertainty set, incorporating newly learned information only reactively after measurements are collected. As a result, they cannot exploit guaranteed future uncertainty reduction during planning and may produce unnecessarily large reachable tubes even along informative trajectories. For example, a drone traversing an uncertain but learnable wind field should be able to plan knowing that it can measure, estimate, and compensate for the wind during execution. Ignoring this future learning can degrade performance or prevent task completion, while also leading to myopic planning that fails to seek informative trajectories that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Addressing these challenges requires jointly modeling the state and parameter-estimate dynamics while efficiently forecasting the worst-case learning guaranteed under all admissible uncertainties. -1In this work, we close these gaps with A-SLS, a scalable robust adaptive policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for future learning during planning. Building on system-level synthesis (SLS) anderson2019system , we augment the physical state with the online parameter estimate so that estimator evolution becomes part of the closed-loop dynamics. We propagate bounded parameter uncertainty and parameter-estimate shifts over the planning horizon, while adaptive SLS responses preserve correlations among process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tighter reachable tubes. Crucially, this enables assured future learning: for each candidate trajectory, we forecast the parameter uncertainty guaranteed to remain after future observations, allowing the optimizer to exploit worst-case future tube contraction without assuming favorable measurements. Because informativeness depends on the trajectory, the same formulation can also favor motions that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Finally, the structured SLS policy class admits efficient parallel reachability and robust constraint tightening, enabling GPU-parallel optimization for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Our contributions are: We formulate learning-aware robust adaptive control as an SLS problem that augments the state with the online parameter estimate, returning policies that adapt to online data while remaining robust to residual uncertainty. We derive reachable sets that preserve correlations between disturbances, parameter error, and estimate shifts, enabling tightened robust tubes that account for and guarantee future learning. These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance. We develop a GPU-parallel solver that enables real-time long-horizon control on high-DoF nonlinear systems. We evaluate safety, tube tightness, parameter learning, active information gathering, and scalability on high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems and hardware. Related Work Classic robust adaptive control~ ioannou1984robust,ioannou1996robust,polycarpou1996robust,astrom1995adaptive,cao2008l1 establishes stability guarantees under disturbances and parametric uncertainty. Recent work extends these ideas to nonlinear and unmatched uncertainty using contraction theory~ lopez2019contraction,lopez2020universal,tsukamoto2021learning,gessow2023adaptive and -LPV control~ zhao2024lpv . Other approaches develop SLS-based robust control under parametric uncertainty~ leeman2023robust and robust adaptive control for linear systems~ ho2019scalable . While these methods provide strong stability guarantees, they generally do not optimize long-horizon constrained trajectories or anticipate how planned actions reduce uncertainty; contraction-based approaches also require challenging metric synthesis and online geodesic computation. In contrast, our method uses SLS for robust adaptive nonlinear trajectory optimization, coupling closed-loop reachability with guaranteed future learning and real-time GPU-parallel synthesis. Other methods incorporate adaptation into safety-critical control. Adaptive and robust-adaptive control barrier functions (CBFs) provide forward-invariance guarantees under parametric uncertainty~ taylor2020adaptive,lopez2021racbf,xiao2022adaptive , with later applications to robotics~ minniti2022adaptive,sinaei2026safe . Many reduce online control to small QPs or impose Lyapunov conditions within MPC. However, synthesizing adaptive CBFs/CLFs can be challenging, and these methods typically provide pointwise invariance or stability guarantees without explicitly planning trajectories to improve parameter learning. Our approach instead couples closed-loop reachability and planning through shared uncertainty sources affecting physical states and future parameter estimates, yielding tighter robust tubes while making information gathering part of the trajectory optimization. Robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) combines online model learning with constrained planning. Early work used conservative constraint tightenings or separate robust safety and learned performance models~ adetola2011robust,aswani2013provably . Set-membership identification was later integrated with robust MPC for linear~ lorenzen2019robust and nonlinear systems~ kohler2021robust,sinha2022matched , with extensions addressing convergence~ lu2021performance , safety certification~ didier2021adaptive , adaptation~ pereida2021robust , contraction~ sasfi2023robust , and distributed control~ faliero2026robust . However, most methods exploit learning only after uncertainty updates are observed rather than anticipating guaranteed future estimator evolution, and can be computationally demanding online. Our adaptive SLS formulation instead jointly propagates parameter-estimation and disturbance dynamics, preserves their correlations for tighter tubes, and enables real-time GPU-parallel synthesis. Finally, dual and active-learning MPC recognize that control affects both task execution and future model quality~ mesbah2018stochastic . Persistent-excitation constraints can promote parameter convergence in RAMPC~ lu2023persistent , while~ parsi2023dual embeds predicted set-membership updates in linear MPC for informative exploration. These methods closely align with our planning-to-learn objective. However, persistent excitation is an indirect proxy for task-relevant uncertainty reduction, while exact future set-membership reasoning can be expensive and difficult to scale. Our method instead optimizes worst-case parameter-estimation dynamics within a scalable SLS framework, exploiting assured future tube contraction while retaining robust nonlinear constraints and GPU-parallel computation for long-horizon, high-dimensional systems. title: SOMA: Stack-of-Objects Manipulation using a Quadruped Robot
summary: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.

Introduction Recent work on quadrupedal locomotion has enabled significant maneuverability across diverse and complex terrains doi:10.1126/scirobotics.aau5872, kumar2021rma , and has also enabled gymnastic-style maneuvers such as a running backflip cafe_mpc . However, these platforms still exhibit limitations when executing tasks that require close physical interaction with the environment. Truly autonomous robotic systems must physically interact with their environment and thus act as mobile manipulators 7487545 . Recently, the robotics community has increased efforts in this direction, with promising work combining locomotion and manipulation for quadruped robots, commonly referred to as loco-manipulation. Unlike bipeds, quadrupedal platforms inherently lack dedicated end-effectors for physical interaction. Nevertheless, in zhu2025versatilelocomanipulationflexibleinterlimb,cheng2023legmanip,lin2024locoman,10611307 , the authors used pedipulation, i.e., manipulation using the legs of a quadruped as an on-demand manipulator, to accomplish tasks such as opening spring-loaded doors, pushing lightweight objects out of the way, doing laundry, pushing switches, and even collecting rock samples in the wild. While these strategies prove effective for versatile manipulation, most prior work cheng2023legmanip, 10611307 strictly constrains the robot's mobility by prioritizing base static stability, with the notable exceptions of lin2024locoman,zhu2025versatilelocomanipulationflexibleinterlimb . To overcome this limitation, a prominent body of work has successfully integrated robotic manipulators onto quadruped bases, achieving significant progress in mobile prehensile loco-manipulation ferrolho2023rolomarobustlocomanipulationquadruped, Mittal_2022, dadiotis2025dynamic, fu2022deep, liu2024visual, 10611066, zhou2026learning, zhu2025versatilelocomanipulationflexibleinterlimb . Despite these advancements, dedicated manipulator-base systems face severe physical constraints when deployed in complex environments. The increased spatial footprint and payload capacity limits of mounted arms hinder operation in tightly confined spaces and restrict the maximum load the system can manipulate. This gap becomes particularly critical in search-and-rescue operations, where robots must navigate narrow passages and interact with heavy, unstable debris under shifting dynamic loads. Consequently, achieving heavy-duty physical manipulation within highly constrained, unpredictable, and hazardous environments remains an open challenge. Quadrupedal robots can manipulate objects without dedicated arms either by deploying individual limbs or by leveraging their entire body for pushing interactions. While limb-based manipulation enables fine control over lightweight objects, whole-body pushing provides a compelling mechanism for transporting heavy or bulky payloads. Although non-prehensile pushing was historically underexplored latombe1991robot , foundational work by Mason established the underlying mechanics and motion planning challenges of contact-driven manipulation mason_ijrr . Modern optimization-based techniques have since made this problem more tractable by formulating pushing as a multi-contact planning problem graesdal2024towards . Recently, these optimization frameworks have been extended to quadrupedal platforms to enable body-pushing behaviors rigo2022contactoptimizationnonprehensilelocomanipulation, sombolestan2023hierarchicaladaptivelocomanipulationcontrol . However, planning through contact remains inherently difficult mason_ijrr , and current optimization methods rely heavily on pre-specified environmental models and fixed robot parameters. As a result, existing controllers struggle to generalize across diverse or unpredictable environments, leaving generalizable, whole-body pushing locomanipulation an open challenge. To address these limitations, we leverage learning-based paradigms 11128271, jeon and propose SOMA, a novel framework designed for whole-body object-stack manipulation on quadrupedal platforms (see Fig. fig:soma ). Built upon a hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture make4010009, jeon , SOMA decouples control into a high-level manipulation planner that commands a low-level locomotion policy. We extend prior work by incorporating explicit control over the robot's base height, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This vertical degrees-of-freedom integration enables the quadruped to intelligently manipulate and reconfigure complex stacks of objects from arbitrary initial states to target poses. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: A learning-based framework for quadruped whole-body manipulation of a stack of objects. Our approach incorporates direct robot base height commands, enabling full 3D pushing strategies---a crucial component missing from previous methods that restrict the robot to a predefined height and, consequently, to 2D planar pushing strategies. The proposed policy successfully reasons about latent physical parameters of the stack---such as object mass, geometry, inter-object friction, and ground-surface friction---thereby enabling robust generalization across diverse problem instances. We evaluate the robustness of our method through extensive simulations. The proposed framework achieves a success rate of when reposing a single box-shaped object and when manipulating a double box stack, consistently meeting stringent accuracy thresholds of in orientation error and in position error. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our proposed method in the real world by deploying it on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot. We run an extensive suite of experiments by varying the geometry, mass, and number of objects in the stack the robot must rest on in the real world. Methods This work targets the following problem: [Stack of Objects] problem:stack A quadruped robot is tasked with pushing a stack of objects in a 3D space to steer the bottom-most object to a target destination while ensuring the remaining objects do not fall. Specifically, the robot must move object from its initial pose to a final goal pose , where represent the orientation matrices and represent the position vectors. The robot must complete the pushing and reorientation tasks within a maximum time , using any part of its body. We assume that the bottom-most object is taller than the maximum height the robot can reach, that is, the height its base can reach when the legs are fully extended. Thus, to push effectively, the robot must use its entire body and contact the bottom object at different heights. Furthermore, the interaction must remain controlled; that is, the robot must avoid aggressive maneuvers and is prohibited from rolling or excessively tilting objects. A trial is deemed successful if the robot maneuvers the bottom object to within a position error and a yaw orientation error of the target goal pose without compromising the stack. Conversely, an episode terminates as a failure if the robot falls, causes any upper object to drop, or fails to achieve the target pose within the allowable error margins. title: KODA: Kinematics--Observation Data Alignment for Humanoid Learning from Human Egocentric Demonstration
summary: Training humanoid whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies requires costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and controller-compatible whole-body state-action labels. Egocentric human demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA (Kinematics-Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific whole-body state-action supervision. KODA first generates a simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this canonical record and regenerates whole-body state-action supervision for co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets, suggesting potential for further scaling.
full_text: Introduction Humanoid robots combine locomotion and dexterous manipulation in a versatile platform for operating in environments designed for people. Realizing this potential requires policies that coordinate body posture, mobility, and bimanual manipulation across the whole body. Whole-body vision--language--action (VLA) models aim to learn such coordination from onboard observations and task instructions~ jiang2026wholebodyvla,hu2026openhlm . Training requires corresponding robot observations, whole-body states, and action supervision compatible with the deployment whole-body controller (WBC) interface. Collecting these demonstrations on the target humanoid is costly, limiting coverage across tasks, objects, and environments. Human demonstration interfaces and egocentric datasets provide RGB images, camera poses, and sparse bilateral hand-position references at scale~ chi2024universal,hoque2026egodex,punamiya2026egoverse . Their success on fixed-base arms~ chi2024universal and in dexterous manipulation~ zheng2026egoscale,liu2026egoengine motivates extending human-data supervision to whole-body VLAs. Approaches such as EgoVLA, WholeBodyVLA, and MotionWAM learn human-derived priors for humanoid policies but still depend on target-humanoid demonstrations for adaptation~ yang2025egovla,jiang2026wholebodyvla,zheng2026motionwam . Target-humanoid data collection therefore remains a bottleneck. Other work converts human demonstrations into robot-oriented supervision. EgoHumanoid uses whole-body human measurements and a shared end-effector-and-navigation action space for co-training~ shi2026egohumanoid . HALOMI trains policies on human demonstrations using head--hand command labels tied to a dedicated controller~ zhao2026halomi . These methods produce supervision tied to particular action interfaces, creating data silos that limit reuse across whole-body controllers; their outputs do not directly provide the whole-body states and compatible actions needed for other WBC interfaces. Their converted episodes also require observations corresponding to the generated robot motion. Fixed-offset reprojection~ shi2026egohumanoid shifts the human camera without following the generated robot trajectory, leaving this observation--motion correspondence unresolved. Moreover, retaining only controller-tuned commands limits reuse to that controller's command space and tracking behavior. A reusable record must support adaptation to different deployment controllers. We target a distinct data-conversion setting: augmenting an existing controller-specific humanoid whole-body dataset from egocentric RGB, camera poses, and hand references. This setting requires three capabilities: (i) generating simulator-checked whole-body trajectories from sparse human references; (ii) synthesizing onboard observations aligned with the generated robot motion; and (iii) instantiating the same converted record as compatible state--action supervision for different deployment controllers. To address these three challenges, we present KODA (Kinematics--Observation Data Alignment), a framework that converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data. The conversion proceeds in three stages, as shown in Fig.~ fig:cem-inner . First, KODA generates a whole-body trajectory from sparse human references using a fine-tuned tracker. Sampling-based command optimization improves reference tracking while maintaining trajectory feasibility in simulation. Second, KODA derives camera poses from the generated trajectory and synthesizes corresponding onboard observations. The aligned motion and observations, together with the task instruction, form a canonical record for the target humanoid. Third, KODA optimizes the selected deployment controller's commands to track the fixed canonical trajectory, producing compatible state--action supervision for co-training with matching real-robot demonstrations. Changing controllers regenerates the state--action supervision while retaining the canonical motion and robot-view observations. Our contributions are: (a) A data-conversion framework that constructs whole-body robot motion and corresponding onboard observations from egocentric human demonstrations. (b) A canonical representation and controller-specific control command generation procedure for generating compatible state--action supervision from the same converted records across deployment interfaces. (c) Real-world evidence of the training value and scaling potential of converted human demonstrations on four G1 loco-manipulation tasks. With 50 robot demonstrations per task fixed, adding 100 converted human demonstrations per task increases macro-average success by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points under SONIC and HEFT, respectively, on object conditions covered by human training clips but absent from robot demonstrations. This metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated data budgets under both interfaces. Related Work Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Humanoid data collection methods use direct teleoperation, human imitation, or whole-body tracking to obtain robot demonstrations. OmniH2O, HOMIE, HumanPlus, and TWIST2 provide interfaces for whole-body teleoperation or imitation learning~ he2024omnih2o,ben2025homie,fu2024humanplus,ze2025twist2 . OmniRetarget preserves human--object and human--environment interactions during retargeting, while SONIC tracks whole-body motion for physically grounded control~ yang2025omniretarget,luo2026sonic,xie2025kungfubot,han2026kungfubot2 . WholeBodyVLA learns loco-manipulation from vision and instructions, while OpenHLM and MotionWAM study whole-body humanoid policy and action-model training jiang2026wholebodyvla,hu2026openhlm,zheng2026motionwam,xie2026textop . These approaches establish the control and learning foundation for humanoid loco-manipulation, but their supervision is collected or represented in a target-robot interface. Egocentric Data and Cross-Embodiment Alignment Egocentric interfaces and datasets provide a scalable source of visual and motion supervision. UMI records robot-compatible gripper trajectories and images, while EgoDex and EgoVerse provide large-scale RGB data with camera and hand-motion annotations~ chi2024universal,hoque2026egodex,punamiya2026egoverse . and EgoVLA use human data for embodied pretraining, and EMMA, EgoEngine, and Ego2Robot combine human video with robot learning or robot-data synthesis~ wei2026psi0,yang2025egovla,zhu2026emma,liu2026egoengine,wang2026ego2robot . Related cross-embodiment methods address appearance and viewpoint transfer through cross-painting or robot-view augmentation~ chen2024mirage,chen2024rovi . For humanoids, EgoHumanoid uses whole-body measurements, fixed-offset view alignment, and training-time perturbations~ shi2026egohumanoid . HALOMI adopts this view alignment and reference adaptation based on the cross-entropy method (CEM) for a dedicated controller~ zhao2026halomi . KODA also uses command optimization, but derives onboard views from generated whole-body motion. Its canonical motion--observation records can be reused to augment manipulation datasets for compatible WBCs through controller-specific command generation and state recording. System Framework sec:method KODA converts egocentric human episodes into robot-view observations, canonical whole-body motion, and controller-compatible state--action data for VLA training as shown in Fig.~ fig:koda-overview . The conversion has three stages: Whole-Body Motion Generation in Sec.~ sec:kinematic_generation produces a simulator-checked trajectory from sparse human references; Robot Onboard View Generation in Sec.~ sec:robot_view_generation uses the corresponding body--camera trajectory to synthesize aligned observations, forming a controller-independent canonical record; and Control Command Generation in Sec.~ sec:vla_training tracks this motion with the selected controller to derive its state--action supervision. The canonical motion and observations are reused across interfaces, while controller-specific states and commands enable co-training with matching real-robot demonstrations. Qualitative demonstration timelines are provided in Appendix~ app:qualitative . Problem Setup sec:problem_setup Let denote the target humanoid and a deployment controller with its action interface. All sequences use the target control clock . After geometry recovery, an RGB episode is represented as , where is the egocentric RGB image, is observed or estimated depth, is the source-camera pose, contains the bilateral 3-D hand keypoints, and is the task instruction. Camera poses and hand keypoints come from source annotations or offline recovery. When source depth is unavailable, KODA estimates it from RGB using the metric-depth model of Depth Anything 3~ lin2025depthanything3 . Depth, camera poses, and hand references must share a consistent metric coordinate system. Human episodes form .
