The canonical trajectory provides a common motion reference for robot-view synthesis and controller-specific tracking. The mappings and act episode-wise on datasets: The mapping retains the canonical observations and instruction, adding state features and optimized command labels in 's interface as described in Sec.~ sec:vla_training . Converted and real-robot episodes share a format and jointly train the VLA policy with parameters to predict . Whole-Body Motion Generation sec:kinematic_generation Given the camera poses and hand references in , Whole-Body Motion Generation outputs the simulator-checked canonical whole-body motion . Contact-Aware Hand Retargeting HAWOR~ zhang2025hawor estimates world-space MANO hand poses from egocentric RGB. Following AnyTeleop~ qin2023anyteleop , KODA retargets them to obtain initial robot wrist poses and active finger-joint values using MANO palm geometry and a calibrated wrist-to-palm transform; distal mimic joints follow a fixed coupling map~ qin2023anyteleop . Contact-aware refinement then adjusts this initialization on reliable contact frames. To identify these frames, EfficientSAM3~ zeng2025efficientsam3 segments hand/forearm pixels, while nearby valid non-hand depths provide object-surface samples. Reliable contact frames are identified from multi-finger proximity, depth, and local surface consistency, then temporally filtered; without reliable contact, the initialization is retained. At contact frames, wrist and finger poses are refined to preserve hand--object geometry. Following OmniRetarget~ yang2025omniretarget , selected human landmarks and corresponding robot-hand points are paired with the same nearby object samples to form connected world-frame interaction meshes. Each vertex descriptor is its offset from the uniformly weighted mean of its neighbors. We optimize wrist poses and finger joints to minimize differences between corresponding human and robot descriptors, preserving the demonstrated hand--object geometry. During optimization, object samples remain fixed, robot points are recomputed by forward kinematics, wrist translations, local rotations, and finger corrections are bounded, and deviations from initialization are penalized. Corrections are interpolated between contact frames and held constant outside their range. title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $ρ$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $ρ$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$ρ$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($ρ=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
full_text: Appendix~ app:proofs Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, more expensive module, and differ both in how the module intervenes (latent refreshing, value-guided resampling, action-suffix reuse) and in when it is invoked. The invocation question has just begun to be mechanized by trigger mechanisms, but these come with no shared objective, no measured costs, and no evaluation standard that separates schedule quality from slow-module quality. We provide the missing account. We formalize invocation as a calibrated decision problem under a query budget, show that fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated scheduling are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI), and prove a renewal baseline that locates the economics: under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is periodic, and the gain of any adaptive trigger is governed by the cost ratio and the temporal dispersion of collapse. Published systems span an order of magnitude on ; measuring FiS-VLA on one RTX 4090 places it at the low end, one slow refresh costing \,ms, about one fast action ( \,ms) or denoising steps, which explains why its hand-tuned cadence is reasonable and bounds what any trigger can gain there. A direct test confirms the prediction: on a controlled testbed the calibrated advantage over the fixed cadence vanishes under homogeneous collapse and grows monotonically with collapse heterogeneity. A calibrated router instantiates the account: on a synthetic testbed with matched budgets it Pareto-dominates all three baseline families ( vs.\ success at a query rate), and we characterize its boundary, not only its wins: the advantage is insensitive to estimator variance but vanishes once the estimator loses validity on most steps, the requirement any trigger mechanism must meet to pay. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) systems increasingly adopt a dual-system architecture: a fast policy executes at control frequency, while a slower, more expensive module intervenes occasionally to correct or re-plan. This pattern appears in trained systems, where the slow layer is a large VLM conditioned on the fast policy's latents (Fast-in-Slow~ fis2025 ) or performs value-guided best-of- resampling (Hume~ hume2025 ), and in zero-training systems built on frozen LLMs, where a gate decides when to reuse predicted action suffixes (RoboICL~ roboicl2026 ). These systems differ in how the slow module acts. Our starting observation is that they also differ in when it acts, and that this second choice has just begun to be mechanized: OneTwoVLA learns a decision token that toggles between reasoning and acting; the concurrent TUD trigger invokes the generalist on high predictive uncertainty~ yang2026tud ; System Switch defers to a reasoning model on low confidence~ bailo2026systemswitch . What these mechanisms lack is an account of the problem they solve: no shared objective, no measured costs, no evaluation standard that separates schedule quality from slow-module quality, and no prediction for when adaptivity beats a hand-tuned fixed ratio at all. Thesis. We give that account (Figure~ fig:architecture ). We model slow-module invocation as a calibrated decision problem under a query budget; show that existing fixed schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); and locate the economics of the problem on a cost-asymmetry continuum that spans three orders of magnitude across published systems and that we measure at both ends ( on FiS-VLA hardware, from the RoboICL deployment's reported API costs). This yields four contributions. A decision-theoretic account with a cost baseline. We define VoI as the expected quality gap between the slow-corrected and fast-only actions, weighted by the probability that the fast policy collapses in state (Section~ sec:method ). Fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated scheduling are degenerate cases of VoI routing (Propositions~ prop:fis -- prop:jev ). A renewal baseline (Proposition~ prop:continuum ) then locates the regimes: under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is periodic with interval , so fixed ratios are hard to beat at low and low collapse heterogeneity, while adaptivity pays as either grows. This explains why hand-tuned cadences are reasonable on embedded-latent systems and why triggered invocation concentrates on separate-VLM systems. A calibrated router with its boundary characterized. A lightweight router estimates VoI online and queries the slow module only when the estimate exceeds the query cost. We characterize where this construction breaks, not only where it works: the advantage is insensitive to estimator variance but vanishes when the estimator loses validity on most steps, which is the requirement any trigger mechanism must meet to pay (Sections~ sec:exp-noise -- sec:exp-breakdown ). A leak-free measurement standard. We contribute staleness curves, routing frontiers, failure attribution, and calibration reliability as a four-measure battery for slow-query policies (Section~ sec:protocol ), with an explicit leak-free rule. On 929 deployment traces from the RoboICL release the rule is not decoration: the same features reach AUC post hoc but ( ) leak-free, so without it the early-warning capability of schedule statistics would be overstated by roughly . The traces also fix the precision of frontier claims themselves: skip decisions cluster by episode at design effects of -- , so a frontier estimate over decision points carries the information of about one thousand episodes (Proposition~ prop:dispersion ). Schedule compilation. The measured quantities are not only diagnostic. A renewal compiler turns a task's measured staleness value function into a per-task refresh period; on controlled task families the compiled period tracks the closed-loop oracle at a cost gap of at most , the compilation is a sample-average approximation whose optimality gap admits a statistical certificate~ mak1999 , and the underlying trade-off inherits the cost flatness of the Harris--Wilson order-quantity problem~ harris1913 , so moderate cost-estimate errors degrade the achieved schedule only at second order; and the validation budget itself has an optimal allocation, concentrated on the near-ties of the cost bowl, which roughly doubles the probability of recovering the oracle period at a fixed budget (Remark~ rem:ocba ). On the FiS backbone the compiler sends every task to the boundary its measured (nonpositive) value function dictates (Section~ sec:exp-distill ). Adaptive triggers, fixed periods, and compiled schedules become commensurable as different amounts of measurement invested in the same cost functional. Evidence. On a synthetic testbed with matched query budgets, calibrated routing dominates the Pareto frontier of the fixed-ratio, always-query, and reuse-gate baselines (Section~ sec:exp-synthetic ). On real systems, we apply the protocol to all 929 deployment traces released by RoboICL (Section~ sec:exp-roboicl ): failed episodes query the slow module less densely and run with greater staleness, and the effect is category-dependent, so no single fixed ratio can exploit it. title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
summary: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.
full_text: 10 Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. Introduction Predicting how actions affect the physical world and learning to generate actions are closely related problems~ nvidia2025cosmos . World models predict future observations from specified actions~ zhu2025uwm,quevedo2025worldgym , while world-action models (WAMs) use video generation to guide action generation~ liang2025videopolicy,ye2026dreamzero . These complementary objectives motivate studying world and action modeling within a unified framework. Video foundation models support policy learning by predicting future observations~ liang2025videopolicy,shen2025videovla,ye2026dreamzero . One line of work~ yuan2026fastwam,bi2025motus,fan2026aim uses mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architectures~ liang2025mixture , in which action tokens attend to bidirectional video representations~ yang2024cogvideox,kong2024hunyuanvideo,nvidia2025cosmos,wan2025wan . These visual representations serve as effective policy priors and support strong manipulation performance. Related studies~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,bi2025motus,nvidia2026cosmos3 jointly model video and action generation within shared architectures, further demonstrating how video generation benefits action learning. In parallel, causal WAMs~ li2026lingbotva,ye2026gigaworldpolicy,ye2026dreamzero use directional attention to couple video and action generation, aiming to capture causal dynamics in a more physically consistent way. =1em These results demonstrate the value of video prediction for action learning, yet the interaction between action-conditioned world modeling and action generation under temporal causality warrants further study. With bidirectional backbones augmented with an action-inference branch, the video branch often retains its pretrained attention~ yuan2026fastwam , reflecting the premise that existing visual representations suffice as policy priors. Causal WAMs allow video tokens to attend to actions, but these actions are noisy variables under joint denoising~ ye2026gigaworldpolicy,ye2026dreamzero . Joint generation therefore differs from forward dynamics prediction conditioned on specified clean actions. Conditioning video generation on ground-truth actions makes forward dynamics an explicit learning objective, raising our first question: Within the same framework, action generation may in turn provide a learning signal for visual prediction, motivating the converse question: Existing architectures provide a straightforward basis for unified causal training, allowing us to investigate these questions within a shared model. In a causal MoT framework, Fig.~ fig:action-conditioning illustrates two endpoints: an all-clean setting, where a world model predicts video conditioned on clean ground-truth actions, and an all-noisy setting, where noisy action tokens serve as generation targets while conditioning video prediction. The figure also shows an representative WAM formulation that prevents video tokens from attending to action tokens. Both WAM formulations are organized around action generation through denoising, limiting action-to-video information flow: the video branch receives only noisy actions or no action information at all. To connect explicit forward-dynamics learning with action generation, we consider , a unified causal model that supports both all-clean and all-noisy conditioning, together with a partial-clean setting, which uses a clean action prefix to condition both future-video prediction and denoising of the remaining noisy suffix. Each training batch mixes the three settings, enabling us to examine reciprocal benefits between forward-dynamics learning and action generation within the same causal model. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple simulated and real-world environments to examine whether world and action modeling benefit each other under unified causal training. Our results provide positive answers to both questions. First, under 's unified causal training, incorporating clean-action conditioning into world model learning substantially improves the policy's action-prediction performance, outperforming the evaluated WAMs with action-masked or noisy-action-conditioned video branches. Second, learning to generate actions also improves action-conditioned world modeling, showing that the benefits can be reciprocal in this setting. We further analyze the interaction between the two learning tasks. Related Work World Action Models World-action models bring predictive world representations into policy learning. One line of work uses generated videos as visual plans or synthetic demonstrations, recovering executable actions through inverse dynamics or goal-conditioned controllers~ du2023unipi,du2023vlp,jang2025dreamgen . Other approaches integrate visual forecasting into the policy itself, using predictive video features~ hu2024vpp,pai2025mimicvideo,liao2025genie or jointly learning future observations and actions~ wu2023gr1,liang2025videopolicy,shen2025videovla,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,fan2026aim,wang2026openwam . These formulations use temporal supervision and video pretraining to improve policy generalization and data efficiency. Recent work also separates predictive learning from the cost of future synthesis. Efficient WAMs retain video co-training while reducing or bypassing future-video generation at deployment~ yuan2026fastwam,li2026lightwam . Latent and condition-space approaches couple future-representation prediction with action generation~ su2026worldguidance,lin2026jepawam,du2026actualizer , while representation distillation transfers world-model features to policies without adding a generative process at inference~ dao2026thaw . We build on these predictive approaches by making the visual consequences of specified actions an explicit learning target during policy training. World Models World models learn transition dynamics for planning and policy optimization, either in compact latent spaces~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamer,assran2025vjepa2 or through visual forecasting~ wu2024ivideogpt,huang2025vid2world . Large-scale video pretraining provides reusable visual dynamics priors~ nvidia2025cosmos,wan2025wan , while robotic world models develop control interfaces that relate these priors to concrete robot commands. Frame-level action injection and spatially grounded kinematic conditioning support fine-grained, controllable rollouts~ zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld,wu2026oscar . Latent-action pretraining offers a complementary route to learning interaction dynamics from unlabeled videos before adapting to robot controls~ gao2025adaworld,gao2026dreamdojo . These predictors increasingly serve as learned simulators for policy evaluation and improvement, supplying imagined rollouts and synthetic experience~ quevedo2025worldgym,guo2025ctrlworld,qiu2026gesim,jiang2025world4rl . Their dynamics priors can also be transferred directly to policy learning~ huang2026a2world . These applications require predictions that follow the supplied actions, a property distinguished from visual plausibility in recent evaluations~ chen2026worldecho . Our work also treats actions as learning targets, using action-generation supervision to strengthen the representations underlying these predictions. Unified World and Action Modeling Unified models support world prediction and action generation through shared representations and flexible conditioning~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,bi2025motus,nvidia2026cosmos3 . This line spans bidirectional diffusion frameworks~ shen2025videovla,nvidia2026cosmos3 and causal designs with autoregressive or directional information flow~ li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero,ye2026gigaworldpolicy . Existing studies report both reciprocal benefits and task trade-offs. For example, WorldVLA~ cen2025worldvla interleaves discrete image and action tokens in a shared autoregressive model, coupling action generation with action-conditioned next-image prediction. Joint training improves both action generation and long-horizon visual prediction. By contrast, Cosmos~3~ nvidia2026cosmos3 reports that joint learning with video improves action prediction under bidirectional video--action diffusion, but co-training with action prediction leads to a small decline in video-generation fidelity. These findings arise from different modeling settings: WorldVLA demonstrates mutual benefits through discrete autoregressive image--action modeling, whereas Cosmos~3 studies joint video--action learning with bidirectional attention. Together, they leave open how temporal causality shapes the learning of physical dynamics and the resulting benefits for video and action prediction. We investigate this interaction within a shared causal video--action MoT framework, explicitly coupling action-conditioned forward-dynamics learning with action generation to examine their reciprocal benefits. title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
summary: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/

A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at . Introduction sec:intro A truly useful assistant in everyday life does not only respond to requests, but also anticipates when help would be valuable. This may involve handing over an object at the right moment, putting away an item after it has been used, or preparing something that will be needed in the next step. By contrast, robot assistants are still commonly evaluated as systems that execute explicit user commands~ openvla, pi05 . For robots to play the role of capable assistants in household, and home-office settings, they must move beyond waiting for instructions and learn to recognize when intervention would be helpful. This has motivated growing interest in proactive robot assistance: robots that infer when help may be useful and act in advance of explicit commands. One line of work in proactive robot assistance predicts task progress in structured sequential tasks~ pace, liu2023proactive, stouraitis2023predictive . However, these approaches are largely confined to robots that perform a single task by following a fixed protocol (e.g., chair assembly), and are ill-suited to generalist robots tasked with open-ended housekeeping. Recently emerging generalist Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) openvla, gr00t, black2024pi_0, pi05 may appear to offer an alternative, but robotics datasets remain scarce across the diverse scenarios such settings demand. As a result, end-to-end models that map perception directly to action face clear limitations even when equipped with reasoning, and proactive tasks, where intent is often underspecified, have received little attention. In response, recent work has adopted a System 1–2 design~ kahneman2011thinking that explicitly separates a high-level reasoning module from a VLA that executes atomic tasks cui2025openhelix, song2025hume, chen2025fast, han2024dual . This separation simplifies learning, since the VLM decides when and what to help with while the VLA need only carry out the prescribed action. We adopt this structure, which in turn places the burden of proactivity squarely on the high-level VLM. The central challenge, then, is accurately predicting human intention at the high level~ buyukgoz2022two , and recent approaches leverage pretrained, large-scale VLMs to do so in open-ended settings~ eventdriven, roboomni, intentionvla . Yet zero-shot prediction remains unreliable when the same observable behavior corresponds to different desired outcomes across users: one person setting out a mug wants coffee, another wants hot water for tea ( ). A fixed, pretrained predictor cannot resolve such ambiguity, because the missing information is not in the scene but in the individual user's habits. Crucially, this missing information can be learned during deployment. In housekeeping settings, an individual's behavior is highly repetitive, so even a handful of past interactions reveal stable preferences, and corrective feedback gathered once can be reused whenever a similar situation recurs. This suggests that a proactive robot should not treat each deployment as zero-shot, but should accumulate experience about its specific user over time. We therefore investigate a test-time learning approach for the high-level VLM, building a robot that personalizes quickly from few interactions, continues adapting after deployment, and carries user feedback forward into future behavior. To this end, we introduce Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a continually updated deployment-time memory that records when assistance is needed and what assistive task should be issued for a particular user. PAM structures this memory as a finite-state machine over the user's activity, where states represent activity phases, transitions represent progress between phases, and per-state assistance entries store the assistive opportunities associated with each phase. In our five-day scenario, the user repeatedly performs a daily activity; PAM is updated across these days so that the robot can provide increasingly appropriate assistance. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=1.5em] We propose a memory-based agentic framework for proactive robot assistance. By conditioning the high-level VLM on user-specific routine context, it decides both when to assist and what task to issue without explicit user requests. We propose Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a memory following a finite-state-machine structure with activity phases, transitions, and per-state assistance entries. It uses user and activity context to reduce ambiguity in assistance needs. We develop a self-evolving memory loop whose reflector revises PAM offline after each day using observed behavior and user feedback. This enables the robot to learn the user's routine, adapt to changes, and incorporate user feedback without retraining. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models sec:rw_vla Robot manipulation has advanced through visuomotor imitation-learning policies~ act, chi2023diffusion and generalist VLAs~ openvla, black2024pi_0, pi05, gr00t , with subsequent work exploring chain-of-thought reasoning~ ecot, cotvla, rth , spatial grounding~ tdvla, spatialvla , and world-model predictions~ vpp, dreamvla, starry . However, jointly optimizing action execution and high-level reasoning in a single network causes the two objectives to compete under limited robot data. In response, recent work adopts a System 1--2 design~ kahneman2011thinking that explicitly separates a slow reasoning module from a fast action executor~ han2024dual, song2025hume, chen2025fast, cui2025openhelix, gr00t . The reasoning module interprets the scene and reasons about how to solve the task, while the executor generates low-level actions for robot control conditioned on the high-level outputs. We build on this division of roles, using a VLM to predict proactive tasks and a VLA to execute the selected atomic skills. Proactive Assistance in Embodied HRI sec:rw_proactive A prominent line of work on proactive robots studies assistance in structured sequential tasks, where the human activity is already organized into known subtasks. In these settings, robots estimate task progress or subtask completion to provide help at the right moment~ liu2023proactive, stouraitis2023predictive , such as handovers in assembly~ pace or ingredient delivery in cooking~ litsouschef . This direction is especially effective when the task sequence, progress measure, and assistance opportunities are known in advance. Another line of work models object usage patterns in daily environments to anticipate future assistance needs~ stom,predicting-routine-object-usage,longproactive . These methods move beyond single structured tasks, but they typically require substantial interaction logs or curated observations for training, limiting their flexibility across diverse everyday routines and rapidly changing user behavior. With the recent progress of foundation models, proactive assistance has begun to move toward more general intent inference. Some systems rely on non-verbal cues such as visual scene changes~ eventdriven , human-object interactions~ hoi4abot, rahimi2026intentvlm , or gaze~ gazeguided, gaus2026act to infer assistive intent, while others draw on verbal cues such as indirect instructions~ intentionvla , speech~ roboomni , or dialogue~ sarch2025grounding,helper . However, intent inference from momentary cues alone remains ambiguous: the same cue can imply different assistance needs depending on the user, context, and activity history. We address this by conditioning the proactive decision on a user-specific memory accumulated across days, so that assistance is grounded not only in the current cue but also in how this user has typically acted and been assisted. Evolving Memory for Test-Time Adaptation sec:rw_memory Recent LLM-agent systems use external memory to support test-time adaptation without weight updates, allowing an agent to accumulate and reuse experience across episodes. These works span verbal self-reflection~ reflexion , reusable skill libraries~ voyager , workflow or experience extraction~ expel,awm , and long-term memory~ memorybank,genagents . However, their memories are generally designed for text-centric agents, games, or instruction-following tasks, rather than for deciding when a robot should proactively assist during an evolving human activity. PAM organizes assistive opportunities into activity phases, per-state assistance entries, and transitions, preserving the context in which each opportunity arises. The task predictor uses this context to decide when assistance is needed and what assistive task should be issued given the user's current activity and learned routine. Method sec:method Our goal is to learn and store a user's routine in memory, then use it to decide when to assist and what task to perform in real time. The system should also adapt quickly to routine changes without retraining. To this end, we design a proactive assistance system built around Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) ( ). A VLM task predictor uses observations and PAM to predict whether assistance is needed and, if so, selects a task for the VLA executor to perform. After each day, a VLM memory reflector updates PAM offline using the day's recorded video. Real-Time Task Prediction and Execution via System 1--2 Architecture sec:method_tasksetter Our task predictor serves as System~2, selecting assistive tasks without task-specific user instructions. At each 1-Hz step, it receives the latest video frames, PAM as text, and the fixed instruction, ``Proactively help the user before they ask.'' It uses the routine stored in PAM to interpret the observations and outputs either a task expressed in natural language or NO ACT. Explicit thinking mode is disabled for real-time inference. The predicted task is passed to the VLA executor, which serves as System~1 and generates low-level robot actions. For example, the predictor selects ``bring milk'' as the user pours cereal. The executor then carries out this task by picking up the milk and placing it next to the user. The simple solution is a flat list of trigger--action pairs, but this provides limited context for interpreting cues within the user's routine. title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce , where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge. Our code and data are available at . Introduction sec:introduction Completing a task specified by a language instruction does not necessarily mean following instructions on how to perform it. For example, ``put the carrot on the plate'' specifies what a robot should accomplish, whereas ``grasp the carrot by its green end'' specifies how to accomplish it. This distinction is particularly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models, which generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions~ brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, bjorck2025gr00t . Following instructions about how to act would enable VLAs to incorporate corrections, refine actions, and adjust their behavior through language, as widely practiced in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs)~ ouyang2022training, madaan2023self, shinn2023reflexion, lee2024volcano, cheng2025vision, driess2023palm . We distinguish these capabilities as What-level and How-level instruction following. What-level instructions specify the task itself, while How-level instructions specify how to execute an already determined task, such as where to grasp an object or which path to take. Existing VLA research has largely focused on the What level, evaluating or improving robustness to paraphrased or replaced task instructions~ zhou2025libero, fei2026libero, hou2026langgap, fang2026vision, kim2026libero, yang2026vision, lian2026langforce, fan2026interleave, zhan2026stable . Meanwhile, systems requiring How-level guidance typically restrict it to predefined commands~ shi2025hi, belkhale2024rt, chen2026steerable or replace language corrections with visual symbols or externally generated recovery actions~ zeng2026diagnose, lin2025failsafe . Consequently, whether VLAs can directly follow free-form How-level instructions, and what limits this ability, remains largely unexplored. We therefore ask: Do current VLAs reflect How-level instructions in their actions, and if not, what prevents them from doing so? In this work, we systematically diagnose How-level instruction following in current VLAs through two complementary settings. First, in offline correction, we collect failed episodes and rerun them with three alternatives: a simple retry with a different seed, a language correction generated from the observed failure, and an inverted correction that reverses the actionable content of the original correction. Comparing these alternatives allows us to determine whether a VLA uses the information in a correction rather than merely benefiting from another attempt. Second, in online intervention, we examine a dual-system design~ shi2025hi in which a VLM monitors robot execution and provides corrections or sub-step instructions to the VLA during the task. Together, these settings evaluate instruction following under favorable and controlled conditions in offline correction and under deployment conditions in online intervention. Across general VLAs~ black2024pi_0, chen2025internvla, community2026starvla and models designed to strengthen instruction following~ yang2026vision, lian2026langforce , both settings reveal a consistent limitation, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a) and (b). In offline correction, corrections succeed less often than simple retries and do not clearly outperform inverted corrections. In online intervention, How-level instructions generally fail to improve task success, while frequent interventions substantially degrade performance. These findings suggest that current VLAs do not reliably use How-level instructions to guide their actions, even when designed to follow task instructions more robustly. To understand this limitation, we investigate the structure of VLA training data. In standard robot datasets, each episode is paired with a single instruction shared across all timesteps~ walke2023bridgedata , and these instructions exhibit limited linguistic diversity~ wanna2026limited . Although the robot's actions change throughout an episode, the instruction typically describes only the task. Language may therefore serve primarily as a task identifier, without teaching the model how instructions should influence task execution. We hypothesize that this training structure limits How-level instruction following. An attention-level analysis provides indirect support: models assign different amounts of attention to corrections, yet their actions fail to reflect them regardless of the attention received, suggesting that the limitation is not specific to a single architectural component. We test this hypothesis by introducing enriched instructions that describe the robot's movements at different segments of an episode, while keeping the underlying demonstrations unchanged. Fig.~ fig:teaser (c) shows how these instructions differ from the original instruction shared across an episode. Across five VLA model families, enriched instructions maintain comparable task success while substantially improving responsiveness to How-level guidance. In particular, actions follow the directions specified by corrections in about 84 of evaluated episodes. The original models and controls trained on the original instructions with the same training budget reach about 53 , close to the 50 chance level. However, this improvement does not consistently translate into higher task success. One possible explanation is that task success on standard benchmarks depends largely on the scene~ lian2026langforce and on chance~ jang2026verifier , and many failures can be recovered through retries alone. Thus, task success may not reliably reflect whether a model actually follows the additional instruction. To measure How-level instruction following more directly, we introduce~ , an Instruction-Necessity benchmark built on SIMPLER~ li2024evaluating , in which the conditions required for success are given only in How-level instructions. Its tasks require following a specified path around a transparent barrier, grasping a particular part of an object, or placing an object at an instructed location. None of the evaluated models, including those trained with enriched instructions, reliably follows these instructions, suggesting that the gained responsiveness falls short under demanding conditions and does not transfer to out-of-distribution (OOD) How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge for current VLAs. Our contributions are summarized as follows. Diagnosis of How-level instruction following. We introduce offline correction and online intervention, revealing that current VLAs do not reliably follow How-level instructions even when designed for instruction following. Training data hypothesis and enriched instructions. We identify episode-level instruction supervision as a potential cause and show that enriched segment-level instructions improve action-level responsiveness without consistently improving task success. . We introduce an Instruction-Necessity benchmark that requires How-level instruction following for success, revealing remaining limitations of current VLAs. Related Work sec:related_work Following in VLAs. Recent studies have questioned whether VLAs genuinely follow language instructions or rely on visual cues and learned patterns. LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026libero , and LangGap~ hou2026langgap show that VLAs often exhibit limited behavioral changes when task instructions are modified or removed, while LIBERO-CF~ fang2026vision reveals their tendency to rely on visual priors even when different tasks share the same scene. These findings are consistent with the limited linguistic diversity of robot datasets~ wanna2026limited and observations that standard SIMPLER~ li2024evaluating tasks can often be completed without language instructions~ jang2026verifier . In contrast, LIBERO-Para~ kim2026libero reports that paraphrasing task instructions can substantially degrade performance in LIBERO-Goal~ liu2023libero , where multiple tasks share the same scene. Together, these studies suggest that VLA behavior may depend on visual priors or familiar instruction patterns rather than the meaning of language instructions. However, they primarily examine whether VLAs identify what task to perform, leaving their ability to follow instructions specifying how to perform a given task unexplored. Another line of work makes VLAs follow task instructions more robustly. InstructVLA~ yang2026vision and ChatVLA~ zhou2025chatvla preserve the multimodal understanding of the VLM backbone. LangForce~ lian2026langforce and Residual Semantic Steering~ zhan2026stable reduce the policy's reliance on visual priors so that the task follows the instruction rather than the scene, even when the instruction is paraphrased. Spatially guided training~ ye2026spatially and interleaved image-text instructions~ fan2026interleave help the policy locate the object in the instruction. These methods aim to identify the intended task and object robustly from the instruction, and whether they also enable How-level instruction following remains unknown. Therefore, our diagnosis includes InstructVLA and LangForce. and Hierarchical Control. Language has also been used to guide robots beyond the task instruction. In hierarchical control, an LLM or VLM plans the task, while the low-level policy executes only a fixed set of skills or commands learned during training, such as atomic subtasks, language motions, or structured steering commands~ ahn2022can, huang2022inner, shi2025hi, belkhale2024rt, shi2024yell, chen2026steerable . Training on such commands makes the low-level policy follow them, but it serves as an executor of predefined commands rather than as a general policy that both perform the task and interprets How-level language. Failure correction and recovery methods likewise convert How-level corrections into visual symbols~ zeng2026diagnose or replace them with recovery actions generated by a separate VLM~ lin2025failsafe . In both lines of work, free-form How-level guidance bypasses the VLA. Whether a VLA can directly follow free-form How-level instructions, and why it fails to do so, has therefore not been diagnosed. Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation policy and training data. A VLA policy maps an observation and a language instruction to an action , where may be an action chunk and is the random seed that governs the stochasticity of the policy, such as the noise of a diffusion or flow-matching action head. The policy is trained on demonstrations , where each episode pairs every timestep with the same instruction . - and How-level instruction following. We decompose an instruction into , a conceptual split rather than a computational one. The What-level component specifies the task, namely which object to manipulate and what to do with it, and the How-level component covers everything else that can help perform the task, such as the path to take, where to grasp or place an object, or context about the scene. title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $π_{0.5}$ as LTM-$π$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$π$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
full_text: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on as LTM- , our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM- achieves 58.54 success on RoboMME and 80.5 on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67 to 87.50 , while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00 , versus 87.50 without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25 to 82.50 . Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control. Our dataset, training code, and inference code have been publicly released at: . Introduction r 0.45 fig:teaser Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained visual and linguistic representations with action generation to follow diverse manipulation instructions~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Yet the current observation may omit information needed for the next action. A robot placing three objects into a bag must remember completed transfers; one tracking an occluded object must retain the effects of earlier interactions. Similar scenes can therefore require different actions depending on the preceding history, motivating explicit memory for robotic control~ dai2026robomme,chung2026rethinking . Existing memory designs retain visual observations, summarize experience in language, or update a recurrent state~ shi2025memoryvla,qu2026lamemvla,torne2026mem,cherepanov2026muvla . Dense visual histories consume substantial context, whereas sparse sampling can omit intermediate interactions. Language summaries abstract away visual detail but may miss fine-grained motion. Recurrent representations support compact updates but must continually decide what to preserve in a bounded state. These trade-offs raise a representational question: For many manipulation tasks, the relevant history is the sequence of changes induced by robot--environment interactions. Latent action models encode an observation pair into a compact code from which the later observation can be reconstructed conditioned on the earlier one~ bruce2024genie,ye2024lapa . This objective encourages the code to capture temporal changes. While latent actions have been used for policy pretraining and world-model control~ ye2024lapa,bu2025univla,gao2026dreamdojo , we study their use as an ordered episodic memory for action generation. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which encodes consecutive observations with a frozen latent action model and projects each code into one memory token. The policy receives a delayed transition prefix alongside the instruction and current observation. Each code depends only on an adjacent observation pair, allowing encoding to overlap action execution. We instantiate LTM on as LTM- , with a lightweight adapter and causal attention that permits persistent KV caching. Sparse initial-frame anchors provide visual grounding for video-conditioned tasks. The policy and adapter learn from robot demonstrations without memory-specific semantic annotations. At inference, the frozen encoder supplies transition codes directly to the policy, without an external reasoning model or intermediate language generation. We evaluate LTM- with two frozen latent encoders, CD-LAM and DreamDojo, on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem. With the original benchmark data, the DreamDojo variant reaches 58.54 average success on RoboMME, compared with 17.93 for the reported memory-free baseline, and 80.5 on LIBERO-Mem, compared with 42.5 for the strongest baseline included in our comparison. We then isolate the effects of memory content and inference lag. Replacing observation-dependent latent transitions with fixed random representations reduces RoboMME success from 57.67 to 44.50 , supporting the contribution of transition-specific content beyond temporal-progress cues. Using a five-step lag reduces estimated latent-encoder blocking from 114.25\,ms to 9.47\,ms relative to zero lag, with a small change in success (57.88 to 57.67 ). We next test how LTM benefits from broader demonstration coverage. We expand RoboMME from 100 to 1,000 episodes per task family and increase training from 40K to 120K steps. With the same encoder and policy architecture, success rises from 57.67 to 87.50 (Figure~ fig:teaser ). All four tracks improve; Reference, the weakest base-data track, gains 47.50 percentage points. Extending training to 120K steps on the original data alone yields no appreciable gain, supporting the benefit of broader demonstration coverage. LTM- exceeds the reported PonderPounce result with data by 11.96 points overall, under different data budgets and supervision assumptions. Scaling does not fully resolve the challenge of composing local transitions into persistent object states: VideoUnmaskSwap and ButtonUnmaskSwap reach 74 and 62 , versus 100 for their non-swap counterparts. In a Cup Swap diagnostic, process supervision achieves 97.93 final-state recovery from latent transitions, compared with 2.40 under final-state-only supervision. These results demonstrate that latent transitions preserve recoverable multi-step interaction information and highlight the importance of intermediate supervision, motivating language-guided reasoning and process supervision to address remaining temporal-composition challenges. To bound execution-memory growth, we merge the most similar adjacent projected tokens under the same quota during training and inference. On RoboMME-10x, a 200-token budget retains 84.00 success versus 87.50 uncompressed and reduces mean transition-token count by at least 38.26 on profiled training queries. Finally, we evaluate LTM- on a Galbot G1 robot in a real-world repeated pick-and-place counting task. LTM- improves average success from 11.25 for the memory-free baseline to 82.50 , demonstrating that transition memory also helps track completed interactions during physical manipulation. Our contributions are threefold: We propose Latent Transition Memory (LTM), a memory representation that uses compact latent transitions between consecutive observations as historical context instead of retaining the full visual history. This focuses memory on interaction-induced changes and enables the policy to use past experience without external reasoning-model calls or memory-specific semantic annotations. We develop LTM- , integrating transition memory into 's inference context through a lightweight adapter. Causal attention, persistent KV caching, and asynchronous transition encoding support efficient online control. Experiments on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem demonstrate strong memory-dependent manipulation performance, with a measured policy inference time of 66.71\,ms on an H100. We characterize transition-memory information, data scaling, and context-budget trade-offs. Ablations distinguish transition content from temporal cues; tenfold RoboMME data expansion raises success from 57.67 to 87.50 ; process-supervised Cup Swap decoding recovers final states with 97.93 accuracy; and a 200-token budget retains 84.00 success. Finally, real-robot counting experiments improve success from 11.25 to 82.50 . Related Work Vision-language-action models. VLA models transfer pretrained visual and linguistic representations to robotic control. RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 predicts tokenized actions, and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla provides an open-source generalist policy. ~ black2024pi0 introduces flow matching for continuous action generation; ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 and LingBot-VLA~ wu2026lingbotvla extend generalization through heterogeneous co-training and multi-embodiment data. These advances do not remove partial observability: the appropriate action may depend on events absent from the current observation. RoboMME~ dai2026robomme and LIBERO-Mem~ chung2026rethinking evaluate this need for execution memory. Memory mechanisms for VLAs. RoboFlamingo~ li2023roboflamingo models history through a sequential policy head; HAMLET~ koo2025hamlet and VLA~ cherepanov2026muvla use learned memory tokens. MemoryVLA~ shi2025memoryvla and LaMem-VLA~ qu2026lamemvla retrieve evidence from explicit memory banks. SAM2Act+~ fang2025sam2act extends a multi-view manipulation policy with a spatial memory bank, encoder, and memory attention. Object-centric approaches retain a different unit of history: SlotVLA~ hanyu2025slotvla models object slots and their relations, while E-SlotSSM~ chung2026rethinking studies the progression of object-centric memory states. GMP~ gao2026gatedmemorypolicy learns when to activate cross-attention over cached image and action tokens. RoboMME also compares symbolic, sampled-frame, and recurrent memories with several policy interfaces~ dai2026robomme . LTM instead retains an ordered sequence of changes between observations, rather than appearance tokens or a recurrent summary of the episode. Temporal prediction also informs memory-based control: HiF-VLA~ lin2025hifvla incorporates motion representations, MemoryVLA++~ shi2026memoryvlapp combines retrieved history with imagined futures, and MemoryVAM~ jiang2026memoryvam injects compressed visual memory into both video prediction and action decoding. MEM~ torne2026mem combines recent video with long-term textual memory, HiMe~ ji2026hime separates working memory from long-term planning, and WeaveLA~ zhu2026weavela passes latent summaries of completed segments to subsequent subtasks. MemER~ sridhar2025memer retrieves keyframes for a high-level vision-language model that generates instructions for a low-level policy. PonderPounce~ choi2026ponderpounce uses a separate pretrained multimodal context model to asynchronously supply continuous cognition tokens to its action model. Its RoboMME training recipe includes transition, subgoal, and demonstration-reasoning supervision. In 2AM~ hu20262am , an agent maintains episodic memory and guides an episodically stateless action model through subtask language and optional 2D spatial hints. These designs delegate historical interpretation to a higher-level model or interface. LTM instead exposes observed transitions directly to the action policy, without invoking a separate reasoning model or generating intermediate language during control. SimpleMemVLA~ yin2026simplememvla retains timestamped video in its VLM's native context and reuses the prefix cache through streaming prefill. Its action head receives representations of generated subtask text, with subtask annotations produced offline by a cloud VLM. This is a training-time annotation dependency, rather than a requirement for cloud-model calls during control. T Mem~ liu2026t2mem places a fast-weight memory between the VLM and action expert and updates it through self-supervised test-time gradients. Like LTM, it learns from action demonstrations without an external reasoning model or memory-specific annotations. Our distinction is therefore the memory representation and update rule: LTM appends frozen pairwise transition codes to a persistent sequence, without test-time gradient updates. title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA

Introduction sec:introduction VLA models bring the semantic knowledge of large pretrained VLMs into robot control, enabling a single policy to follow diverse instructions across objects and scenes openvla,pi0,fastwam . This capability, however, is commonly coupled to repeated backbone execution: each action chunk re-encodes the current images and language instruction with a large model. The robot must continuously observe the environment and revise its actions, but the instruction and overall task remain largely unchanged. Must the large VLM backbone also be re-run at every control decision? When manipulating objects, people typically work out the goal and identify the relevant objects before acting. As they reach, grasp, and place, they adjust their movements from what they see and feel without reinterpreting the whole task before every small action. This suggests two timescales: task understanding can remain stable, while control must respond continuously to changes in the scene. This motivates a policy that establishes task context once and then stays responsive to live observations throughout execution. Prior work reduces VLA inference cost by changing action representations or generation procedures pi0fast,fastwam . These improvements leave a separate question: must a large model recompute task context for every action chunk? Can a VLA think once about the task and still manipulate effectively as the scene changes throughout an episode? A fixed memory cannot represent the current world state: objects and arms move, and the visible scene changes during execution. The central challenge is to use live observations to query fixed task context at every control decision. We address this with ---You Only Think Once. A frozen 4B VLM encodes the instruction and initial multi-camera views into layer-wise key--value task memory at the start of an episode, then leaves the repeated control loop. The online actor continually processes current camera views and proprioception, with short visual history in the RoboTwin configuration. Query fusion combines learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current arm state and wrist-view features to form action queries. The action decoder uses these queries to read visual tokens and task memory, and an action head predicts an action chunk in one forward pass. The memory remains fixed, but the observations and predicted actions change at every control decision. The policy therefore remains closed-loop even though its task memory is fixed. We evaluate on RoboTwin 2.0 robotwin2 , LIBERO libero , and LIBERO-Plus liberoplus . On RoboTwin 2.0, it reaches 92.46 success in the Clean setting and 92.40 under domain randomization. obtains 95.95 on standard LIBERO and 79.11 on the LIBERO-Plus protocol. On RoboTwin, same-hardware measurements against Faster-WAM (HUST), DM0.5, and Fast-WAM show a 10.9--17.1 reduction in amortized policy inference time after including its one-time initial call, and its post-prefill online resident memory is 1.22~GiB. Task-memory swaps cause large performance drops, showing that the actor depends on episode-matched memory in our evaluation. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce an episode-level VLA architecture that represents one-time task understanding as fixed, multi-layer memory, moving a frozen 4B VLM outside the repeated control loop. We develop an online actor that fuses learned queries with live visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context across VLM depths, enabling action-chunk prediction in one forward pass. Across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, we show that this separation preserves competitive closed-loop performance while reducing RoboTwin amortized inference cost by 10.9--17.1 ; controlled memory interventions verify that the actor uses episode-matched context. Related Work sec:related-work Efficient VLA policies. Generalist VLA policies couple pretrained VLM representations with action generation through autoregressive tokens, flow matching, or specialized action heads openvla,pi0 . Recent work reduces the cost of each policy invocation through parallel continuous-action decoding and action chunking openvlaoft , or through more compact action tokenization pi0fast . These methods primarily optimize action generation while retaining repeated processing of new observations by the VLM backbone. Our focus is instead the frequency of backbone invocation: removes the frozen VLM from the control loop after one episode-level prefill. HyperVLA amortizes task conditioning by encoding the instruction and initial image into the generated parameters of a compact base policy, which then maps each current observation to an action~ hypervla . instead keeps the online actor shared across episodes and retains task context as explicit, layer-wise key--value task memory; at every control decision, query fusion combines learned queries with current feedback to form action queries that retrieve from this fixed memory. Reusing computation across control steps. VLA-Cache reuses representations of visually stable tokens between adjacent observations while selectively recomputing changed or task-relevant content vlacache . World-action models reduce online cost by omitting test-time future generation fastwam , sparsifying video--action interaction fasterwamhust , or attaching a shallow action module to a deep video backbone fasterwamnoah . These approaches reduce the work performed at each online call, but retain a large visual or video backbone in the repeated control path. instead fixes task context at episode start and delegates changing-state estimation entirely to a lightweight online actor. Method sec:method Overview Figure~ fig:architecture illustrates the two stages in the RoboTwin setting. Given an instruction and initial multi-camera views , a frozen VLM constructs task memory once per episode: The online actor comprises visual encoders, query fusion, an action decoder, and an action head. At each control decision, its input encoding stage maps current views , proprioceptive state , and optional visual history to online input representations: Here collectively denotes visual tokens and per-arm feedback. The prediction stage fuses learned queries with this feedback, then uses the action decoder and action head to read task memory and predict actions: Task memory stores episode-level context. At each action-chunk boundary, the actor combines current visual and proprioceptive observations with this fixed memory to predict the next action chunk. Episode-level task memory sec:memory The upper path in Figure~ fig:architecture uses a frozen DM0.5~ dm05 4B VLM to contextualize the instruction with the initial views. We retain the key and value tensors from all 34 Transformer layers: Retaining all 34 layers allows the actor to retrieve task context at different VLM depths. The memory remains fixed throughout the episode, and the VLM leaves the control loop after prefill. Online actor sec:actor Live inputs. In the RoboTwin configuration shown in Figure~ fig:architecture , the online actor receives current head and two wrist images, short head-camera history, and robot state. Each camera has a separate trainable DINOv2~ dinov2 encoder, with weights shared across frames from that camera. Visual tokens carry learned slot embeddings and time offsets, distinguishing past from current evidence. These tokens feed Cross-Visual attention; the CLS token from each current wrist view separately feeds query fusion. Query fusion. We initialize learned queries for each future time step and arm : Query fusion combines these learned queries with each arm's current state and wrist-view CLS token to form action queries. For arm , we project its seven-dimensional proprioceptive state and wrist-view CLS token, concatenate them with its role embedding, and fuse the features through an MLP to obtain arm feedback . A gated residual MLP combines each normalized query with the corresponding feedback and adds the result to the query. The same arm feedback is reinjected through a layer-specific gated residual before each subsequent decoder layer. Each action query represents one arm at one future step and can attend to visual tokens from all cameras. Current feedback updates the queries at every chunk boundary, allowing the same fixed task memory to be read differently as execution progresses. Action decoding. Each of the four action decoder layers follows the four stages shown in Figure~ fig:architecture . attention coordinates queries across future time steps and the two arms. attention reads visual tokens from current views and available history, grounding each query in visual feedback. attention then retrieves relevant task context from the fixed task memory, and the feed-forward network (FFN) updates the query. Together, these stages ground each action query in both the current visual--proprioceptive state and episode-level task context, enabling task-aware action prediction that remains responsive throughout execution. Within Cross-Memory attention, a KV memory adapter determines which VLM depths each decoder layer reads. Decoder layer learns scores over the memory layers, initialized to favor its depth-aligned layer: After bringing keys into a common rotary-position~ rope space with , the mixed memory is The queries read with one grouped-query cross-attention~ gqa operation. A key-side segment embedding distinguishes instruction from initial-image tokens. A linear action head predicts in one forward pass, without iterative denoising. For single-arm LIBERO, the same two-stage design uses agent-view and wrist images, one set of action queries, and a action chunk. The reported LIBERO configuration uses current frames without visual history.
