title: VLA-$Δ$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables, including appendices. Code: https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$Δ$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$Δ$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $π_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
full_text: Introduction Building generalist robot policies that follow natural-language instructions in diverse environments is a long-standing goal of embodied intelligence. Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ RT2023,kim2024openvla,GR00T2025,Pi02024,intelligence2025pi_,zheng2026x,community2026starvla,li2024cogact have recently emerged as a promising paradigm toward this goal. Built on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), VLAs inherit rich semantic knowledge and visual understanding from large-scale vision-language pretraining. They use the VLM backbone to encode task instructions and visual observations, mapping these representations to robot actions and achieving strong performance across diverse benchmarks. Despite this progress, VLAs often exhibit failures revealing a limited understanding of physical dynamics. For example, a policy may close its gripper before reaching the target object, or continue toward the placement location after a failed grasp. In such cases, the policy appears to replay a memorized trajectory rather than respond to the evolving scene. These failures suggest that reliable manipulation requires reasoning about how the robot and its environment should change as the task progresses. A key reason is that most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions and lack explicit supervision of the intermediate physical state changes. They tend to overfit observation--action correspondences instead of capturing how physical states change over time. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:introduction , existing studies Li2026ZR0,WorldVLA2025,VLAJEPA2026,JEPAWAM2026 introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction to guide action generation by implicitly modeling state changes. (b) Reasoning VLAs such as ECoT~ ECoT2024 autoregressively infer task plans and object locations before generating actions. However, their chain-of-thought supervision focuses on high-level task planning and state reasoning, together with sparse visual localization. It describes what should be done next, but not how the physical states of the robot and objects change between current and future states. (c) World Action Models (WAMs)~ cai2026internvla model state changes by generating future images. These methods provide denser visual details, but future-image reconstruction mainly enforces consistency in scene appearance and does not explicitly identify which changes are necessary for task completion. Moreover, generating future images typically introduces additional inference cost. (d) Latent-WAMs~ chen2026lawam move future prediction into a latent space, reducing the cost of visual reconstruction. However, their latent representations still model only future visual states, rather than signals tied to physical states and motion interactions. Overall, these approaches supervise either high-level task semantics or future visual appearance , but rarely supervise the physical state transition itself , i.e., how object poses, spatial relations, and robot--object contacts change from the current state to the future. Yet it is precisely these physical changes that directly define which actions the robot must take. To bridge this gap, we propose to explicitly model physical state transitions as learning targets. Such transitions should be both linked to task intent and grounded in concrete visual information: task semantics alone cannot specify how objects move, while visual appearance alone cannot indicate which changes matter for the task. Our core design is to extract physical state-transition information between the current and future states, encompassing both task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes. We aim to learn transition representations that capture task semantics while preserving motion details, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. We therefore introduce VLA- , a general framework using physical state transitions as explicit learning targets. The framework incorporates learnable Physical State Difference Queries into the vision-language backbone to form a unified transition representation conditioned on current observations and task instructions. We shape this representation through two supervision pathways: direct prediction and autoregressive generation. ~Structured Transition Slots provide structured supervision for variables including spatial positions and contact states, encouraging a semantic division of labor among Queries and giving the transition representation clear physical meaning. ~Optical Flow provides dense visual motion supervision, encouraging the representation to preserve motion details of objects and grippers. ~Future-State Difference Text provides coherent semantic supervision for task progress, spatial displacement, contact changes, and associated physical constraints through autoregressive generation. Together, these three signals guide the Query representations to jointly encode task semantics and visual motion changes, supporting continuous action generation. We construct a pretraining dataset comprising approximately 484 hours and 24 million frames and derive physical state-transition supervision signals from it. The three supervision signals are introduced only during pretraining, while downstream fine-tuning uses only the action-learning objective. This training scheme allows the physical state-transition knowledge acquired during pretraining to provide a representational foundation for downstream policy learning and adapt to the continuous control requirements of specific tasks. During deployment, the model directly generates actions without decoding intermediate supervision targets. VLA- achieves strong performance in both simulation and real-robot experiments. VLA- achieves a success rate of 98.40 on LIBERO and outperforms all compared methods under both the Clean and Random settings on RoboTwin. In real-robot experiments, it outperforms by 5.5 . These results suggest that physical state-transition supervision during pretraining helps the model focus on task-relevant motion changes, enabling it to benefit from pretrained transition representations during downstream fine-tuning. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose VLA- , a general framework using physical state transitions as explicit learning targets. By explicitly modeling task semantics and visual motion changes, it provides more direct supervision for continuous action generation. We curate approximately 484 hours and 24 million frames of robot demonstrations and develop a complete automated data annotation pipeline to generate large-scale, multilevel physical state-transition annotations for model pretraining. VLA- achieves the highest success rates among the compared methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin and outperforms in real-robot experiments. Method Overall Architecture of VLA-Δ As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:architecture , employs learnable Physical State Difference Queries to organize vision-language information into a physical state-transition representation for continuous action generation. The overall architecture follows the vision-language backbone and action-expert design of GR00T N1 GR00T2025 , using Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct and a 9-layer Diffusion Transformer. At time , the model receives multi-view visual observations , a task instruction , and the robot proprioceptive state , and predicts a continuous action chunk of length , . The visual observations and task instruction are first encoded into a contextual sequence , which is then fed into the vision-language backbone together with the learnable Query parameters . We extract the final-layer hidden states at the Query positions to obtain the transition representation : We shape this representation through two pathways: direct prediction and autoregressive generation. The direct prediction pathway reads the designated Query hidden states to predict structured variables, , where , and dense optical flow, . The autoregressive generation pathway predicts Future-State Difference Text, . Under the attention constraints illustrated in the right panel of Fig.~ fig:architecture , text positions can attend only to the Queries and preceding text, and cannot directly attend to the context . Therefore, information from the current observations and task instruction must pass through the Query representation before contributing to difference-text prediction. The action expert attends to through cross-attention and combines it with the independently encoded robot proprioceptive state . It then transforms Gaussian noise into a continuous action chunk through flow matching: , . The three auxiliary supervision signals are used jointly with action learning only during pretraining, while downstream fine-tuning optimizes only the action-learning objective. During deployment, the model retains the Query representation extraction and action-generation pathways without decoding the auxiliary supervision targets. Multilevel Physical State Transition Learning Structured Transition Slots Supervision. Physical State Difference Queries lack explicit constraints on their semantic roles when trained solely through action prediction. To encourage transition representations to encode physically meaningful information, we introduce Structured Transition Slots, which organize task-relevant state variables and their changes into nine categories of supervision targets with predefined semantic roles: task progress, task phase, target position, gripper position, motion and relative displacement, interactable position, gripper state transitions, contact transitions, and obstacle risk. This supervision encourages the assigned Queries to develop a soft semantic division of labor while preserving information exchange among Queries, allowing them to jointly support action generation. Figure~ fig:structured-slots presents an example of Structured Transition Slot annotations for a complete manipulation episode. Further details appear in Appendix~ sec:appendix-state-transition-annotations . We assign a subset of Queries to these structured targets. For each slot category, a lightweight prediction head reads the corresponding Query hidden representations to output . The overall structured objective is , where denotes the weight assigned to each target category. These structured targets provide direct supervision for learning key state variables. Dense Optical Flow Supervision. Structured Transition Slots supervise predefined state variables and their changes, but do not fully capture fine-grained visual motion during object movement, gripper approach, and local alignment. To complement this information, we introduce Optical Flow supervision using dense two-dimensional displacements between current and subsequent observations from the same viewpoint, encouraging Query representations to preserve local motion details in the image plane. We use a lightweight optical flow decoder that reads only the final hidden states of the last difference queries and decodes their motion information into dense optical flow. The total loss is defined as , where is the average error over all valid pixels, and is the average error over motion pixels whose target flow magnitude exceeds a predefined threshold. Optical flow alone does not distinguish task-relevant motion from other image motion. We therefore combine it with Structured Transition Slots and Future-State Difference Text, jointly constraining transition representations through state semantics and visual motion objectives. Future-State Difference Text Supervision. Structured Transition Slots and Optical Flow supervise physical state changes through predefined state variables and dense visual displacements, respectively. To better support action generation, transition representations also need to capture the relationships among these changes, including how object motion and contact transitions jointly advance the current subgoal and which physical constraints must be satisfied throughout this pr

title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.

title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://juliusju572.github.io/x-fly/
summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
full_text: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42\,ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78 of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present , a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, reaches 74.18 SR on test-seen and 51.73 on test-unseen, compared with 16.45 and 18.43 for full-chunk BC and 32.04 and 29.46 for DreamFly. Introduction Aerial VLN asks an embodied agent to follow a free-form instruction through a large urban environment and terminate within a target radius~ liu2023aerialvln,gao2025openfly . Compared with indoor graph navigation~ anderson2018vln,chen2021hamt , the agent must produce continuous translation and rotation, cope with large viewpoint changes, and recover from control errors that alter every subsequent observation. Success therefore depends on two coupled abilities: flying to the described goal, and deciding when the goal has been reached. Recent aerial agents condition on large vision-language models (VLMs), which makes every policy query expensive~ deng2026dreamfly,zhu2026fsdvln . Action-chunk policies predict several future controls per query~ zhao2023act,chi2024diffusionpolicy , yet aerial VLN agents such as DreamFly execute only the first control and query again~ deng2026dreamfly . Executing the complete chunk amortizes policy inference across its controls: for our fast--slow policy, executing all eight cuts model inference from 195 to 42\,ms per executed waypoint (Sec.~ sec:setup ). Full-chunk execution also changes where the policy is queried. The aircraft moves through eight controls before new visual feedback can correct it, so the states at which the policy is next queried, its decision anchors, drift away from the expert trajectories it was trained on. Expert-only data cover these learner-visited anchors poorly in two ways: they contain no chunk that starts at an off-route learner pose and returns it to the route, and their positive STOP labels are confined to expert terminal windows, leaving the anchors where the learner itself arrives poorly represented. We call this the full-chunk support gap. On test-seen, switching BC from single-step to full-chunk execution drops SR from 46.57 to 16.45 (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), although navigation failures barely change (28.02 vs.\ 30.77 ); no-stop failures account for 47.78 of the full-chunk outcomes (Sec.~ sec:failure ). Reaching the goal is not the same as stopping there. addresses both sides of the gap with two training stages applied after multi-domain BC (Fig.~ fig:training ). Recovery DAgger~ ross2011dagger runs the learner with the deployed full-chunk executor and labels every visited anchor with a smooth chunk that decays the learner's offset and reconnects to the future expert segment; the first anchor inside the success region receives a positive STOP label. Recovery reduces navigation and no-stop failures, while premature stopping remains common. Flow-GRPO~ liu2025flowgrpo then compares closed-loop attempts of the same task and updates the chunked flow controller and a separate Bernoulli STOP policy from their outcomes. With eight controls per decision, reaches 74.18 SR on test-seen and 51.73 on test-unseen, all from explicit in-region STOP. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=1.25em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] We study full-chunk execution in aerial VLN and characterize the support gap it creates at learner-visited decision anchors, with separate effects on goal reaching and termination. We present , a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial navigation that combines multi-domain BC, recovery supervision at learner-visited anchors, and closed-loop outcome optimization of chunked control and STOP. We demonstrate improved full-chunk navigation on OpenFly and characterize distinct stage-level gains: recovery improves goal-region reachability and reduces no-stop failures, while outcome post-training further reduces premature termination. Related Work Aerial vision-language navigation. VLN was first studied on discrete indoor navigation graphs~ anderson2018vln,fried2018speaker,wang2019rcm,hong2021vlnbert,chen2021hamt,chen2022duet . Continuous VLN removes the graph abstraction~ krantz2020beyond , and AerialVLN and OpenFly extend the setting to long-range urban flight~ liu2023aerialvln,gao2025openfly . Recent aerial agents use hierarchical planning, causal memory, diffusion policies, world-action prediction, and fast--slow reasoning~ wang2025traveluav,zhang2025citynavagent,deng2026dreamfly,zhao2026worldvln,liu2026imagineuav,zhu2026fsdvln . We adopt a fast--slow backbone and study a different axis: the training distribution shift created when such a policy executes a complete chunk before replanning. Learning when to stop. Graph VLN agents treat STOP as one action of a discrete vocabulary, and several works show that termination deserves dedicated modeling, through a separate stop policy~ xiang2020stop or progress estimation~ ma2019selfmonitoring . DreamFly adds a lightweight termination head trained on top of its frozen navigation policy~ deng2026dreamfly . A continuous-waypoint policy has no intrinsic STOP coordinate, so also uses a separate Bernoulli head, but supervises it at the learner's own arrival anchors and optimizes it jointly with control from closed-loop outcomes. Flow policies and action chunks. Diffusion and flow-matching policies represent multimodal continuous actions and emit action sequences~ chi2024diffusionpolicy,lipman2023flow,black2025pi0 . Action chunking amortizes policy inference~ zhao2023act ; temporal ensembling, bidirectional decoding, and real-time chunking address the resulting loss of reactivity at inference time~ zhao2023act,liu2025bid,black2025rtc . Fast--slow VLA systems separate reasoning from control~ xu2025vlacache,li2026think . keeps inference unchanged and instead repairs the training distribution that full-chunk execution induces. Closed-loop imitation and reinforcement learning. DAgger reduces covariate shift by labeling learner-visited states~ ross2011dagger . DART injects noise into demonstrations~ laskey2017dart , HG-DAgger relies on a human corrector~ kelly2019hgdagger , and ChauffeurNet synthesizes perturbed driving trajectories that return to the route~ bansal2019chauffeurnet . TravelUAV applies continuous-trajectory DAgger to aerial navigation with a teacher that searches forward along the reference~ wang2025traveluav . Our labels are instead collected at the anchors produced by full-chunk execution, follow the route by the number of executed controls, reconnect within one chunk, and add STOP labels at the learner's arrival anchors. On the RL side, RCM and EnvDrop combine imitation with RL for VLN~ wang2019rcm,tan2019envdrop , RefineFly and WorldVLN post-train aerial policies in closed loop~ wang2026recoverfly,zhao2026worldvln , and diffusion and flow policies are optimized by treating denoising as a Markov decision process~ black2024ddpo,ren2025dppo,liu2025flowgrpo,zhang2025reinflow . We use Flow-GRPO's stochastic transitions and add a factorized STOP objective to refine recovered full-chunk behavior. Method Problem: the full-chunk support gap sec:problem An episode consists of an instruction, onboard RGB observations, and executed controls, and ends at a STOP decision, the control budget, or an abnormal event such as a collision. The fused policy is queried only at decision anchors , one every executed controls. At each anchor it outputs a control chunk with and a STOP decision . If , the first controls of are executed open loop before the next anchor. We deploy . BC supervises only at anchors sampled from expert trajectories, , whereas deployment queries the policy at , the anchor distribution induced by the learner's own -step execution. Larger tends to move farther from , because more controls separate consecutive corrections. Two supervision signals are then missing on the support of : [leftmargin=1.25em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] Control gap. At an off-route anchor, no expert chunk starts at the learner's pose and remains coherent for steps until the next decision. Termination gap. Positive STOP labels come only from expert terminal windows, not from the anchor where the learner itself first enters the success region. BC (Sec.~ sec:bc ) provides the initial policy, Recovery DAgger (Sec.~ sec:recovery ) supplies both missing labels at the anchors this policy visits at , and Flow-GRPO (Sec.~ sec:grpo ) refines the recovered policy from closed-loop outcomes. Policy and BC initialization sec:bc The policy (Fig.~ fig:policy ) follows the fast--slow design of recent aerial agents~ deng2026dreamfly,zhu2026fsdvln . Learned query banks extract cached observation and instruction features from a frozen VLM and fresh current-frame features from its visual tower; these tokens, ego state, and a masked history of executed controls form the fusion sequence, with navigation queries as cross-attention memory. The fused representation conditions a rectified-flow controller and a separate STOP head, so control and termination have distinct likelihoods. Each control is a body-frame increment of translation and yaw. A two-layer DiT is trained by rectified flow~ lipman2023flow : with expert chunk , noise , and , where is the fused conditioning. Six Euler steps generate a chunk at inference. BC trains the query banks, fusion layers, controller, and STOP head on 849,106 valid decision windows from the UE, 3DGS, and AirSim domains of OpenFly, with positive STOP labels at expert terminal windows; the VLM and visual tower stay frozen. Auxiliary regularizers are listed in Appendix~ sec:impl . Recovery DAgger at learner-visited anchors sec:recovery We run the current learner in training scenes with the deployed full-chunk executor and record observations at its anchors. Labels must follow demonstration order, since a nearest-point match can point backward when a route passes near itself. We therefore index the expert route with a monotonic cursor that advances at each collected decision by the number of controls actually executed, rather than searching forward along the reference for a match as in TravelUAV~ wang2025traveluav . With learner pose at anchor and offset , the recovery target is for . The offset factor equals one at , decays with zero slope at both ends, and vanishes at , so the target starts at the learner pose and rejoins the future expert segment after one chunk (Fig.~ fig:training b). Yaw uses the same decaying offset, wrapped to the shortest signed angle, and consecutive target poses are converted to body-frame controls as in BC. Recovery targets are constructed only during training. STOP labels follow goal-region entry rather than the cursor. Collection runs with STOP disabled and is truncated at the first anchor inside the 20\,m success region, which is labeled STOP with a hover target; every earlier anchor is CONTINUE with its recovery target, and an anchor still outside the region after the cursor has reached the expert endpoint keeps a target toward the goal. Truncation also removes post-arrival anchors whose labels would point backward. Recovery thus adds STOP positives at the learner's own arrival anchors, complementing the expert terminal windows

title: CarryOn: A Dual-Loop Harness for Personalized and Reliable Robot Assistance
summary: While generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open-world manipulation, real-world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like "make me a sandwich" requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures. To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user-level and scene-level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control-based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference-consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety-finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Robot assistance ultimately aims to serve people in their everyday lives. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced this goal by learning to execute diverse manipulation instructions across tasks and environments~ black2024pi_0,kim2024openvla,brohan2023rt . Large-scale robot datasets further support learning across tasks and embodiments~ o2024open,team2024octo,bousmalis2023robocat . However, progress in instruction-conditioned manipulation alone does not bridge the gap to everyday assistance. A robot must know both what to do to meet the user's needs in the current environment and how to carry it out reliably as physical conditions change. Bridging this gap requires a system that connects context-sensitive task decisions with reliable execution. A harness is the system surrounding a base model that orchestrates execution and decides how the model plans, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results~ weng2026harness . Language-agent systems illustrate how memory and reflection can support decisions across interactions~ packer2023memgpt,park2023generative . In the field of robotics, hierarchical VLA systems connect high-level requests to manipulation instructions~ shi2025hi . Recent concurrent works on embodied harnesses use memory to steer frozen VLAs and coordinate heterogeneous policies~ zhang2026harness,huang2026roboharness , or evolve runtime critics and recovery skills from execution experience~ ding2026zetta . These works mainly focus on how to improve VLA models' performance in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. However, for everyday assistance, reliable execution must also be coupled with deciding what is appropriate for the user in the current situation. We study this connection through personalized robot assistance, which exposes two challenges. First, task decisions must remain aligned with the user's needs as interactions and scenes change, and the same request can require different actions. Learning preferences or identifying personal objects~ wu2023tidybot,lee2025bring provides context, while in reality the context can be dynamically changed and thus requires revision in stored memory. Second, the resulting plan must be supported by reliable physical execution: impending hazardous contact calls for intervention~ hu2025vlsa to ensure safety, while a failure that has already occurred calls for repair~ vats2025recoverychaining to ensure robustness. The harness must connect these responses to the intended task and retain failure experience to improve later recovery. Consider a user who asks a robot to ``serve me food'' (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The robot should respect an earlier vegetarian preference without requiring it to be repeated in the query. It may look beneath a remembered cover for a carrot, but finding meat instead must change its original plan. Even when the ingredient is suitable, an obstacle or a lost grasp can interrupt delivery to the bowl. The harness must preserve the user's dietary requirement when observations change the plan, restore progress when a grasp fails, and use that failure to improve later recovery. We present , a dual-loop harness that connects adaptive task decisions with reliable execution for personalized robot assistance. Its central design makes task context and recovery behavior persistent, revisable parts of the runtime around a frozen VLA. The planning loop determines what to do for the user and scene, and the execution loop protects and repairs the active subtask. Visual feedback connects them, informing plan revision and determining whether execution should advance or invoke recovery while retaining the task goal. The planning loop supports contextual adaptation through memories. User context expresses needs and preferences, while scene context helps determine where and how they can be fulfilled. The planner combines both with the current multimodal request and available observations to select an endpoint and supported subtasks. Dialogue revises user context, and observations trigger explicit scene-memory updates before subsequent plans proceed. Memory thus participates in a feedback loop: it guides action, while the resulting evidence updates what later plans can rely on. The execution loop supports physical reliability through fast proactive shielding and slower reactive recovery. A fast proactive shield predicts gripper and carried-object motion and filters commands against geometric contact constraints. After a failure, slower, event-triggered recovery skills repair the physical state so the interrupted task can continue. Offline reflection then uses failures of the current recovery version to revise its parameters and strategies, retaining successive versions in a skill library for later attempts. Immediate protection and reactive repair operate within an episode, and accumulated experience changes recovery behavior across attempts. This design keeps the VLA fixed while allowing the recovery pathway to improve through repeated reflection. Contributions. In this paper, we present a dual-loop harness, called , with the features of personalization and reliable execution. The planning loop of the harness connects persistent user and scene contexts with observation-driven revision, supporting personalized task decisions across interactions, scenes, and query modalities, while the execution loop combines proactive geometric shielding with reusable and iteratively refined recovery skills. Real-world studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our harness in planning preference-oriented tasks across diverse users and scenes. Notably, our method strongly increases recovery success rates from 13 to 80 using refined skills, and reduces the constraint-violation rate from 52.6 to 6.1 . Related Work sec:related_work TidyBot learns placement preferences that generalize to later requests~ wu2023tidybot , while Bring My Cup personalizes through reference-image memory and visual prompting~ lee2025bring . Embodied personalization studies memory across user interactions~ kwon2026embodied,lee2026personalizing , and language agents retrieve and consolidate experience for subsequent decisions~ packer2023memgpt,park2023generative . Unlike previous works, connects persistent preferences with revisable scene knowledge: user memory constrains task selection, while the scene memory guides later actions. Code as Policies generates programs over perception and control APIs~ liang2023code . Language-model planners ground instructions through affordances, feedback, and multimodal observations~ ahn2022can,singh2022progprompt,huang2022inner,huang2023voxposer,driess2023palm,zhu2023vima , while uncertainty-aware planners decide when to act or seek information~ ren2023robots . Hierarchical VLA systems connect instructions to visuomotor execution~ shi2025hi ; RoboHarness uses memory to orchestrate heterogeneous policies~ huang2026roboharness . Harness VLA combines a frozen contact-rich primitive with analytic operations and memory-guided retries~ zhang2026harness . In contrast, retains the VLA to execute manipulation and couples persistent personalization with action filtering and physical repair. Both loops share the active task, preserving the user-conditioned goal through recovery and using observed outcomes to govern task progression. Vision-language models provide semantic failure feedback~ zhang2026safevla , while FailSafe trains failure reasoning and recovery from generated failure recovery cases~ lin2025failsafe . RecoveryChaining learns local policies that return control to nominal controllers~ vats2025recoverychaining , and Zetta evolves runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy~ ding2026zetta . Language agents accumulate experience through memory and reusable skills~ shinn2023reflexion,zhao2024expel,wang2023voyager . In our method, confines refinement to control-based recovery: offline reflection revises supported parameters and strategies, retaining successive skills for later attempts. This separates immediate repair from experience accumulation while leaving the VLA and geometric shield fixed. Latent-space safety filters use reachability analysis in learned world models~ nakamura2025generalizing ; AnySafe adapts such filters to parameterized constraints~ agrawal2025anysafe . VLSA adds a barrier-function safety layer~ hu2025vlsa , and Code-as-Monitor generates executable constraints for failure monitoring~ zhou2025code . In our design, the proactive shield predicts the spatial response to policy-predicted actions and filters actions according to minimum-distance constraints between the gripper or carried object and task-specific obstacles. This provides a check before hazardous contact, complementing recovery after failure without online learning. Method sec:method uses a dual-loop harness to adapt task decisions to the user and environment and to support reliable physical execution. The planning loop turns a request into subtasks using persistent user and scene knowledge, then updates that knowledge through dialogue and observation. The execution loop runs a pretrained VLA, checks its actions for collision risk, and invokes control-based recovery skills when manipulation fails. Experience is retained in two forms: context for future planning and recovery experience that supports successive revisions of a versioned skill library. Fig.~ fig:architecture summarizes the runtime, and the following sections describe how each form of experience is used and revised. Overview of Given a request and an optional reference image, the planner combines user memory , scene memory , and descriptions of the available skills to produce a plan. Each planned subtask specifies an instruction , an endpoint that provides the requested skill, and optional dependencies on earlier subtasks. Endpoints include manipulation stations and information-gathering tools, so a plan can request an observation or external information before deciding what to manipulate. At a manipulation endpoint, the frozen VLA predicts action chunks from observation and the subtask instruction . A geometric shield filters these chunks using task-dependent contact constraints before execution. The Visual Judge compares recent camera images with the scene at the start of the subtask to assess progress toward . It reports running, success, or failed: success advances the plan, while failure invokes recovery on the same subtask. Observation results return to the planner for plan and memory updates. The Planning Loop: Personalization across Interactions and Scenes sec:method-know Planning with persistent, revisable context A personalized plan must satisfy the user's needs and account for the environment in which the task will be carried out. Since the current request may leave both kinds of information unstated, we maintain user and scene memories as complementary planning context. User memory supplies preferences and object references established in earlier conversations. We store preferences, habits, and reference images of the user's objects in user-specific profiles, which enter the planner context with each request. The planner is instructed to apply the requesting user's profile when selecting subtasks. The profile is combined with the current instruction, so planning accounts for both retained preferences and the user's present request. Scene memory provides planning context for deciding where and how to carry out the task in the current environment. We store object inventories and descriptions by place. The planner combines these records with the available skill descriptions to select an endpoint and decide whether an observation is needed before manipulation. If the target is hidden or its location needs checking, the planner requests an observation. title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55 on LIBERO-40, 33.4 on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6 on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4--9.5 on LIBERO-40, 9.7--18.3 on CALVIN, and 3.2--4.2 on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Generalist policies such as OpenVLA, , and \ provide a foundation for learning diverse manipulation skills kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Further specialization can improve individual domains, leaving useful capabilities distributed across separate policies. Multi-teacher consolidation seeks to transfer these capabilities into one student whose learned parameters are shared across domains. Across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN, the student must accommodate distinct observation and native action interfaces while integrating specialist supervision through the same learned parameters. Teacher-generated data provide a direct route to capability transfer xu2025rldg,xiao2026pld . During deployment, however, the student may encounter observations that differ from the teachers' demonstrations: a missed grasp changes both the next observation and the recovery action required. On-policy distillation (OPD) obtains teacher guidance at inputs induced by the student, following the principle of interactive imitation learning ross2011dagger,agarwal2024gkd,zhong2026vlaopd . For flow-based policies, the choice of supervision also extends inside action generation. A teacher can supply a final action chunk or local velocity predictions at intermediate states along the student's noise-to-action trajectory. Flow-based VLA consolidation therefore involves two evolving input distributions. The student's executed actions determine which environment observations it encounters, while its velocity field determines which intermediate states it traverses during action generation. Guidance on teacher demonstrations can leave both distributions mismatched to the deployed student. Recent work develops student-trajectory supervision for continuous generators and robot policies fang2026flowopd,oh2026fastopd,liu2026wamopd . For cross-domain consolidation, the central design question is how to couple teacher guidance to the shared student's behavior at both levels as its capabilities evolve. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework for consolidating domain-specialized flow-based VLAs into a shared student. The framework couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories, aligning supervision with the evolving student at both the environment and action-generation levels. Each frozen specialist supplies local velocity targets in its domain. We aggregate weighted domain-loss gradients to update the student once, then use the updated policy to collect new environment experience and action-flow trajectories. The student shares learned parameters while retaining the preprocessing, normalization, and action decoding required by each domain interface. Teachers are used only during training. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt] We introduce a two-level on-policy framework that consolidates domain-specialized flow-based VLAs through teacher supervision on student-induced environment and action-generation states. We demonstrate cross-domain capability consolidation in a shared \ student. It outperforms the SFT initialization, Action Loss OPD, and Teacher-rollout SFT on all aggregate metrics across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN. We characterize the roles of supervision targets and joint input sources through matched comparisons. Learning curves establish persistent advantages over endpoint matching, while suite-level results and domain-weight comparisons identify how transferred capabilities are distributed across tasks. Related Work sec:related On-policy distillation. OPD places teacher supervision on states or sequences generated by the current student. Its foundations connect interactive imitation learning with policy distillation: DAgger queries an expert on learner-visited states to address distribution shift ross2011dagger , while czarnecki2019distilling analyze how sampling and optimization choices affect policy transfer. In language models, GKD trains on student-generated sequences using teacher distributions and allows different divergence objectives agarwal2024gkd . MiniLLM instead optimizes sequence-level reverse KL through a policy-gradient formulation gu2024minillm . These approaches share student-induced sampling but differ in how teacher feedback becomes a learning signal. More recent work demonstrates token-level reverse-KL supervision for reasoning and behavior recovery in language-model post-training lu2025onpolicydistillation . Our framework extends this principle to both environment and action-generation states in closed-loop control. Multi-teacher capability consolidation. Policy distillation offers a route from specialized policies to a shared model rusu2016policy . In language models, MOPD consolidates domain experts through student-generated trajectories, while Open-MOPD and D -MOPD study capability imbalance and domain scheduling ma2026mopd,gao2026openmopd,sun2026d3mopd . DN-MOPD calibrates domain feedback and UP-MOPD constrains optimizer-generated updates, addressing interference during joint training li2026dnmopd,zhu2026upmopd . Controlled studies also find competitive off-policy alternatives after method-specific tuning and teacher-trajectory filtering xie2026rethinking . In robotics, RLDG and PLD transfer expert behavior through generated data; PLD additionally collects recovery experience from base-policy states xu2025rldg,xiao2026pld . DualVLA integrates complementary teacher capabilities, MergeVLA combines parameters with task-specific components, and MM-Nav consolidates navigation experts through student execution fang2025dualvla,fu2025mergevla,xu2025mmnav . Online RL can supply strong flow-based specialists for subsequent transfer chen2025pirl . We consolidate known domain experts into a shared action policy across distinct manipulation benchmarks. Distillation for continuous generation. Diffusion Policy uses iterative denoising for action generation, while Flow Matching learns velocity fields for continuous generation chi2023diffusionpolicy,lipman2023flowmatching . Flow-OPD transfers image-generation expertise through student-trajectory supervision with cold-start training and manifold anchoring fang2026flowopd . DiffusionOPD derives transition-matching objectives along student generation paths, including a squared velocity error for Gaussian transitions and direct transition matching for deterministic sampling li2026diffusionopd . FlowMap-OPD further separates rollout-state acquisition from distributional supervision in few-step flow-map generators li2026flowmapopd . For robot policies, FastOPD combines teacher velocity targets on student-generated action states with self-consistency for lightweight deployment, conditioned on dataset observations oh2026fastopd . Multi-task CFM distillation combines teacher-field matching with demonstration-based flow matching at action--noise interpolation states deshmukh2026multitaskcfm . Shallow- , SnapFlow, and DriftOPD pursue compression or one-step generation through teacher distillation, self-distillation, or offline policy learning jeon2026shallowpi,luan2026snapflow,jun2026driftopd . We retain the existing action-generation interface and focus on cross-domain capability consolidation. On-policy supervision for embodied policies. In closed-loop control, the student also determines the observations that condition future actions. VLA-OPD queries teachers on student environment rollouts and uses token-level reverse-KL supervision zhong2026vlaopd . PIVOT-Q selectively supervises vulnerable states visited by quantized VLAs, while uncertainty-aware distillation studies when teacher guidance should be trusted ruan2026pivotq,ren2026uaopd . Two distinct WAM-OPD studies extend this direction to world action models. yang2026wamopd use joint video--action supervision on fixed collected histories, constructing action-flow targets from teacher actions and noise. Concurrent work by liu2026wamopd explicitly formulates on-policy sampling over both observation histories and denoising states. Its main method combines a fixed history pool, fresh student denoising paths, and prefix weighting to reduce environment interaction; its experiments also include Online OPD with renewed rollouts. Our framework directly couples renewed student environment rollouts with local teacher velocity guidance on student action-generation paths. Across LIBERO, Meta-World, and CALVIN, we examine how this two-level supervision consolidates domain specialists into one student, and compare both the supervision target and the joint source of its inputs. title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
summary: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
full_text: Training-free target-aware refinement of a 3D Gaussian language map. An LLM turns a free-form request into a target word, and the refined map localizes it (green stars), whereas the baseline misplaces the ``outlet'' (red cross). The localized goal then guides a quadruped robot. fig:teaser Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: INTRODUCTION A reliable spatial representation is central to robotic autonomy, since a robot must understand its environment before it can act within it across tasks such as localization, navigation, and manipulation. The recent emergence of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2021nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d has made photorealistic spatial representation possible. Moreover, by combining these representations with vision language models~ radford2021learning , a scene is no longer restricted to a fixed set of semantic labels, and open-vocabulary NeRF and 3DGS representations~ kerr2023lerf,zhou2024feature,qin2024langsplat have become possible, allowing the space to be queried with arbitrary natural language. However, existing methods for building such language maps tend to fall toward one of two ends of a spectrum, and we instead pursue the practical middle ground, precise localization of user-specified targets without giving up open-vocabulary generality. Closed-set methods are trained per scene with semantic supervision~ li2024sgs,zhu2024sni and are accurate on their predefined labels, but cannot be queried with any word outside that set. Open-vocabulary methods instead distill vision-language features and respond to arbitrary text~ kerr2023lerf,qin2024langsplat,zhou2024feature . Yet because the distillation blends surrounding context into each feature, the resulting relevancy can be spatially diffuse, so a query often yields a plausible heatmap whose peak is not always precise enough to serve directly as a navigation goal. We first tried to sharpen such maps with a training-free post-processing, but found that the limitation is already present in the 2D features themselves, whose top-ranked retrieval is often wrong before any lifting to 3D. Purely post-hoc processing is therefore insufficient, which motivates injecting the target text directly into the features. To this end, we propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Given a small set of user-specified target words, we localize each target in every training view with a text-promptable segmenter, retain the open-vocabulary base from a class-agnostic segmenter, and encode both with a vision-language model. Within each target region the visual embedding is then blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient decides how much prior is injected, while non-target regions are left untouched. Such coefficients are conventionally treated as hyperparameters, swept over a grid or set by heuristics. Injecting too much overwrites the region's visual embedding and erodes the appearance cues and general queryability that make the map open-vocabulary. We therefore formulate the problem as finding the smallest coefficient that still lets each target win, and we solve it in closed form. Each detection yields this minimum as a flip point, and the per-target strength is read off the knee of the capture curve that the flip points form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. This minimal injection, together with the untouched non-target regions, is what keeps the refined map open-vocabulary. Because the refinement acts only on the 2D features before distillation, it is pipeline-agnostic and drops into different language maps as a plug-in module, from dense feature fields to object-level maps. It also carries over to language-goal localization, where the map must turn a query word into a 3D goal position. We observe a failure mode rooted in the geometry of contrastive vision-language embeddings~ liang2022mind,mu2017all . Text embeddings cluster around a shared direction, so injecting them plants this common component in the map, and under the standard cosine read-out every query then retrieves the same dominant regions. A centering step in the read-out removes this common mode. Notably, centering barely changes the base map but is decisive on the refined one, after which the refined map localizes goals more reliably than the base across Replica~ straub2019replica , ScanNet~ dai2017scannet , and HM3D-Semantics~ yadav2023habitat . We summarize our contributions as follows: A training-free, target-aware refinement that makes user-specified targets reliably retrievable while keeping the map open-vocabulary, with each target's injection strength obtained in closed form instead of tuned. A centered read-out that identifies and removes the query-agnostic bias of injection, turning the refined map into a reliable source of language-goal locations. Consistent gains in segmentation and localization on three benchmarks, plug-in transfer to field-based and object-level maps, and a real-world demonstration on a legged robot. Related work Open-vocabulary 3D language maps Semantic mapping has long attached labels to reconstructed geometry, but classical systems remain closed set, recognizing only the categories their segmenters were trained on~ mccormac2017semanticfusion . Open-vocabulary maps remove this limit by distilling vision-language embeddings into 3D, first over point clouds and implicit fields~ peng2023openscene,jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion,kerr2023lerf and more recently into 3D Gaussian Splatting~ qin2024langsplat,zhou2024feature,wu2024opengaussian , with closed-form solvers reducing the distillation cost~ xiong2025splat,jun2025dr and online variants embedding language during SLAM~ lee2025lego,ha2026langgs . Dedicated benchmarks now track the open-vocabulary quality of such maps~ kassab2026openlex3d . All of these works concern how to build the map, and to our knowledge none refines the language field of an already-built one, so our training-free, target-aware refinement is complementary to all of them. Language-goal localization and navigation A language map supports many downstream tasks, and this work concerns the one closest to deployment, turning a query word into a navigation goal. Spatial memories built from vision-language features have enabled language-driven navigation over grids and implicit fields~ huang2023visual,shafiullah2022clip,lee2025lamp , zero-shot object search~ gadre2023cows , scene graphs queried through language model reasoning~ werby2024hierarchical,gu2024conceptgraphs , and Gaussian memories for goal retrieval~ zhou2025lagmemo , evaluated under object-goal navigation protocols~ batra2020objectnav,khanna2024goat . Across these systems the goal is typically read out by raw cosine similarity between the query embedding and the stored features. We show that this standard read-out breaks once text embeddings are injected into the map, and that a centering step in the read-out restores and then surpasses the base retrieval. Method sec:method Our method refines an existing 3D Gaussian language map so that user-specified targets become reliably retrievable while the map stays open-vocabulary. For every training view we localize each target, blend its visual embedding toward the target text by a coefficient obtained in closed form, and lift the refined per-view features into 3D. At query time a centered read-out turns the refined map into 3D goal locations for navigation. Fig.~ fig:method summarizes the pipeline. Problem Setup sec:setup We are given a posed 3DGS scene whose language field is built from multi-view vision-language features. Each Gaussian carries an L2-normalized feature in the joint embedding space, and a text query scores Gaussians by the cosine similarity , where denotes the text encoder. The application additionally provides a small set of target queries with text anchors . A target region is retrieved only when its features score higher for than for every competing anchor. Densely distilled features frequently fail this test, since distillation mixes surrounding context into each feature and the argmax drifts toward larger context categories. In this setting, our goal is to refine the features so that two conditions hold. First, each target must win this comparison reliably, so that querying retrieves its own instances rather than the surrounding context that currently absorbs them. Second, the map must remain open-vocabulary, so features that belong to no target must stay unchanged, and even the target features should move only as much as needed. To this end the refinement introduces, for each target, one injection coefficient that blends the target features toward the text anchor as a convex combination of the two. The problem we solve is choosing each as the smallest value for which still wins, with no tuned hyperparameter. Target-Aware Feature Injection sec:inject We construct a target-aware feature map for every training view and then lift the per-view maps into 3D, in our implementation with a closed-form feature splatting solver~ xiong2025splat . For each view, a class-agnostic segmenter, instantiated with SAM\,2~ ravi2025sam in automatic mask generation mode, produces masks that cover the view, and a vision-language model, for which we use SigLIP\,2~ tschannen2025siglip , encodes each masked region into a -dimensional embedding. These region embeddings form the open-vocabulary base of the map. For each target word , a text-promptable segmenter, SAM\,3~ carion2025sam , localizes the target with a per-target mask in the same view. The shared encoder embeds that region into , and the text anchor comes from the paired text encoder. Regions outside the target masks keep their visual embeddings, so the base is preserved by construction. title: Uni-PNP: Unified Prehensile and Non-prehensile Policy Learning for Generalizable Object Pose Reaching
summary: Object manipulation often requires combining non-prehensile actions with grasping. However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy that jointly learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation for object pose reaching across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39% success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP.

However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39 success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91 on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP . Introduction Robotic manipulation can be broadly divided into prehensile and nonprehensile modes. Prehensile manipulation moves an object while holding it in a stable grasp. Nonprehensile manipulation moves an object without grasping, through actions such as pushing or tipping. We often combine these skills in everyday activities. For instance, a phone lying flat on a table leaves little clearance for a direct grasp. We slide and tilt the phone while closing our fingers, creating room to secure and lift it. Nonprehensile contact creates access for grasping, while a secure grasp enables controlled lifting and repositioning. However, prior work typically develops prehensile and non-prehensile capabilities separately, and combines them either by preparing objects for a grasp using non-prehensile manipulation~ preafford2024,gomp2026 , or by planning sequences of prehensile and non-prehensile primitives~ hacmanpp2024,spin2025,adaptpnp2025 . Treating the two modes as separate skills limits their ability to learn unified manipulation behaviors. Moreover, prior methods depend strongly on the geometry of the environment, object, and gripper. Several grasp-preparation strategies exploit environmental features such as edges and walls to obtain extrinsic dexterity~ zhou2023extrinsic,preafford2024,kobashi2025occluded , requiring suitable environmental supports. GOMP~ gomp2026 uses a learned graspability field to guide non-prehensile manipulation toward configurations suitable for subsequent grasp execution. Furthermore, these methods are constrained to the gripper geometry seen in training, which is inconvenient for real-world deployment. Cross-gripper policies learn grasp poses from grasp synthesis ~ adagr2021,graspgenx2026 . However, geometry influences manipulation beyond grasp pose selection: it also determines the contact interactions and resulting object motions. These geometry-dependent effects motivate jointly learning prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation across diverse objects and grippers. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy for prehensile and non-prehensile (PNP) object manipulation. Our policy reaches target object poses across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first construct a contact-dynamics dataset by sampling object--gripper contact configurations and recording the resulting object motions under gripper actions. We then pretrain a compact geometry encoder to predict these motions, learning a representation of geometry-dependent contact dynamics for the policy. Finally, we train the policy on these features through a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum. The policy first learns grasping and repositioning with smaller, readily graspable objects. Training then continues on an object set whose initial configurations are challenging for direct grasping, encouraging the policy to discover non-prehensile interactions and combine them with grasping. We evaluate Uni-PNP in simulation on 1,218 objects from this challenging set and 249 unseen objects from a different distribution, using grippers drawn from a training catalog of 200 geometries and the unseen Panda gripper. Uni-PNP achieves 76.39 pose-reaching success on training objects and grippers, and 57.91 on unseen objects with the unseen Panda gripper, outperforming the pose-reaching baselines across all settings. We complement these benchmarks with real-world experiments and an analysis of emergent manipulation skills, including tip-assisted grasping and table-assisted reorientation. Our contributions are: We introduce Uni-PNP, a unified policy that learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation jointly for object pose reaching. We construct a contact-dynamics dataset and propose motion-prediction pretraining to learn a compact geometry representation across varied objects and grippers. We demonstrate effective object pose reaching and generalization to unseen objects and grippers in simulation and real-world experiments. Related Work Learning-based Non-Prehensile Manipulation Non-prehensile manipulation changes an object's pose through contacts such as pushing and pivoting ~ mason1986,lynch1996,hou2018pivot . Recent learning-based methods unify non-prehensile manipulations by directly mapping geometric observations to actions~ corn2024,unicorn2025,dywa2025,dapl2026 . CORN~ corn2024 and HACMan~ hacman2023 improve generalization across object shapes through contact-aware representations and end-to-end interaction learning, while other methods use parameterized primitives or policy decomposition~ kim2023decomp . Nevertheless, these approaches focus on non-prehensile repositioning itself; a non-prehensile policy alone does not secure the object for stable lifting. Grasp and post-grasp repositioning therefore remain separate objectives in most existing systems. Combining Prehensile and Non-Prehensile Manipulation -Oriented Preparation and Affordance-Guided Manipulation. Many methods treat non-prehensile actions primarily as grasp preparation. Push--grasp systems coordinate pushing and grasping to improve grasp accessibility~ dogar2010,xu2021pushgrasp,zeng2018 . Affordance-based methods predict regions or object configurations that support a subsequent grasp~ preafford2024,gomp2026 , with language-conditioned affordances extending this idea to task-specific manipulation~ yuan2025robopoint . GOMP~ gomp2026 learns a graspability field and directs non-prehensile motion toward configurations suitable for grasp execution. Several approaches obtain extrinsic dexterity from walls, edges, slots, or slopes~ zhou2023extrinsic,preafford2024,kobashi2025occluded , making execution dependent on suitable support geometry. Separating preparation from grasp execution introduces a handoff between the two stages, whose effectiveness depends on the intermediate object configuration and available support. Integration of Prehensile and Non-Prehensile Skills. Another line of work explicitly plans contact modes or sequences of manipulation skills. External pushes, shared grasping, and contact-mode planning coordinate finger contacts with environmental support~ chavandafle2014,chavandafle2017,hou2020shared,cheng2021contact,cheng2022contact . HACMan++~ hacmanpp2024 selects spatially grounded motion primitives, AdaptPNP~ adaptpnp2025 revises primitive sequences and intermediate object poses using execution feedback, and SPIN~ spin2025 learns connectors between independently trained skills before distilling their planned trajectories into a policy. For skill-library approaches, the available primitives and transition conditions constrain the behaviors that can be composed. Contact-mode planners instead explore modeled contact interactions without necessarily requiring a predefined skill library. In contrast, Uni-PNP learns coordinated arm and gripper actions through a unified policy. Geometry Representations for Contact-Rich Control Point-cloud encoders such as PointNet~ pointnet2017 provide geometric features for downstream learning. Self-supervised pretraining develops these features through correspondence matching~ pointcontrast2020 , completion of occluded geometry~ occo2021 , and masked prediction of discrete tokens, point geometry, or latent representations~ pointbert2022,pointmae2022,point2vec2023 . For robotic control, PointPatchRL~ pointpatchrl2024 combines masked reconstruction with reinforcement learning, while 4D visual pretraining learns features through future prediction~ fourdp2025 . These objectives do not explicitly supervise the object motion induced by gripper contact. Contact-based representations focus on the geometry through which forces can be applied. CORN~ corn2024 predicts contact between an object and the gripper, while UniCORN~ unicorn2025 extends contact prediction to pairs of arbitrary geometries. Their supervision identifies where contact occurs but does not specify the motion it produces. DAPL~ dapl2026 incorporates physical attributes and action-conditioned dynamics prediction to represent contact-induced scene motion. Its encoder is refined using trajectories collected by the RL policy, tying the learned representation to the task-specific interaction distribution explored during training. Method Our goal is to achieve generalizable object pose reaching: bringing an object from an arbitrary stable initial pose to a specified target pose across different two-finger grippers. This requires combining non-prehensile contacts that reposition or reorient the object with prehensile actions that secure it for the final motion. To this end, we pretrain a geometry encoder to predict object motion induced by gripper contact under varying physical conditions. The learned representation conditions an actor--critic policy, which is optimized with a curriculum from ordinary grasping scenes to challenging object configurations. title: Trajectory-based Diffusion from One-shot Human Video for Generalizable Manipulation
summary: Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations. However, most existing approaches require labor-intensive data collection with additional teleoperation systems, which hinders scalability. Human videos represent a natural source of data that implicitly contain knowledge of manipulation behaviors. However, transferring them to robots remains challenging due to the visual domain gap and the absence of explicit action labels. In this work, we introduce TDV, a trajectory-based framework that leverages data generation to enable generalizable manipulation. TDV focuses on task-relevant objects by leveraging plug-and-play 6D pose estimation techniques to extract object trajectories from human videos, thereby mitigating the impact of irrelevant backgrounds and varying viewpoints. As a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, trajectories are inherently independent of the visual domains and different embodiments, enabling efficient data generation. Our method outperforms previous approaches on RLBench simulation tasks, achieving near 100\% success rates across seven tasks. In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques.
full_text: Our method is capable of generating a large number of valid trajectories from a single human video, enabling strong spatial generalization. Moreover, it exhibits robust performance under variations in the visual domain during deployment. fig:surface Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations.
