In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques. INTRODUCTION Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks without the need for manually configured heuristic rules. Most existing imitation learning approaches rely on proprioceptive states and visual data collected directly from the robot system, typically obtained through additional teleoperation systems operated by humans~ act, DP, fu2024humanplus . However, this approach is inefficient and presents significant challenges in scaling up data collection. In addition to images and text, there is a vast amount of human demonstration videos available on the internet, which inherently encode procedural knowledge for performing various manipulation tasks. Nevertheless, extracting meaningful perceptual information and actions from these videos for robot manipulation remains a non-trivial challenge. This problem involves two main aspects: the significant gap in visual domains and the lack of robot action information. Some studies utilize flow as an intermediate representation~ flowcorl, generalflow, Gen2Act, ATM , which captures the motion trends of task-relevant objects and exhibits robustness to visual discrepancies introduced by different embodiments. However, these methods require the camera viewpoint during deployment to be consistent with the one used during data acquisition, which limits their scalability in practical applications~ xue2025demogen . For manipulation tasks, the primary focus is on the state changes of task-relevant objects, rather than the agent executing the actions, thereby enabling cross-embodiment deployment. We find that object-centric representations, such as 6D object pose~ affordance, hsu2024spot, omnimanip , can effectively capture the real-time state of the object while mitigating the effects of irrelevant background and different viewpoints. A trajectory composed of a sequence of 6D object poses encapsulates the state transitions during the manipulation process. The previous method~ hsu2024spot requires pre-generated grasp poses for the object and fails to fully exploit the advantages of trajectory representations in scaling datasets~ mandlekar2023mimicgen , which is crucial for enhancing the generalization of manipulation. To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework, TDV, which enables generalizable manipulation across different embodiments from one-shot human demonstrations, as shown in Fig.~ fig:surface . Our framework is structured into three stages. To eliminate the influence of viewpoint changes, we represent trajectories relative to the reference object frame. Then, the resulting trajectories provide a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, enabling efficient data augmentation through simple trajectory scaling and interpolation. Finally, we then use the augmented dataset to train a trajectory-based diffusion policy, which achieves robust generalization across diverse manipulation tasks and supports multi-procedure execution conditioned on high-level task descriptions. During deployment, the pose of the moving entity is detected in real time and fed into the history sequence of the diffusion policy, enabling closed-loop execution. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework (TDV) that learns manipulation policies solely from human videos, significantly improving data collection efficiency and enabling scalable policy learning across diverse tasks. We leverage an object-centric intermediate representation based on trajectories to enable effective learning and cross-embodiment generalization. Our experiments demonstrate that TDV achieves strong spatial generalization and remains robust under complex backgrounds and diverse camera viewpoints. Related Works Learning from Human Videos Many efforts have been made to learn scalable manipulation policies from non-robotic data, particularly human videos~ Gen2Act,VideoDex,H-InDex,DBLP:conf/icra/ChaneSaneSL23 . The main idea is to extract meaningful representations from massive visual data and transfer them to robotic tasks. For instance, R3M~ r3m and MVP~ DBLP:conf/corl/RadosavovicXJAM22 pretrain visual representations on the large-scale internet human video dataset Ego4D~ ego4d , aiming to extract manipulation knowledge beneficial for robot learning from first-person perspective videos. However, due to the heterogeneous nature of the data sources and significant domain gaps, transferring pre-trained representations to specific manipulation remains challenging. To address this issue, some methods~ DBLP:conf/corl/KumarZ0J022,DBLP:conf/corl/SiebZHKF19 leverage in-domain human videos, where humans and robots perform the same manipulation tasks in identical environments. Another approach leverages transferable representations, such as affordances~ vbc, humanwild and flows~ flowcorl, Gen2Act, generalflow , combined with additional action policies. Object-Centric Manipulation To exclude background and task-irrelevant objects, many researchers focus on developing effective object-centric representations, which possess visual robustness and cross-scene generalization capabilities. The primary representation include point clouds~ GROOT , Gaussian splatting~ gs , 6D object pose estimation, neural implicit fields~ NDF , and other related methodologies~ robosee, flowcorl, 3dda, hsu2024spot . Owing to the development of visual foundation models, previous work~ GROOT has segmented the object point cloud from the scene point cloud in a modular manner and used it as input for the imitation policy, which are robust to background changes. Rather than directly using point clouds, Kerr et al.~ robosee combined 3D Gaussians with object part motion to construct a 4D Differentiable Part Model. Among object-centric representations, the 6D object pose is comparatively straightforward and efficient. Pan et al.~ omnimanip instructed the LLM to construct constraint relations based on the coordinate of task-relevant objects, and performed real-time 6D pose tracking during closed-loop execution to optimize the trajectory. To enable real-time object tracking in videos based on the generated object mesh, we divide the process into two steps: initial mask generation and mask tracking. We use the task description as a text prompt for GroundingSAM~ groundingsam to obtain the initial mask corresponding to the task-relevant object. Compared to visual images, using trajectories as an intermediate representation offers significant advantages in terms of computational efficiency and data augmentation~ mandlekar2023mimicgen . title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation
summary: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.
full_text: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human–robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines. Introduction Recent robot manipulation models are evolving toward World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future scene evolution and robot behavior, enabling predictions of interaction outcomes cosmospolicy2026,lingbotva2026 . However, scaling real-world robot data requires dedicated hardware, human operation, and physical deployment, making broad coverage of tasks, objects, and scenes expensive. In contrast, human manipulation videos are abundant and capture diverse task processes and object interactions, making them an attractive source of additional experience for robot learning droid2024,humanvideosurvey2026,mimicplay2023 . Yet humans and robots differ substantially in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms, so concrete human actions cannot be directly reused as robot supervision whirl2022,xskill2023,uniskill2025 . This leads to the central question of this work: A complete human manipulation sequence contains two types of information: object-interaction relations that support task progress, and concrete motion realizations that are closely tied to the human embodiment. For long-horizon manipulation tasks, we first organize continuous execution into local task processes using temporally extended subtasks, thereby avoiding the requirement that the robot reproduce human motion step by step. However, defining a subtask only specifies the local scope within which transfer takes place; it does not further determine which information within that scope should be preserved together with the task experience. Retaining only the task intention or boundary states of a subtask may discard the conditions and interaction relations that determine how a local effect is realized, whereas retaining the complete human execution trajectory reintroduces substantial embodiment-specific motion details. We study this selective information-preservation problem through the lens of causal beams pearl2009causality . Given a structural model and a specific context, a causal beam allows part of the inputs to be projected out in a context-dependent manner, while requiring the actual values of the retained variables to sustain the actual outcome of the current mechanism and the projected mechanism to retain nontrivial responsiveness to its retained inputs. This perspective motivates separating task-level abstraction from contextual information selection. Task-level variables provide an abstraction of execution, while causal-beam conditions constrain which semantic dependencies are retained within a specified model. Based on this, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST) . CBST first learns manipulation-related temporal representations through human-video pretraining and grounds them, under robot demonstration supervision, into a candidate SCM instantiated from shared manipulation templates. A contextual subtask-conditioning module then selects a contextual causal beam from the candidate SCM according to the current execution context, producing the local task effect, relevant conditions, and their effect-relevant dependencies. This structural information conditions the target robot WAM, while concrete actions are still generated from the robot's current state and its own action space. CBST therefore combines human-video representation transfer with causal-beam-constrained selection of contextual subtask information for robot execution. Our contributions are summarized as: (1) We study human-to-robot learning from the perspective of cross-embodiment transfer, focusing on which task-progress structures should remain transferable after embodiment-specific motion is discarded; (2) We propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST), which combines a shared candidate manipulation SCM with learned contextual causal beams to preserve effect-relevant conditions and dependencies for conditioning robot WAMs; (3) We systematically evaluate CBST on WAMs including LingBot-VA and Cosmos Policy, examining the contributions of human video pretraining, context-specific causal selection, and their effects on robot control. Related Works Human-to-robot transfer aims to exploit abundant human demonstrations while addressing the embodiment gap between human and robot execution. Motion-oriented approaches seek representations that remain useful across embodiments while retaining execution information. WHIRL aligns human and robot videos to infer task intent and initializes robot policy learning from third-person human demonstrations whirl2022 , while EgoMimic uses egocentric human videos with 3D hand tracking, cross-domain alignment, and joint training on human and robot demonstrations egomimic2025 . Latent Action Pretraining (LAPA) instead learns discrete latent actions from videos without robot action labels and subsequently maps them to robot actions using limited robot data lapa2025 . Other approaches move toward higher-level transferable representations. MimicPlay learns latent plans from large-scale human play videos and uses them to guide a low-level robot controller mimicplay2023 ; XSkill discovers cross-embodiment skill prototypes from unlabeled human and robot videos and maps them to robot actions with a conditional policy xskill2023 ; Translating Robot Skills learns unsupervised correspondences between skill sequences across morphologically different agents translatingskills2022 ; and UniSkill learns embodiment-agnostic skill representations that allow skills extracted from human video prompts to guide robot policies trained on robot data uniskill2025 . More recently, Gen2Act generates human future videos for novel tasks and conditions a robot policy on the generated motion information gen2act2025 . Temporal abstraction organizes long-horizon behavior into reusable units beyond primitive actions. The options framework formalizes temporally extended policies through initiation sets, internal policies, and termination conditions options1999 , while later robotic methods model skill feasibility and composition, such as SayCan saycan2022 and relational skill-precondition learning. Another line of work represents task progress through intermediate subgoals: Video Language Planning generates hierarchical visual and language plans vlp2024 , TaKSIE conditions visual subgoal generation on task progress taksie2025 , and Latent Space Backward Planning recursively constructs intermediate latent goals from the final task goal lbp2025 . More recent world-model methods integrate such temporal abstraction directly into planning: Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models learns dynamics at multiple temporal scales and uses high-level latent subgoals to guide low-level planning hwm2026 , while SAGE similarly exploits temporally extended latent subgoals for action-sequence generation sage2026 . World models learn predictive dynamics to support action selection and planning. Early latent-dynamics approaches such as PlaNet perform planning directly in learned latent spaces planet2019 , while more recent methods extend this idea to visual robot manipulation: DINO-WM predicts future visual features for zero-shot planning dinowm2025 , V-JEPA~2-AC learns action-conditioned latent dynamics for model-predictive control vjepa2_2025 , and IRASim models fine-grained action-conditioned visual futures for simulation and planning irasim2025 . Recent World-Action Models further unify future prediction with action generation. WorldVLA jointly models visual and action tokens in an autoregressive framework worldvla2025 ; Cosmos Policy generates robot actions together with future-state images and value estimates cosmospolicy2026 ; LingBot-VA jointly learns future-frame prediction and policy execution in a shared visual--action latent space lingbotva2026 ; and -WM further combines video prediction, action generation, and action evaluation within a unified model tau0wm2026 . Problem Definition and Analysis Problem Formulation Robot manipulation is a sequential decision-making process: given a task instruction \(g\), the robot generates actions based on the available information and obtains new observations through interaction with the environment. Let \(s_t\) denote the robot observation at time \(t\), comprising visual input and available proprioceptive measurements, and let \(a_t\) denote a robot action. The interaction history is \(h_t=(s_0,a_0, ,a_ t-1 ,s_t)\). We consider a world-action model (WAM) that jointly models robot actions and future observations conditioned on the interaction history \(h_t\) and task instruction \(g\). Given \(h_t\) and \(g\), the WAM generates an action chunk and predicts future observations through the joint conditional distribution \(p_ (A_t,S_t^+ h_t,g)\). Here, \(A_t=(a_t, ,a_ t+H-1 )\) denotes an action chunk of length \(H\), and \(S_t^+=(s_ t+ )_ T_H \) denotes the future-observation sequence at offsets \( T_H \ 1, ,H\ \). After executing the action chunk, the robot updates the interaction history using newly acquired observations, forming a closed-loop control process. Causal Beams sec:causal_beams We use a recursive structural causal model \(M=(U,V, F)\), where each non-root variable \(V_i V\) is determined by a structural mechanism \(V_i=f_i( _i,U)\). A context \(U=u\) determines the actual values \(V_i(u)\). For the causal-beam construction, the parent set of each mechanism is partitioned as where \(C_i\) denotes the retained parents and \(N_i\) the remaining parents. title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
comment: 26 pages, 8 figures. Haitao Shen and Hanyu Liu contributed equally
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.

Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA~2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for robot learning, achieving strong performance across many manipulation tasks~ baseline_openvla,baseline_pi05 . Beyond direct action supervision, recent studies increasingly introduce additional learning objectives into VLA training, including geometric representation alignment and spatial or 3D structure prediction~ intro_spatial_forcing,intro_glad . Among these, latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction have become two representative forms of supervision. Latent action abstracts visual transitions into compact tokens that characterize how the scene changes over time~ intro_lapa,intro_villax , whereas future vision encourages the policy to predict future representations, providing supervision about how the scene is expected to evolve~ intro_gr1,rw_flare . Because executable actions are the ultimate outputs of robot policies, direct action prediction is typically treated as the dominant training objective, while LA and FV prediction are introduced as auxiliary supervision. Prior studies have examined latent-action formulations and integration strategies~ intro_pixels_to_tokens,intro_what_matters , showing that such supervision can benefit downstream policy learning. More importantly, LA and FV are not merely auxiliary in effect: by providing learning signals about state changes and task structure, they directly shape the same policy during optimization. Yet, showing that an additional target is useful does not establish that direct action prediction is itself the most effective supervision. We therefore ask (Figure~ fig:framework ): under a fixed training budget, what should robot policies learn to predict, and can assigning LA or FV prediction an equal or larger share of training samples than direct action prediction improve action execution? To investigate this question, we build a unified VLA framework that places a two-stream MMDiT on top of a pretrained VLM, with separate action and auxiliary experts interacting through joint self-attention. We further introduce a sample-level router that assigns each training sample to either action or auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, making their relative training allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets and three FV targets: LA predicts discrete latent tokens extracted by different encoders, whereas FV predicts future features in different visual representation spaces. This unified setup enables a controlled comparison of how different supervision targets shape policy learning, with source-matched controls that change only routing for each FV target; FV prediction still conditions on demonstrated actions. We evaluate our framework on two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO and CALVIN) and four real-robot manipulation tasks, and obtain three main findings. First, suitable LA and FV supervision can outperform action-only training under the same training budget, even when direct action prediction receives only half or fewer of the training samples. Second, FV generally performs better than LA across both simulation and real-robot tasks, while the strongest LA configuration remains competitive on CALVIN. Third, our analyses suggest that LA and FV shape policy learning in different ways: DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets better capture absolute position and task identity, and both can alter policy attention toward task-relevant regions. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit the dominant role of direct action prediction in VLA training and investigate how allocating supervision to LA and FV affects policy learning. (2) We introduce a unified VLA training framework with a sample-level training router that explicitly controls the allocation of action and auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, enabling controlled comparisons across multiple LA and FV targets. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot manipulation tasks, together with representation and attention analyses, and derive systematic findings on action-supervision allocation, the performance differences between LA and FV, and their representation characteristics. Related Work sec:related Supervision beyond action labels. Robot learning draws on supervision beyond action labels, including visual reconstruction and language generation~ rw_voltron , vision-language co-training~ rw_rt2 , and geometric alignment~ intro_spatial_forcing,intro_glad,rw_4d_wam . We focus on two demonstration-derived targets, LA and FV, and study both which target to predict and how to allocate training samples between it and direct action prediction. Latent actions. LAPA and UniVLA pretrain policies with latent actions derived from visual transitions~ intro_lapa,rw_univla . The villa-X framework jointly models latent and robot actions, using latent plans to support action generation~ intro_villax . Analyses examine controllable changes and exogenous noise~ rw_lam_learn , while LARYBench~ rw_lary finds that general visual encoders can outperform specialized latent-action models on its semantic and physical-action probes. Empirical studies compare latent-action formulations, integration strategies, and loss weights~ intro_pixels_to_tokens , and examine links between representation-quality proxies and downstream policy performance~ intro_what_matters . Rather than reweighting losses on every sample, we route each sample to a single objective, and we probe LA and FV sources with the same absolute- and relative-motion readouts. Future vision. GR-1, GR-2, UWM, and DreamZero jointly model future images or videos and robot actions~ intro_gr1,rw_gr2,rw_uwm,rw_dreamzero . Seer and VPP guide action generation with predicted visual states or features~ rw_seer,intro_vpp . FLARE enhances policy learning through future-representation alignment and compares against an action-only baseline trained for longer~ rw_flare . We instead compare against action-only training with the same total budget, vary the action share, and add source-matched FV controls, including allocations where auxiliary prediction receives most samples. title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
summary: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.
full_text: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness. INTRODUCTION sec:introduction A robot must convert a language instruction and a changing visual scene into a temporally coherent sequence of actions. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) systems use a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) as a semantic backbone and attach a diffusion or flow-matching action decoder chi2024diffusion,kim2024openvla,starvla2025,xvla2025 . This recipe gives strong instruction following, but the action interface is commonly learned directly from robot trajectories. The resulting hidden state need not represent the short-horizon visual change that an action is intended to cause. Consequently, the policy has no explicit internal prediction of what its action will do before it is executed. At the same time, large video collections contain abundant information about how objects and hands move, but generally do not provide robot actions. Latent action models (LAMs) address this gap by compressing temporal changes into a compact code ye2025lapa . Existing systems, however, often pretrain a LAM or a latent world model separately and subsequently adapt it to a robot policy. This multi-stage procedure introduces an additional checkpoint and optimization boundary, and it does not guarantee that the learned latent is useful to the final action decoder. We propose TS-WAM (Teacher-Student World-Action Model), a task-adaptation architecture that makes temporal prediction the central interface of a VLA policy without requiring a separately pretrained latent-action model. The model uses an asymmetric pair of VLM branches. The online -VLM receives only the current observation and language instruction. It produces latent- tokens that a small transformer predictor maps to a predicted latent action. The EMA -VLM receives the current and future observations and reads the corresponding target latent action. This temporal information asymmetry turns future visual evidence into a training-only teacher signal while keeping the deployed policy causal. The latent action is coupled to visual dynamics and control. A frozen DINO encoder represents the current and future images as spatial feature grids. A newly initialized latent world decoder predicts the feature displacement conditioned on the current feature and latent action. The predicted future feature is passed to a conditional flow-matching action head together with VLM context and robot state. The policy therefore follows an explicit chain: infer a latent intent, predict its visual consequence, and ground that consequence into an action chunk. The same training procedure can mix robot demonstrations and action-free human videos. Human clips contribute current--future visual pairs to the teacher and world-model objectives, whereas robot clips additionally provide state and action supervision for the flow head. Thus, action-free data expands temporal supervision without providing embodiment-specific action labels. The task-specific world decoder is initialized from scratch and co-adapts with the VLM and policy. This joint objective keeps temporal prediction aligned with the downstream control interface throughout task adaptation. At deployment, the resulting policy uses only the current observation while retaining visual anticipation learned from both data sources. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce vlm-jepa, a self-supervised framework for learning temporal latent-action representations from robot demonstrations and action-free human videos. We propose TS-WAM, a lightweight world-action model that unifies temporal representation learning, visual prediction, and action generation through end-to-end training. It anticipates action consequences to guide control, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world evaluations on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate TS-WAM's strong manipulation performance. RELATED WORK sec:related_work Vision-language-action policies. VLA methods adapt large multimodal models to robot demonstrations and decode continuous action chunks with autoregressive, diffusion, or flow-based heads kim2024openvla,starvla2025,xvla2025 . Their pretrained semantic representations are useful for language grounding, as demonstrated by recent generalist policy and multimodal-control systems wang2025univla,maes2026leworldmodel,parthasarathy2025closing , but the action decoder is typically the only component trained to model robot dynamics. TS-WAM retains the VLM as a semantic context encoder while adding an explicit temporal latent-action and future-feature interface. Latent actions and world models. World models learn compact dynamics for planning and control ha2018worldmodels,hafner2019planet,chua2018pets,hafner2019dream, hafner2023dreamerv3,maes2026leworldmodel,sobal2025pldm . Reconstruction-free models such as DINO-WM predict features from a frozen visual representation zhou2024dino,oquab2024dinov2 , avoiding the cost of pixel prediction. Existing approaches commonly first pretrain on large-scale video or interaction data to obtain latent-action or dynamics supervision, and then fine-tune on robot demonstrations for embodiment-specific control ye2025lapa,bu2025univla . This two-stage pipeline incurs substantial additional computational cost and resource demands. TS-WAM instead jointly optimizes a causally predicted latent action and world-action model within the deployed VLM. Joint-embedding predictive architectures. JEPA methods learn by predicting the representation of a target region or future observation from an encoded context, rather than reconstructing the input in pixel space. A context encoder and predictor estimate the target embedding, which is provided by a separately encoded target. The target encoder is commonly updated by an exponential moving average, providing a stable regression target without explicit negative samples. This objective emphasizes predictable semantic and temporal structure. I-JEPA and V-JEPA apply this principle to images and videos, respectively assran2023ijepa,bardes2024vjepa,assran2025vjepa2,zhang2026deltajepa . Their EMA target encoders provide stable self-supervision for visual representation learning. TS-WAM transfers this principle to VLA: the target is a latent action extracted from a future-aware VLM, while the student is restricted to current observations, making the learned representation directly usable for control. Learning from heterogeneous video. Self-supervised video learning extracts temporal representations without action labels bardes2022vicreg,bardes2024vjepa , but they must still be grounded in embodiment-specific robot actions. LAPA and UniVLA address this gap by learning latent actions from videos and adapting them to robot control ye2025lapa,bu2025univla . TS-WAM uses unlabeled human videos for temporal supervision while jointly optimizing robot actions. Its shared latent-action and future-feature interfaces align video-derived representations with the robot objective throughout adaptation. A second challenge is retaining video-derived knowledge during robot adaptation. Sequential objectives can cause catastrophic forgetting kirkpatrick2017overcoming , motivating continued video supervision during robot adaptation. TS-WAM retains ego-video supervision while learning the robot action objective, anchoring the shared temporal representation to both visual domains. This joint training is intended to mitigate forgetting; verifying skill retention requires dedicated evaluation. Method sec:method TS-WAM introduces a novel integration of the JEPA architecture and delta-lwm with an end-to-end joint training strategy that learns manipulation skills directly from heterogeneous datasets of robot demonstrations and ego videos. Figure~ fig:overview presents the overall architecture. sec:jepa Fig.~ fig:vlm_jepa details the future-distilled latent-action interface, our first contribution. The asymmetric observation inputs allow future-aware temporal supervision while keeping the online prediction causal. latent-action prediction. The online branch inserts learned latent- query tokens into the current image-language sequence. The resulting hidden states are . A lightweight transformer predictor maps them to the latent-action space: where are learned target-query embeddings. The online branch has access only to information available before the action is executed. More explicitly, the predictor projects the latent- tokens and target queries into a shared space, adds separate learned positional embeddings, and applies a self-attention stack to their concatenation. Only the final target positions are retained and projected back to the world-model code space: This explicit bottleneck prevents the latent action from being copied directly from a single VLM hidden state and forces temporal intent to be inferred from the current observation. -aware EMA teacher. The teacher branch uses the same VLM and latent-action mapper but receives the current and future images. It reads target query tokens and produces target . Teacher parameters are updated after each optimizer step by where is the EMA momentum. Gradients do not flow through the teacher. We optionally normalize the detached target over its code dimension and align the online prediction with it using This objective does not reconstruct pixels or require an action label. It asks the student to infer the temporal change represented by the privileged teacher from the current observation alone. At inference, the teacher is pruned. The online VLM and predictor therefore implement a causal map with no extra temporal input or inference-time teacher cost. sec:world_action -step feature-delta visual dynamics. We use a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain spatial feature grids and from the current and future frames. Instead of predicting an absolute future representation, the trainable decoder predicts the motion target The decoder is initialized from scratch for every TS-WAM run. title: Towards bio-inspired visual navigation: a neuromorphic navigation paradigm for MAVs
summary: Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments. Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors. The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module. This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps. The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points. Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption. The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX. Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment. Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.

Introduction In nature, insects and birds can rely on compact visual systems and efficient neural information processing to achieve long-duration, robust navigation in complex environments under extremely limited computational and energy resources~ collett2002memory, bhagavatula2011optic . This ability to perform rapid perception, real-time decision-making, and stable flight under severe resource constraints highlights a significant gap between the navigation capabilities of current small aerial robots and those of flying animals. Over the past decade, advances in visual sensors and artificial neural networks have substantially improved the capabilities of flying robots, especially small rotorcraft MAVs, in environmental perception~ qin2018vins,teed2023deep , autonomous obstacle avoidance~ song2023learning,loquercio2021learning,zhou2022swarm , and closed-loop control~ song2022policy,o2022neural . However, existing MAVs still fall short of the robustness and energy efficiency exhibited by biological visual navigation systems in complex scenarios. Current mainstream navigation systems based on conventional frame-based vision and artificial neural networks~ kaufmann2023champion,yu2025spatial,yu2025depth acquire image frames at fixed intervals and process visual information through dense and synchronous computation, as shown in Fig.~ fig:1 B. Many existing systems~ kaufmann2023champion, wu2026precise rely on visually salient ground features, such as fiducial markers or high-contrast objects, to maintain reliable perception during highly agile flight. In contrast to the sparse and asynchronous sensing and computation of biological systems, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:1 A, this frame-driven paradigm makes it difficult to simultaneously achieve robust perception and high energy efficiency on high-speed, resource-constrained MAVs. More fundamentally, this mismatch in sensing and computation principles may not only constrain navigation performance in increasingly challenging environments, but also limit the potential of conventional architectures to evolve toward more adaptive, efficient, and biologically inspired autonomy. Neuromorphic technologies~ chakravarthi2024recent,gallego2020event,roy2019towards offer a promising route to narrowing the gap between robotic navigation systems and biological navigation systems. Unlike conventional frame-based vision sensors and artificial neural networks, neuromorphic vision sensors, known as event cameras, and spiking neural networks are characterized by event-driven operation, sparse activation, and asynchronous processing, which are intrinsically aligned with biological visual perception and neural computation. Event cameras generate events only when pixel-level brightness changes occur, enabling visual information to be captured with microsecond-level temporal resolution while substantially reducing redundant data. In contrast, spiking neural networks transmit and process information through asynchronous discrete spikes, and can significantly reduce computational power consumption, especially when deployed on neuromorphic processors. In recent years, neuromorphic technologies have attracted increasing attention and achieved significant progress~ klenk2024deep,guan2025deio,zhou2021event,niu2025esvo2,zhu2025depth,ghosh2025event,hu2025ede,gehrig2024low,li2022asynchronous,gehrig2023recurrent,yen2024tracking,fang2021deep,fang2023parallel,yao2025scaling,luo2024integer . Event cameras have demonstrated advantages over conventional frame-based cameras in challenging scenarios involving high-speed motion and complex illumination, and have been widely applied to visual tasks such as pose estimation~ klenk2024deep,guan2025deio,zhou2021event,niu2025esvo2 , depth estimation~ zhu2025depth,ghosh2025event,hu2025ede , and object detection~ gehrig2024low,li2022asynchronous,gehrig2023recurrent,yen2024tracking . In parallel, spiking neural networks have shown the potential to achieve performance comparable to artificial neural networks across various tasks~ fang2021deep,fang2023parallel,yao2025scaling,luo2024integer , while substantially reducing energy consumption. In particular, the rapid development of dedicated neuromorphic processors~ davies2018loihi, akopyan2015truenorth, painkras2013spinnaker,pedersen2019spinnaker,richter2023speck for spike-based computation has made sparse asynchronous computing and practical deployment of spiking neural networks increasingly feasible. These advances highlight the promise of neuromorphic technologies for efficient and robust visual navigation. However, existing neuromorphic navigation studies~ vemprala2021representation, bhattacharya2024monocular,jesusanmi2024investigating,jiang2023neuro often introduce neuromorphic components only at either the sensing or computing stage, and have not yet established a unified end-to-end neuromorphic navigation framework. Some studies~ vemprala2021representation, bhattacharya2024monocular use event cameras to acquire visual information, but still rely on artificial neural networks for subsequent processing. Others~ jesusanmi2024investigating,jiang2023neuro adopt spiking neural networks for decision-making and inference, while their visual inputs still come from conventional frame-based images. This mismatch between sensing and computation weakens the core advantages of neuromorphic systems, including sparsity, asynchrony, and low-redundancy processing, and also limits their potential for low-latency and energy-efficient navigation. In contrast, the integration of event cameras and spiking neural networks can preserve consistent properties across sensing and computation, providing a more promising technical route toward bio-inspired and energy-efficient autonomous visual navigation. With the development of neuromorphic processors, researchers have begun to explore neuromorphic robotic systems and have made preliminary progress in perception and control tasks~ vitale2021event,salt2019parameter,paredes2024fully,jiang2025fully . However, due to the still immature hardware and software ecosystem, the lack of structural information in event streams, the limitations of spiking neural networks in efficient representation and end-to-end training, and the limited number of neurons and operators supported by neuromorphic processors, existing studies have largely remained at the level of relatively simple navigation subtasks, for example pose estimation or motion control, etc. A neuromorphic navigation paradigm for MAVs that integrates event-based sensing, spike-based computation, and neuromorphic hardware deployment in real-world complex environments remains an open challenge. In this paper, we present an end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for visual navigation of MAVs in complex environments for the first time. By integrating an event camera, a spiking neural network, and a neuromorphic processor into a closed-loop navigation system, the proposed paradigm mimics biological visual sensing and computation as shown in Fig.~ fig:1 B, providing a system-level pathway toward robust, low-power, and real-time visual navigation for MAVs. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: First, we present the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic visual navigation paradigm for MAVs that has been successfully transferred from simulation to real-world deployment. By integrating neuromorphic sensing, spike-based computation, and neuromorphic hardware deployment, the proposed framework demonstrates the practical feasibility of end-to-end neuromorphic navigation on resource-constrained MAV platforms. Second, we develop an onboard spiking perceptual representation module that converts asynchronous event streams into compact geometric features for MAV navigation. By compensating for the absence of explicit environmental geometric structure in raw event streams, this module provides navigation-relevant structural representations while alleviating the sim-to-real gap induced by rendering discrepancies between simulation and real-world scenes. Third, we propose an end-to-end MAV navigation policy based on spiking neural networks, enabled by efficient guidance learning and population coding. Guidance learning improves policy training efficiency, while population coding supports informative spike-based representations with a small number of time steps. The learned policy is further deployed on a neuromorphic processor, establishing an energy-efficient and real-time navigation system. Results End-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation system The physical implementation of the end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation system is shown in Fig.~ fig:2 . The system consists of an event camera (Prophesee EVK4), a neuromorphic processor (Intel Kapoho Bay), an edge computing platform (NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX), an x86-based host computer, and a micro aerial vehicle. Considering the limited on-chip neuron resources and the limited set of operators supported by Intel Kapoho Bay, we partition the overall spiking neural network into two modules for deployment: a perceptual representation module and a navigation module. Specifically, the spiking neural networks for depth estimation and feature extraction (perceptual representation module) are deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX in the form of simulated SNNs, which generate event-based geometric representations of the environment. The spiking neural network for navigation (navigation module) is deployed on the Intel Kapoho Bay neuromorphic processor, enabling low-power and real-time action generation. title: Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation
summary: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.

However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives. Introduction Reconstructing 3D scenes and synthesizing novel views from multiple 2D captures is a fundamental problem in computer vision and graphics, with broad applications in robotics, autonomous driving, gaming, and virtual reality. The pioneering NeRF~ nerf represents scenes as an implicit radiance field optimized via volume rendering, while subsequent 3DGS~ 3DGS employs differentiable rasterization of anisotropic 3D Gaussians to achieve real-time, high-fidelity rendering. Despite its success, standard 3DGS requires a time-consuming per-scene optimization process. To address this limitation, a growing line of work has explored feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction~ pixelsplat, mvsplat, depthsplat, mvsplat360, freesplat , which trains generalizable models on large-scale datasets to directly predict 3D Gaussians from input views in a single forward pass. Recent advances have further eliminated the dependency on pre-computed camera poses~ noposplat, anysplat, instantsplat , enabling truly end-to-end reconstruction from uncalibrated images. However, current feed-forward approaches adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm in which one Gaussian is predicted for each input pixel. While conceptually straightforward, this design suffers from three key limitations: (1) Redundancy---textureless or homogeneous regions consume as many Gaussians as detail-rich areas, yielding redundant primitives and wasted capacity; (2) Insufficient coverage---poorly observed regions cannot be faithfully reconstructed, since each Gaussian is predicted independently from a single pixel, without leveraging contextual information from well-observed neighbors; and (3) Input dependency---the total Gaussian count is strictly tied to the input resolution and view count rather than to the scene itself, preventing efficient reconstruction. In this work, we present Anchor3DGS, a feed-forward framework that takes uncalibrated multi-view images as input and outputs 3D Gaussians of the scene (see Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Our key insight is that a scene's 3D structure has no intrinsic connection to the number of input views or pixels that happen to observe it. We therefore propose to lift Gaussian allocation into 3D space: we represent the scene with a set of anchors whose spatial distribution is guided by scene content, while the total number of anchors is a hyperparameter, independent of image resolution and view count. Our framework consists of several key components: (i) Entropy-guided anchor sampling. Our 3D anchor sampling strategy simultaneously ensures broad spatial coverage of the scene and adaptively allocates more anchors to regions exhibiting higher visual complexity, as identified by local information entropy. Entropy automatically guides 3D anchors to where they are needed most: few anchors suffice for low-complexity regions (e.g., white walls or sky), while many anchors concentrate on high-complexity regions (e.g., intricate structures or rich textures). (ii) Multi-view anchor aggregation and local decoding. Each 3D anchor aggregates visual features from all input views under occlusion-aware weighting, and is decoded into a small set of neighboring Gaussians that represent its local 3D region. Anchors also exchange information with each other, allowing those in poorly observed regions to leverage the context from well-observed neighbors and still produce plausible appearances. In contrast, pixel-aligned methods often leave visible holes in such regions. (iii) Feature enhancement. Beyond standard attributes, each Gaussian is also assigned a feature vector. These features are later splatted and decoded by a lightweight network, which compensates for the high-frequency details missing from the coarse splatted RGB image. Extensive experiments across benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our method. In sparse-view settings (3 and 6 input views), Anchor3DGS significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines. In dense-view settings ( input views), Anchor3DGS achieves comparable rendering quality while requiring an order of magnitude fewer Gaussians. This demonstrates that a compact anchor-based representation can match the fidelity of pixel-aligned approaches with greater efficiency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose Anchor3DGS, a novel anchor-based feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces the pixel-aligned paradigm with a compact anchor-based representation, decoupling the Gaussian count from input image resolution and the number of input views. We introduce three key designs—entropy-guided anchor sampling, occlusion-aware anchor aggregation and local decoding, and feature enhancement—which together enable high-fidelity novel view synthesis with fine details. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets with substantially fewer Gaussians than existing methods, demonstrating that our method yields a more compact yet equally effective representation. Related Work Per-Scene Novel View Synthesis. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf pioneered novel view synthesis by representing scenes as continuous density and radiance fields, and optimizing them via differentiable volume rendering. Despite subsequent improvements~ ref-nerf, scaffold-gs, mipnerf360, instantngp, nerf++, frnerf , the expensive ray sampling in volume rendering still prevents real-time performance. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3DGS, 3dgs-advances instead represents scenes as explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians and exploits differentiable tile-based rasterization, achieving real-time speed with superior quality. However, both NeRF- and 3DGS-based methods require accurate camera poses, typically from a costly Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipeline such as COLMAP~ colmap . To remove this dependency, several works~ nope-nerf, cf3dgs, longsplat, robustness attempt to jointly optimize the camera poses and the scene representation. Nevertheless, all these methods still rely on tedious per-scene optimization. In contrast, our Anchor3DGS directly predicts camera poses and 3D Gaussians in a feed-forward pass within seconds. Feed-Forward Novel View Synthesis. Feed-forward novel view synthesis avoids per-scene optimization by learning generalizable priors from large-scale datasets. Early works~ pixelnerf, ibrnet, mvsnerf condition the NeRF representation on image features aggregated from input views, enabling cross-scene generalization without per-scene retraining. Following the success of 3DGS, subsequent feed-forward works~ splatter-image, pixelsplat, mvsplat, mvsplat360, depthsplat, freesplat, volsplat, gs-lrm replace NeRF with explicit Gaussian primitives for higher rendering quality and faster speed. As representative examples, pixelSplat~ pixelsplat employs epipolar attention to infer a dense depth probability distribution for predicting 3D Gaussians from image pairs, whereas MVSplat~ mvsplat incorporates multi-view stereo principles by constructing explicit cost volumes for more accurate geometric reconstruction. A recent line of pose-free feed-forward methods~ noposplat, flare, yonosplat, anysplat further eliminates the reliance on known camera parameters. By leveraging robust geometric priors from 3D foundation models~ dust3r, vggt , FLARE~ flare and AnySplat~ anysplat can simultaneously infer the camera poses of input images and the matching geometry-aligned 3D Gaussians. Despite these advances, all aforementioned feed-forward 3DGS methods typically predict Gaussians in a dense, pixel-aligned manner, resulting in massive redundant Gaussians. Although AnySplat~ anysplat applies post-hoc voxelization for Gaussian reduction, this fails to address the root cause, and the remaining Gaussians are still far from compact. Instead, we decouple Gaussian allocation from the pixel-aligned paradigm and model the scene using a compact set of 3D anchors. A few concurrent works~ c3g, tokengs also attempt to explore compact representations using learnable tokens, whereas we explicitly leverage 3D scene structure and visual complexity to guide Gaussian allocation. Method The key idea of our method is to represent the scene with a compact set of 3D anchors, rather than being strictly bound to the input image pixels. Each anchor represents a local 3D region: it is placed on a geometry-aware scene scaffold, gathers information from multiple views, exchanges information with other anchors, and is finally decoded into a set of local Gaussians. In this way, the scene representation is organized directly in 3D space, with its size controlled by the anchor budget. Concretely, given a set of uncalibrated input images , we first build a multi-view geometric scaffold using a VGGT-based pose-free geometry backbone~ vggt , which predicts camera parameters and per-view depth maps . By unprojecting the predicted depth maps with the predicted cameras, we obtain scene points in 3D space, from which we sample a fixed number of anchors guided by local image entropy. Each anchor is then encoded into a latent token through occlusion-aware multi-view feature aggregation and cross-anchor interaction. Finally, each token is decoded into local Gaussian primitives, yielding the final Gaussian set . Fig.~ fig:pipeline illustrates the overall pipeline of Anchor3DGS. Pose-Free Geometry Initialization sec:geometry Before constructing anchors, we first build a geometry-aware 3D scaffold of the scene. The role of this stage is to lift the uncalibrated input images into a consistent geometric space on which anchors can be placed and reasoned about. To this end, we employ a VGGT-based~ vggt backbone model as a strong multi-view geometry prior. Given input images with , the geometry backbone predicts for each view a camera extrinsic , a camera intrinsic , and a depth map . We denote the overall predicted camera parameters by with . Using , we unproject each depth map into a per-view 3D point map , and denote the resulting set of 3D scene points by . This geometric scaffold serves two purposes in our method. First, the scene points in provide a geometry-aware 3D candidate pool for anchor sampling. Second, the predicted camera parameters allow every anchor to be projected back into the input views, which is essential for subsequent multi-view feature aggregation and occlusion reasoning. Based on this geometric scaffold, our final representation is built as a fixed-size set of 3D anchors with features in scene space. title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
summary: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm towards general robotic control brohan2023rt1roboticstransformerrealworld,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel, black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . In the pretraining stage, the field has evolved from VLMs autoregressively generating over discretized action tokens brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer, kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel, pertsch2025fastefficientactiontokenization to more recent flow-matching action experts coupled with pretrained VLMs nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation, black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld , enabling scalable learning from diverse action trajectories. The paradigm shift was foreshadowed by diffusion-based visuomotor policies chi2024diffusionpolicyvisuomotorpolicy , which established iterative denoising as an effective means of learning multi-modal (i.e., multi-peaked) action distributions. However, the stochasticity that benefits learning also introduces a unique challenge at deployment. Given the same observation and instruction, different noise seeds yield samples of different quality during inference. However, the flow-based VLA model cannot distinguish which action chunk is most likely to succeed. During execution, a robot must commit to one sampled action chunk, which may irreversibly change the physical world. A good action chunk advances the task, while a poor one could directly lead to failure or accumulate errors that drift the trajectory out of distribution ross2011reductionimitationlearningstructured, liu2026streampi, lu2026faster . We empirically show that the policy variance is non-uniform along the task, and failures tend to happen in high-variance segments of the action trajectory, as in Figure~ fig:intuition (a). What if we could detect these critical moments before committing to an irreversible action, and briefly ``rewind'' the decision by spending additional computation? This calls for two components: a trigger that decides when the states are critical and additional computation is worthwhile, and a verifier that determines which sampled action should be executed. To answer the first question, we start with the policy's uncertainty. As shown in (a), when the end-effector is close to a contact-rich interaction region, the trajectory follows a more complex motion pang2023globalplanningcontactrichmanipulation , and internally, the policy uncertainty increases. We therefore combine temporal action variation and cross-sample uncertainty into a training-free two-axis trigger. Computed with two sampled action chunks, the trigger closely tracks the contact information from the environment and aligns well with the policy's intrinsic uncertainty, as shown in (b). We therefore use the trigger to activate repeated sampling and verification at critical decision steps. Once repeated sampling is activated, the second question arises: how should candidate actions be evaluated? We argue that latent world models are a natural fit. The verifier evaluates the quality of action chunk samples by predicting the progress or relative ranking kwok2025robomonkeyscalingtesttimesampling, fan2026dreamavoidcriticalphasetesttimedreaming . Therefore, the model must understand world dynamics and represent the future states resulting from executing the action chunk. In addition, verification is a low-dimensional problem: how much an action chunk advances the task is a scalar judgment, and most camera pixels are irrelevant to it. As a result, pixel-level world models have two pitfalls: (1) the image or video generation incurs substantial latency, making it difficult to deploy at real-time control frequencies; and (2) they solve the harder pixel generation before the easier progress estimation, making the quality of downstream verification unnecessarily dependent on generation fidelity. We compare these paradigms in . This motivates verification in a latent space, which compresses the pixel observation into compact and dynamic-rich features, where we can jointly predict the latent states and task progress. Building on these observations, we recast action randomness not as a hazard to be suppressed but as a resource to select from, with the latent world model as a verifier. Specifically, we claim the following contributions: A latent world model as a verifier. We exploit the action-conditioned latent representation produced by a pretrained latent world model to estimate the progress of candidate action chunks. An empirical characterization of policy stochasticity in flow-based VLAs and the two-axis trigger. We characterize policy stochasticity. Leveraging the temporal action variation and the cross-sampling variance, we propose a two-axis trigger that is action-based and training-free. It detects the critical states and reduces inference costs while preserving the benefits of test-time selection. A simple training, evaluation, and real-robot deployment pipeline. On real-world manipulation tasks, each triggered round of repeated sampling and verification adds 326 ms of latency. Our method improves the average completion score by 14.7 percentage points over the base policy, outperforming baselines, including VLM-based verifiers and pixel-level world model verifiers. Related Work Test-time Enhancement for VLAs. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized according to whether the VLA policy is updated at deployment time. Test-time training methods, such as EVOLVE-VLA bai2025evolvevlatesttimetrainingenvironment and TT-VLA liu2026ontheflyvlaadaptationtesttime , perform online policy optimization during deployment using dense reward signals. Rather than relying on external reward estimation, T VLA chen2026trustinstinctsconfidencedriventesttime derives intrinsic rewards from the policy's own confidence to enable self-supervised adaptation. Another line of work keeps the pretrained VLA policy frozen and improves action quality through either gradient-free selection or gradient-based augmentation. Gradient-free methods xu2026vgasvalueguidedactionchunkselection generally adopt a repeated-sampling-and-selection strategy where a model-based verifier evaluates candidate actions. RoboMonkey kwok2025robomonkeyscalingtesttimesampling uses a VLM-based verifier to select the optimal action, demonstrating a test-time scaling law of autoregressive VLAs. GPC-RANK qi2026inferencetimeenhancementgenerativerobot employs a lightweight pixel-generation model with a downstream estimator to rank candidate actions. DreamAvoid fan2026dreamavoidcriticalphasetesttimedreaming combines a pretrained foundation-level, action-conditioned video generation model with an estimator and introduces a vision-based trigger to reduce computational overhead. In contrast, gradient-based methods such as Guided Action Flow yang2026guidedactionflowqguided backpropagate gradients from the verifier score to refine sampled actions. In this work, we follow the repeated-sampling-and-selection paradigm. Unlike prior verifier-based methods, which rely on VLMs or pixel-level world models followed by downstream signal extraction, our approach uses a latent world model to jointly predict dynamics and estimate task-specific progress, synergizing with an action-based trigger to allocate computation adaptively. We compare more test-time verification methods in Appendix~ appendix:related_work . Latent World Models for Robotics. Building on advances in visual representation learning, prior research on latent world models has developed along two main directions. The first line of work sobal2025learningrewardfreeofflinedata,maes2026leworldmodelstableendtoendjointembedding,zhang2026hierarchicalplanninglatentworld , represented by DINO-WM zhou2025dinowmworldmodelspretrained , V-JEPA 2-AC assran2025vjepa2selfsupervisedvideo and H-JEPA zhang2026hjepaendtoendlearninghierarchical utilizes pretrained visual encoders and trains dynamics predictors to perform zero-shot planning in latent space. Given a goal image, these methods employ search-based algorithms to identify suitable action proposals. The second direction combines latent world models with VLAs. VLA-JEPA sun2026vlajepaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodel , Being-H0.7 luo2026beingh07latentworldactionmodel and Copper-Policy feng2026copperpolicyfocusrepresentationrobust incorporate the prediction objective of latent world models into VLA training, while LaWAM chen2026lawamlatentworldaction introduces a latent subgoal as an additional conditioning signal. These integrated approaches improve overall manipulation performance and generalization. Recent VLAs commonly employ flow-matching-based action generation intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld , which takes random Gaussian noise as input. This noise dependence is typically omitted from the policy notation. We make this dependence explicit: where denotes the random seed used to generate the Gaussian noise, with a distinct seed for each sampling index . Repeated sampling therefore produces a set of diverse action chunks . Executing an action chunk changes task progress; therefore we define the quality of an action chunk as its change in progress, referred to as delta progress, where is the task progress at timestep . Compared with absolute progress, delta progress matches the effect of the action chunk, making it a more direct and intuitive target for action evaluation chen2025robotwin20scalabledata . title: CBF-Based Control Allocation for Omnidirectional Tiltrotor Aerial Robots
summary: Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve. Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs. A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%. These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.
