Introduction mnidirectional aerial robots can regulate position and attitude independently, enabling contact inspection, tool alignment, and six-dimensional physical interaction~ ollero2022,bodie2021,ryll2019 . Fixed tilted-rotor designs obtain this capability through their geometry~ brescianini2016,park2018 , whereas actively tilting platforms can reorient their thrust directions during flight~ ryll2015,allenspach2020 . In the latter case, control allocation must coordinate fast thrust changes with slower servo motion. Servo transients can make a desired wrench infeasible even when the target pose is kinematically admissible. A force and moment achievable after reorientation may lie outside the thrust-limited set at the current tilt angles. Aggressive motion therefore requires an allocator that preserves wrench authority while both the request and the actuation geometry evolve. Wrench tracking and instantaneous feasibility are distinct objectives. Tracking reduces the difference between the desired and generated wrench; feasibility requires an admissible thrust vector at the current rotor directions. Servo motion changes the attainable wrench set. We constrain that motion to retain the requested wrench together with a neighborhood accounting for nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch. Geometric and differential allocators provide direct actuator setpoints, coordinated reconfiguration, and limit handling~ bodie2020,allenspach2020,johansen2013 . Augmented and normalized differential allocation further connect wrench controllers to actuator-rate commands and account for heterogeneous limits~ cuniato2026 . The remaining question addressed here is how to constrain servo reconfiguration so that a specified wrench request remains inside the instantaneous thrust-limited set despite configuration mismatch. Control barrier functions (CBFs) express this objective as constraints on servo motion~ ames2017,ames2019 . For a nonsingular six-channel configuration, inverse allocation gives six lower and six upper thrust margins. An ellipsoidal wrench reserve tightens them against nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch. Their complete derivatives, including the changing reserve, define a servo-rate quadratic program (QP); a downstream differential allocator commands thrust rates for tracking. The contributions are threefold: An exact nominal-to-actual required-thrust identity and a support-based reduction of configuration-robust wrench containment to twelve scalar margins. An explicit servo-rate CBF-QP and a conditional invariance proof connecting nominal margins to desired-wrench feasibility at the actual servo angles, without assuming identical commanded and actual servo velocities. A telemetry-based comparison of a measured-angle CBF variant with geometric allocation (GA), augmented differential allocation (ADA), and normalized differential allocation (NDA) across four scenarios. Recorded force-space views and six-dimensional margins relate tracking performance to instantaneous wrench feasibility. The guarantee concerns existence of an admissible thrust vector; thrust realization and pose tracking also depend on actuator and closed-loop dynamics. Sections~ sec:model -- sec:baselines establish the model and baseline allocators. Sections~ sec:proposed -- sec:guarantee develop the CBF formulation and guarantee. Sections~ sec:simulation -- sec:conclusion present the simulation comparison, design implications, and conclusions. Related Work Actuation Geometry and Dynamic Allocation The attainable wrench set depends on both vehicle design and rotor orientation. Offline tilt optimization improves task-dependent authority~ rajappa2015 , synchronized mechanisms change the flight configuration~ ryll2022 , and independently tilting platforms permit online redistribution of actuator effort~ ryll2015,allenspach2020 . These architectures offer different allocation freedoms. Here, six independently controlled thrust magnitudes form a square wrench map when the six tilt angles are fixed. Constrained allocation has a substantial history. Active-set methods handle bounded least squares~ harkegard2002 , dynamic QPs shape actuator transients~ harkegard2004 , and null-space methods enforce hard joint limits~ flacco2015 . Dual-layer allocation can also modify the requested virtual control when actuator constraints prevent its realization~ yan2021 . A recent predictive allocator accounts for asymmetric motor dynamics by optimizing null-space motion over a horizon~ pretto2026 . Our method instead constrains the servo motion to preserve a specified neighborhood of the desired wrench inside the attainable set. For the quantitative comparison, we use geometric allocation (GA), augmented differential allocation (ADA), and normalized differential allocation (NDA). Section~ sec:baselines gives their essential equations and the differential-allocation (DA) foundation. Power differential allocation (PDA) additionally uses speed-dependent propeller-acceleration envelopes~ cuniato2026 . A calibrated envelope is unavailable for the present propulsion model, so PDA is excluded from this benchmark. A differential allocator uses twelve effective actuator coordinates because servo motion and propeller acceleration both contribute to wrench rate. Instantaneous feasibility instead concerns the six thrust channels at fixed angles. A direction available through coordinated motion may therefore be unavailable through thrust changes alone. The proposed barrier constrains this fixed-configuration set while retaining a differential tracking stage. Barrier Functions and Actuator Feasibility CBFs translate set invariance into control inequalities~ ames2017,ames2019 . Robust, input-to-state-safe, and measurement-robust formulations address uncertainty in the dynamics, actuation, and state information~ xu2015,kolathaya2019,cosner2021 . Integral and high-order CBFs accommodate dynamically extended inputs and higher-relative-degree constraints~ ames2021,xiao2022 . Safety layers have also been studied for aerial physical interaction~ cuniato2022 and reaction-wheel allocation~ yang2025 . Readiness barriers preserve a lower bound on motor wrench-rate authority through a torque-level allocation QP~ silano2026 . More directly, Silano and Saska~ silanosaska2026 use active tilt to preserve a motor-only wrench-rate readiness metric, enforced through motor torques and servo setpoints. Their certificate concerns a lower bound on the log-volume of an attainable wrench-rate approximation. Our constraint follows a specified wrench request: the request and its uncertainty neighborhood must fit inside the instantaneous thrust-limited wrench set. The square inverse map makes this containment test exact, and the equivalent-wrench identity transfers nominal margins to actual-angle feasibility. The distinction is the certified quantity: a desired-wrench neighborhood in the thrust-limited set, rather than a volume measure of motor wrench-rate authority. The certificate is continuous time and conditional on admissible CBF inputs. Sampled-data and delayed-input formulations~ breeden2022,singletary2020 address implementation effects, while command governors and predictive safety filters~ garone2017,wabersich2021 can modify a request that exceeds the available authority. These are complementary extensions to the allocation-level result established here. The present certificate concerns allocation feasibility; outer-loop stability and task-level safety remain separate properties. title: Edit4D: Editable 4D Scene Generation with Textual Control
summary: We introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D scene generation framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background and dynamic character representations. Recent advances in generative models have enabled text-driven dynamic scene synthesis, but editable 4D scene generation remains challenging due to the need to preserve spatial geometry and temporal dynamics. Existing approaches typically generate holistic scene videos, where the background and dynamic characters are coupled, making object-level editing and flexible camera control difficult. Edit4D addresses these limitations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and scene-character composition. Using these prompts, we synthesize multi-view scene images with text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors and reconstruct a background 3D Gaussian splatting representation. We then generate a character image, animate it with an image-conditioned video prior, reconstruct a 4D mesh, and bind Gaussian primitives to obtain a character representation. Finally, both components are composed through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. A global scene refinement is then performed to improve harmonization and rendering consistency. By integrating stage-specific components, Edit4D enables controllable camera motion, flexible object-level editing, and the practical construction of editable 4D scenes. Project page: https://chanwo0kim.github.io/Edit4D/

Project page: Introduction sec:intro Advances in large-scale text-to-image models such as DALL-E~ DALL-E and Stable Diffusion~ LDM have rapidly accelerated visual content generation. This progress is especially evident in video generation, where models such as Sora~ liu2024sora and Veo~ GoogleDeepMind2025Veo3 demonstrate strong photorealism, temporal coherence, and scene complexity. Building on these advances, recent research has shifted toward 3D and 4D content creation. In particular, 4D generation aims to capture both spatial structure and temporal evolution, requiring multi-view consistency, temporal coherence, and stable 3D geometry. Despite progress in diffusion models, general 4D scene generation remains challenging and has yet to reach the level required for widespread commercial use. Existing text-to-4D methods can be broadly divided into object-level and scene-level approaches. Object-level methods~ bahmani20244dfy, zheng2024unified often produce multi-view consistent dynamic subjects by focusing on a single foreground object, but they do not generate complete scenes with backgrounds. Scene-level methods~ yu20244real,liu2025free4d synthesize complete dynamic scenes as a single holistic representation, making object-level editing difficult. Moreover, because geometry is reconstructed from a limited set of generated viewpoints, rendering quality often degrades under novel-view changes. These challenges are further amplified by the scarcity of large-scale dynamic-scene datasets, which forces many methods to rely on distillation from image or video generative priors. Although such priors provide useful supervision, the resulting 4D content remains constrained by their quality and failure modes. Furthermore, when artifacts appear in the generated content, even localized errors require regenerating the entire sequence, making correction costly and prone to inconsistencies with the original output. In real production workflows, where expert-driven refinement is often necessary, this lack of editability becomes a significant limitation. These observations suggest that constructing 4D scenes as composable assets, rather than as a single monolithic video, offers a more flexible alternative. Asset-based generation naturally aligns with graphics workflows, allowing creators to manipulate and replace scene components with greater control. However, editable 4D scene construction remains underexplored, as existing pipelines often couple backgrounds with dynamic elements and make independent editing difficult. To address these limitations, we introduce Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes from separate background scene and dynamic character representations. Given a user instruction, Edit4D first decomposes it into stage-specific prompts for background, dynamic character, and composition. We then generate the 4D scene through parallel background scene and dynamic character generation, followed by scene--character composition. The background scene is reconstructed as a 3D Gaussian representation from multi-view images synthesized using text-to-image and camera-conditioned generative priors. For the dynamic character, we generate a reference video by animating a character image, reconstructing a temporally consistent 4D mesh, and binding Gaussian primitives to obtain a dynamic character representation. The composition stage localizes the target placement region with text-guided masks and optimizes the character pose using contact-aware constraints. We further perform a global scene refinement to improve appearance consistency and rendering details. Extensive experiments show that Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent 4D generation methods, while additionally supporting controllable camera motion. We illustrate the overview of our method in Fig.~ fig:teaser . We summarize our contributions as follows: We propose Edit4D, an editable text-to-4D framework that constructs 4D scenes by composing separate background and dynamic character representations through a stage-specific generation pipeline. This component-wise design enables independent editing, flexible control, and scene recomposition within a unified 4D space. We introduce a text-guided composition method that automatically places a dynamic character into a background scene. Our method localizes target region from text and optimizes character position with contact and penetration constraints, reducing the need for manual placement. Edit4D achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with recent 4D generation methods while preserving high perceptual quality. Beyond generation quality, it supports camera control and fine-grained object-level editing. Related Works sec:related 3D and 4D Scene Generation Text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly with the development of large-scale generative models. Score distillation sampling (SDS)-based methods~ poole2022dreamfusion, wang2023prolificdreamer, chen2023fantasia3d, liang2024luciddreamer, zhuo2024vividdreamer, lin2023magic3d synthesize 3D content by aligning rendered views with text-conditioned diffusion priors, but they are computationally expensive and often suffer from view-dependent artifacts and the Janus problem. Recent multi-view guided methods address these limitations by generating geometrically consistent views and then lifting them into 3D representations. Text-conditioned~ li2024instant3d, shi2023mvdream, li2024dual3d, huang2025mv and image-conditioned~ voleti2024sv3d, liu2023one, liu2024one, liu2024syncdreamer, yang2024hunyuan3d approaches follow this paradigm to improve visual fidelity and efficiency. More recently, data-driven models~ zhao2025hunyuan3d, wu2024direct3d, tang2024lgm trained on large-scale 3D datasets generate 3D from text or image inputs. Building on these advances, recent text- or video-to-4D methods~ pan2024efficient4d, ren2023dreamgaussian4d, ren2024l4gm, singer2023text, sun2024eg4d, yin20234dgen, zheng2024unified, bahmani20244dfy, yu20244real, liu2025free4d synthesize dynamic 3D content using diffusion guidance, multi-view generation, or SDS-based optimization. Object-level methods such as 4Dfy~ bahmani20244dfy and Dream-in-4D~ zheng2024unified can produce temporally coherent and multi-view consistent dynamic objects. Scene-level methods such as 4Real~ yu20244real and Free4D~ liu2025free4d instead generate complete dynamic scenes, improving photorealism or temporal consistency through video-conditioned reconstruction or point-guided denoising. However, these methods typically perform holistic 4D synthesis, making it difficult to isolate and control individual scene components after generation. In contrast, Edit4D constructs 4D scenes from separate representations, enabling fine-grained modification while preserving spatio-temporal coherence. Scene Representation Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2021nerf established a foundation for neural 3D scene representations through volumetric rendering. Although NeRF achieves high visual fidelity, its slow rendering speed motivated more efficient variants such as Instant-NGP~ mueller2022instant and HexPlane~ cao2023hexplane , which leverage hash-based or tensor-decomposed encodings. More recently, Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d introduced a rasterization-based representation using Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rendering with high visual quality. This line of work has been extended to dynamic 4D representations, including NeRFPlayer~ song2023nerfplayer , 4D-GS~ wu20244d , and Grid4D~ xu2024grid4d , which jointly model spatial structure and temporal motion. However, accurately recovering geometry remains challenging when optimization relies mainly on photometric supervision. Recent methods such as SuGaR~ guedon2024sugar and 2D Gaussian~ Huang2DGS2024 redesign Gaussian primitives to align with underlying surfaces, while structure-guided frameworks like GaussianAvatar~ moon2024gaussianavatar, hu2024gaussianavatar and Mani-GS~ gao2025mani attach the Gaussians to deformable meshes for stable geometry. Scene Composition With recent advances in segmentation foundation models~ kirillov2023segment, zhang2024evf , mask-based composition methods in 3D neural scenes have been actively studied. By leveraging 2D masks from segmentation or text-to-mask models, prior methods localize editable regions for object removal and inpainting, ensuring reliable composition~ bartrum2024replaceanything3d, ye2024gaussian, shahbazi2024inserf . More closely related to our work, human-scene placement methods aim to place human in 3D scene with physically plausible contact while reducing interpenetration artifacts. PROX~ Hassan_2019_ICCV fits SMPL-X~ SMPL-X:2019 bodies to scenes using contact and penetration constraints, and POSA~ hassan2021populating learns a body-centric contact representation for plausible placements. Furthermore, COINS~ Zhao:ECCV:2022 and Narrator~ xuan2023narrator refine using contact optimization to encourage natural human-scene contact. However, these methods typically assume reconstructed real scenes, supervised interaction data, or manually prepared assets. In contrast, Edit4D performs text-driven scene--character composition, allowing dynamic characters to be automatically placed into generated background scenes through text-guided segmentation and contact-aware optimization. Method We propose Edit4D, a unified framework for generating editable 4D scenes from textual descriptions. As shown in Fig.~ fig:method , our framework composes independently generated background scenes and dynamic characters into a unified 4D representation, enabling object-level editing and recomposition. We first describe our editable 4D scene representation based on Gaussian splatting. title: Onboard Lightweight LLM Reasoning for Human-Aware Safe UAV Navigation
summary: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.

Introduction sec:introduction UAVs are increasingly deployed for delivery, inspection, and monitoring in environments shared with people~ saunders2024autonomous, aela2024uav, fang2024strategies . Such environments are not only dynamic but semantically heterogeneous: a pedestrian, a moving truck, a parked car, and a hedge all constrain the feasible trajectory, yet they imply very different risk and should not receive identical avoidance behavior. Conventional pipelines optimize trajectories well when the environment is accurately modeled~ Hanover2021PerformancePAA, liu2017ral , but they treat obstacles as geometry: occupancy maps and detections say where an object is, not how it should modify clearance, priority, or motion response~ 10802806 . We call the resulting deficiency the human-aware safety gap: a geometric planner assigns a person and a lamp post the same clearance, and its map carries no notion of who or what is being avoided. Human-aware planning should instead maintain larger, category-dependent clearance around people and preserve short-term awareness of them through temporary occlusions. Our goal is therefore not to model people merely as dynamic obstacles, but to preserve category-specific safety semantics when planning around them: closing the gap means producing context-dependent safety constraints---clearance, dynamism, and persistence that depend on the object's category and the operating context---and delivering them to the planner in real time, onboard. Large language models (LLMs) offer the abstraction needed to produce such constraints~ li2025large, Yue2025ASOA , and LLM-based monitoring and planning has begun to appear in robotics~ sinha2024real, wu2024hierarchical, wang2025contact . Sinha et al.~ sinha2024real pair a fast embedding classifier with a slow generative fallback, but the vehicle must wait while the large model reasons; contact-aware planners~ wang2025contact model interaction physics rather than grounding live observations. Prior landing methods~ niu2021vision, zhang2023coni focus on cooperative targets and typically assume obstacle-free landing zones. We ask instead: Three system-level obstacles stand in the way. (i) LLMs cannot consume raw imagery or 3D geometry, and end-to-end vision-language models (VLMs) are too heavy for Size, Weight and Power (SWaP)-limited platforms~ bai2025qwen25vltechnicalreport ; we therefore decouple a light vision-language encoder (VLE)~ li2022blip from a text-only LLM and ground its output with depth. (ii) Lightweight LLMs that fit onboard hallucinate~ Sun2025OnionEvalAUA ; we stabilize them with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)~ Lewis2020RetrievalAugmentedGFA over a safety knowledge base and constrain decoding to a JSON grammar. (iii) Semantic guidance must not break real-time control; the LLM never commands the vehicle but adjusts planner-level constraints (unsafe regions and margins) consumed by a model-based planner and controller. A fourth obstacle emerged only after closed-loop deployment among pedestrians: with a 2\,s map decay, a brief occlusion removes a person's constraint from the map before they reappear, so the pipeline needs object persistence in addition to semantics. This paper contributes: (1) a semantic-to-spatial grounding pipeline that turns RGB-D observations into obstacle-specific risk and 3D safety constraints; (2) a RAG-stabilized, grammar-constrained lightweight LLM reasoning module, whose per-class verdicts are cached so that the LLM reasons once per category rather than per frame, with a cache-miss reasoning pathway for categories outside a fixed semantic policy; (3) persistent obstacle identities with occlusion-aware holding in the planner map; and (4) an onboard feasibility study on Jetson-class hardware together with closed-loop Gazebo experiments in urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles and in autonomous landing, with an analysis of perception under the limited input resolution that onboard compute imposes. Method sec:methodology Fig.~ fig:TopOverview shows the three subsystems. Perception converts RGB-D frames into semantic and spatial primitives; Reasoning maps them to obstacle-specific safety parameters; Action keeps a persistent obstacle set and injects it into a model-based planner. Perception: Shared VLE, Segmentation, and 3D Grounding sec:scene-understanding A single frozen BLIP ViT-B/16 encoder~ li2022blip ( 86M parameters) serves two heads, avoiding redundant visual computation onboard. The captioning branch is BLIP's original decoder and yields a short zero-shot scene description ( tokens) that identifies potential hazards. The segmentation head is a lightweight decoder we train on top of the encoder: multi-scale features from layers , , and are projected to a common width with convolutions and fused via skip connections~ ronneberger2015u ; a text prompt (e.g., ``person'', ``car'') conditions the fused map through FiLM~ perez2018film , before four resize-convolution up-blocks (bilinear upsampling followed by a convolution, which avoids checkerboard artifacts~ odena2016deconvolution ) produce the mask . Each connected component of that exceeds an area threshold is back-projected through the time-aligned depth map with intrinsics , after rejecting depths more than from the in-mask median. The result is a list of tuples at 10\,Hz. Reasoning: From Semantics to Safety Parameters sec:semantic-reasoning LLM-populated verdict cache. The LLM does not run per frame; it runs per class. The first time a class label appears, its name and the scene caption are sent through retrieval and the LLM, which returns a semantic verdict ; the verdict is stored in a per-class cache and reused for every later detection of that class at no inference cost. The cache is therefore not a hand-written lookup table but the accumulated output of the reasoning module: it is warm-started with the verdicts the same RAG--LLM path produced for the categories the segmentation head is prompted with (person, car, truck), and it grows whenever a new label is encountered. This mechanism is designed to extend the pipeline beyond a fixed semantic policy: labels absent from the cache can trigger retrieval-grounded reasoning and subsequently be handled like cached categories. In our 20-run urban benchmark, however, every observed label hit the warm cache, so no online LLM query was issued after initialization; the landing ablation in Sec. IV-B isolates the contribution of the reasoning path itself. In our 20-run urban benchmark every label hit the warm cache, so no online LLM query was issued after initialization; the landing ablation in Sec.~ sec:landing isolates the contribution of the reasoning path itself. Because a novel object can appear at any moment, the full stack is loaded at start-up rather than lazily, and a verdict that fails grammar validation falls back to a conservative default box rather than discarding the object. Hybrid retrieval. For an unknown class, the caption and class name query a local safety knowledge base (KB) with a hybrid search: dense retrieval (bge-small-en-v1.5, \,MB) captures synonyms (``pedestrian'' ``person''), while sparse BM25 anchors high-priority keywords (``truck''). Scores are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion~ cormack2009reciprocal , , , and only the top- segments enter the prompt to avoid attention dilution in small models~ fang2025attentionrag . Edge inference and grammar-constrained output. Reasoning runs Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct on llama.cpp with importance-matrix 4-bit quantization~ frantar2022gptq and a statically allocated KV cache for constant memory and predictable latency. A GBNF grammar restricts decoding to the expected \ "is dynamic": yes|no, "bbox size": float\ schema, which substantially reduces malformed generations and removes the need for a separate free-form parsing stage. Following Code as Policies~ liang2022code , the LLM is deliberately restricted to semantic risk (dynamic or not, how much clearance) and does not produce waypoints: small models are poor at Euclidean arithmetic~ bubeck2023sparks , and encoding dense geometry into the prompt inflates context and degrades reasoning~ liu2024lost . Action: Persistent Obstacles and Planner Constraints sec:action Persistent identity and occlusion hold. A per-frame detection list is not enough for planning near people: temporary occlusions (e.g., a pedestrian passing behind a parked vehicle) create gaps in detections, and with a fixed voxel decay the corresponding constraint leaves the map within seconds, motivating short-term persistence in the planner map. We assign each detection a stable object id by greedy nearest-neighbor association within its class (gate \,m, time-to-live \,s) and publish the semantic box together with that id. The planner map keeps, per id, the last-seen time and last known box; an object whose age is below a hold time (3\,s) stays in the map at its last position, and only afterwards are its voxels released. Holding in place rather than extrapolating is deliberate for pedestrians, whose heading is not persistent; vehicles can be extrapolated with a tracked velocity when available. Human awareness thus enters the planner through differentiated clearance and persistence policies rather than by treating people as generic occupied space. Ids also expose a metric we use in Sec.~ sec:results : how many objects are carried across detection gaps. Unsafe regions in the planner. Every dynamic object yields an axis-aligned box of side bbox size around ; the unsafe set is . The planner interface is intentionally minimal so that the back end can be swapped. title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling policies to predict low-level actions conditioned on natural-language tasks and visual observations~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,team2025gemini,cai2026xiaomi . By leveraging large-scale pretraining and large vision-language backbones, VLAs demonstrate strong generalization across objects, scenes, and task specifications, making them increasingly attractive for deployment in versatile manipulation systems. Despite their impressive capabilities, deploying these models in closed-loop control is often limited by inference efficiency~ chi2025diffusion . At every control step, high-resolution (e.g., 224 224) and frequently multi-view observations are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens~ kim2025fine,intelligence2025pi_ that dominate the compute and latency of the vision-language-model (VLM) backbone during action prediction, far outweighing the few text tokens of a short task. Yet not all visual tokens contribute equally to action prediction. In a typical manipulation step, only a small subset of tokens carries decision-critical information (e.g., the target object/place or the gripper--object contact region), while the rest are redundant or even distracting~ xu2025vla,yang2025efficientvla,jiang2025better . Reducing the number of visual tokens processed by the large-language-model (LLM) backbone, without sacrificing task performance, has therefore become a key direction for accelerating VLA inference~ pei2025action,tan2025think,wang2025specprune . However, directly applying VLM-specific token compression methods~ bolya2022token,chen2024image,zhang2024sparsevlm to robotic control is often suboptimal, because these methods are designed for single-shot vision-language understanding, where the objective is to preserve global semantic content for perception tasks such as detection, captioning, or generation. Unlike image-based VLMs that process a single image, or video-based VLMs that encode a fixed sequence of frames, a VLA interacts with the environment through actions that directly shape its subsequent observations: at each step the agent receives a new observation conditioned on its previous action and predicts the next one. Visual tokens are thus not representations of a static scene but components of a sequential decision process, which sets token compression for VLA apart from its VLM counterpart in two respects. The first is that token relevance is governed by the task rather than by generic visual saliency (now standard practice in language-guided pruning), which we adopt as our importance signal rather than claim as a contribution. The second, and the focus of this work, is that the amount of decision-critical visual information varies drastically across control steps: some steps (e.g., target localization) rely on broad scene context, whereas others (e.g., grasping or contact) depend on a small, localized region. A single fixed compression rate is therefore inherently mismatched, wasting computation when the useful information is concentrated, and discarding necessary context when broader information is required. Motivated by this, we propose FastVLA, a training-free visual token compression framework for efficient VLA inference whose core is a temporally adaptive, per-step compression rate. At each step, FastVLA scores visual-token importance with task-to-vision attention which is a training-free signal that a controlled comparison shows is more reliable for action prediction than vision-only or fused attention and then, crucially, decides how many tokens to keep from the shape of the resulting importance distribution. Specifically, it estimates the effective number of tokens the decision depends on via an inverse-Simpson uniformity measure, and maps this quantity through an online sliding-window calibration to a timestep-dependent compression rate: when the current step concentrates on few tokens relative to its recent history it prunes aggressively, and when the decision draws on broader context it prunes conservatively. By allocating the token budget where each decision needs it, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone computation, speeds up action prediction, and improves closed-loop responsiveness, without caches or training. We evaluate FastVLA on three open-source VLA models including OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , and CogACT~ li2024cogact , across the widely used LIBERO~ liu2023libero and SIMPLER~ li24simpler benchmarks, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59 and action latency by 9-32 (up to a speedup) while maintaining task success, yielding a comparable or even better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing training-free compression, pruning, and reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20 ( speedup) and raises the control frequency by up to 25 at comparable success. In summary, our contributions are: We propose FastVLA, a training-free, plug-and-play visual token compression framework that accelerates closed-loop VLA inference. We design a step-adaptive compression policy that sets a timestep-dependent token budget from the inverse-Simpson uniformity of the importance distribution under online sliding-window calibration. We validate FastVLA on OpenVLA/OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO), CogACT (SIMPLER), and a physical Franka Research 3 robot, achieving substantial compute and latency reductions in simulation and a real-robot speedup with comparable task success. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Manipulation Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a general-purpose paradigm for robot manipulation, predicting actions directly from natural-language tasks and visual observations and generalizing across objects, scenes, and task specifications. Early work such as SayCan~ ahn2022can combines language-conditioned planning with learned low-level skills, while RT-1~ brohan2022rt and RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt scale language-conditioned visuomotor learning with large robot datasets and web-scale vision-language pretraining. In parallel, PaLM-E~ driess2023palm and Octo~ team2024octo highlight the benefits of large pretrained representations across tasks and embodiments. More recently, foundation VLA models including OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , CogACT~ li2024cogact , and ~ black2024pi_0 / ~ intelligence2025pi_ demonstrate strong robustness and open-world generalization via heterogeneous multi-robot data and transformer backbones. Despite their capabilities, these models are typically billion-scale and rely on high-resolution (often multi-view) observations that are encoded into long visual-token sequences and processed by large transformers at every control step. This incurs substantial computation and end-to-end latency in closed-loop control, motivating inference-time methods that reduce redundant visual tokens while preserving task-critical information. Visual Token Compression for Efficient VLA Inference Because most VLA models~ kim2024openvla,kim2025fine,li2024cogact,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_ adopt VLM-style architectures, training-free token compressors built for VLMs are broadly applicable: they prune or merge visual tokens by token similarity (ToMe~ bolya2022token ), shallow-layer or cross-modal attention (FastV~ chen2024image , SparseVLM~ zhang2024sparsevlm , VisPruner~ zhang2025beyond ), or token diversity (DivPrune~ alvar2025divprune ). However, these methods are designed for single-image inference and apply a static pruning policy, so transferring them directly to VLA often degrades control performance. Recent work therefore targets VLA inference along three lines: reuse- and cache-based methods that exploit cross-step temporal redundancy (VLA-Cache~ xu2025vla , FlashVLA~ tan2025think ); importance-estimation methods that add task-, phase-, or motion-aware cues (SpecPrune-VLA~ wang2025specprune , ADP~ pei2025action , VLA-Pruner~ liu2025vla ); and hybrid or learned schemes that go beyond pruning (EfficientVLA~ yang2025efficientvla , LightVLA~ jiang2025better ). These methods still share limitations that FastVLA overcomes. Reuse and caching introduce cross-step state and cache-management overhead, so wall-clock gains can lag FLOP reductions; learned schemes such as LightVLA require training and are tied to a specific backbone, although at equal success they can reach a better compute–latency point than training-free methods. In addition, some VLM/VLA compression algorithms commit to a fixed compression ratio, adapting (if at all) only through auxiliary external signals such as end-effector motion. FastVLA differs on three axes: it is training-free, pruning independently at each step without caches; it conditions token importance on the language task; and, crucially, it makes the compression rate itself adaptive, reading the per-step concentration of task-relevant evidence via an inverse-Simpson uniformity signal calibrated against a short temporal window, spending tokens where the decision needs them and pruning harder where it does not. Method We propose FastVLA, a temporally adaptive and training-free visual token compression method that reduces the number of visual tokens processed by the VLA model's LLM backbone (Fig.~ fig:framework ). FastVLA proceeds in two stages: it first scores visual-token importance with a task-conditioned attention signal, and then, as our core contribution, sets how many tokens to keep adaptively at each step from the concentration of that importance distribution. We present both stages below. Preliminary: Visual Token Compression in VLA Models Methods that reduce the visual-token cost of a VLA backbone fall into three families that differ in what they do to the token sequence. Token pruning permanently discards a subset of visual tokens at one or more layers, shortening the sequence processed by the subsequent layers; the removed tokens are not recovered. Token merging instead aggregates similar tokens into a smaller set of representative tokens, preserving part of the discarded information through pooling rather than hard deletion. Reuse/caching exploits temporal redundancy across control steps: token representations or key-value states computed at previous timesteps are cached and reused for regions that remain unch

title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
summary: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
full_text: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision--language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision--language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: github.com/kyutai-labs/reki . Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become an effective paradigm for language-conditioned robot control. A pretrained vision--language model (VLM) encodes camera views and instruction, based on which a smaller action expert predicts the next actions~ black2024pi0, intelligence2025pi05, nvidia2025gr00tn1,shukor2025smolvla, yuan2026qwenrobot, ma2026internvla . The strongest VLAs today are pretrained partly on proprietary data, and neither these data nor the pretraining pipelines are released~ intelligence2025pi05, yuan2026qwenrobot , making it hard to reproduce their results. Since each new model changes architecture, data and training recipe at once, gains cannot be traced back to a single choice. With REKI, we release the full pipeline, from data curation to deployment. REKI has a simple design, is pretrained on public data only and sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size. It pairs a VLM with a flow-matching action expert, and a memory mechanism gives the policy access to its recent past. Preserving past context can improve control~ octo, liu2025rdt1b, chi2025diffusion , yet most VLAs predict actions from the current observation alone~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, intelligence2025pi05, nvidia2025gr00tn1, shukor2025smolvla, molmoact, spatialvla, rdt2 . Existing ways of incorporating such context, however, often introduce substantial overhead ( ): feeding past frames to the VLM adds their image tokens to every VLM pass~ jang2025contextvla, yuan2026qwenrobot , recurrent methods require sequential training~ cherepanov2026muvla, jiang2026robottt , and others introduce additional, dedicated memory modules to the policy~ shi2026memoryvla, koo2025hamlet . REKI summarises past context through a small set of registers~ darcet2024registers in the action expert. The registers of each frame are cached across chunks ( ). Each frame is thus encoded only once and no separate module, sequential unroll during training or test-time update mechanisms are necessary. This yields clear gains at almost no overhead, and our 2.4B model REKI ranks first among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365 ( ), and generalises to real robots. Our ablations show that memory consistently improves performance, with the most pronounced gains for the first past frame ( ). Beyond task success, we find that memory stabilises action generation: without memory, the policy often oscillates between poses across action chunks, while with memory, such oscillations are about four times rarer ( ). Our contributions are thus three-fold: (i) We introduce REKI, a 2.4B-parameter VLA pretrained on public data, which sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size. (ii) We introduce register tokens in the action expert to act as a memory, which can be cached efficiently, and analyse how this reduces the failure modes of the memoryless policy. We hope REKI serves as a strong and accessible baseline for future VLA research. To foster VLA research, we release the model weights and our optimised training and inference code, from data curation to deployment on a real robot. Related work sec:related Many VLAs release their weights, and often their finetuning code, but not the code or the exact data mixture used for pretraining~ openpi2025, nvidia2025gr00tn1, rdt2, zheng2025xvla, chen2026abotm05 . The strongest VLAs are pretrained partly on proprietary data, collected~ intelligence2025pi05, wang2026qwenvla, rdt2 or synthesised~ yuan2026qwenrobot , and several have no public weights~ intelligence2026pi07, wang2026qwenvla, yuan2026qwenrobot . OpenVLA, Octo and RDT-1B released their full pipeline on public data such as Open X-Embodiment~ kim2024openvla, octo, liu2025rdt1b , followed by SmolVLA, MolmoAct and MolmoAct2, which also releases bimanual data collected by its authors~ shukor2025smolvla, molmoact, fang2026molmoact2 . These releases have helped the research community pretrain models again, change their data or design, and compare them under the same conditions. Models pretrained on larger in-house data, with more recent design choices, have nonetheless kept a lead on most benchmarks. Building on this line of work, REKI is pretrained on a broad mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision--language data, and released in full, from data curation to deployment on a real robot. It reaches the best results among VLAs pretrained on public data on three benchmarks ( ), and is optimised for fast inference ( ). Most of these models act on the current observation alone, yet past context helps a policy identify the task state and recover from failed attempts~ shi2026memoryvla, torne2026mem, gatedmemory , and methods differ in where they pay for it ( ). The most direct approach stacks or compresses past frames in the VLM~ yuan2026qwenrobot, torne2026mem, intelligence2026pi07, jang2025contextvla . Its cost then grows with the window, at least in the vision encoder~ koo2025hamlet . A recurrent state~ cherepanov2026muvla, xiao2026avavla or fast weights~ jiang2026robottt keep the input short, but must be unrolled step by step in training. Others store past features or keyframes in an extra module~ shi2026memoryvla, koo2025hamlet, mark2026bpp, memer . Like VLA and HAMLET, REKI carries the past in a few learnable tokens, but as registers~ darcet2024registers in the action expert. The VLM encodes each frame once, a training window is one batched pass, and at inference memory adds under 1 to the prediction time of a model without memory ( , ). Without memory, a policy can also switch between modes at each new action chunk~ longcontextdp, lian2026intentvla , which is attributed to perceptual aliasing in reinforcement learning~ whitehead1991learning, singh1994learning, mccallum1996reinforcement . In REKI, memory makes such switches about four times rarer ( ), without the extra policy queries of temporal ensembling or bidirectional decoding~ act, liu2024bid . More generally, a policy may condition on every context observed so far, . The camera observations gather the available views, static or embodied. The robot state is expressed as absolute joint angles or an absolute end-effector pose, and the actions as absolute joint angles or delta end-effector poses and yield the next states at a given control frequency. The observations and the instruction are variable-length token sequences. An encoder embeds them into an encoded context whose tokens the expert reads as keys and values in its cross-attention blocks. The state is a single low-dimensional vector. It is pooled into one state embedding , which modulates the expert through its adaptive normalisation~ peebles2023dit , alongside the flow-time embedding. title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
comment: This work has been submitted to the 2027 IEEE Aerospace Conference
summary: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
full_text: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones Elena Wittemyer\\ Stanford University \\ William F. Durand Building \\ 496 Lomita Mall \\ Stanford, CA 94305 \\ elenawit@stanford.edu\\ Grace Gao\\ Stanford University \\ William F. Durand Building \\ 496 Lomita Mall \\ Stanford, CA 94305 \\ gracegao@stanford.edu\\ Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC. Introduction Motivation In a 2028 mission titled ``MoonFall'', NASA plans to send a team of four propulsive drones to the Moon's south pole to rapidly scout the lunar surface noauthor_moonfall_nodate . The drones will use their propulsion systems to complete short `hops' across the surface of the Moon. In-flight, they will use multiple high-definition optical cameras to capture images of terrain that would be challenging to reach from the ground. With these images, the drones seek to build high-resolution models of the lunar surface, which are a critical resource for safe exploration of the Moon. Scientists have developed terrain models for most of the lunar surface using orbital measurements barker_new_2016 . At best, these digital elevation models (DEMs) have a resolution of about 1-5 m/pix; at worst, their resolution is about 60 m/pix aadi_sub-metre_2026 . Even the best DEMs do not have sufficient resolution to resolve smaller rocks or craters. Lunar landers often rely on these terrain models for choosing a landing site; these low-resolution models cannot provide enough information, so lunar landers must rely on sensor measurements moments before landing. Propulsive drones will generate terrain models at sub-meter resolutions, enabling safe landings for future spacecraft and supporting a sustained presence on the lunar south pole. In this work, we consider the problem of autonomous motion planning for propulsive drone-based exploration of the lunar south pole. The first key challenge in motion planning for propulsive drones is landing site safety. At the moment a drone begins a hop, it does not know in advance where it is safe to land. Mid-flight, the drone must be able to identify a site that is not only free of obstacles like rocks or craters, but is also reachable under its dynamics model. It must then calculate and follow some feasible trajectory to reach this safe site. Moreover, it is important that each hop the drone completes is fuel efficient. The planned MoonFall drones have a limited fuel supply and are not designed to refuel; once they are low on fuel, the drones will permanently land and deploy a long-duration payload noauthor_moonfall_nodate . The more fuel efficient a drone's hops are, the more terrain it can cover during its short flying lifespan. Critically, the drone must be able to determine landing site safety/reachability online and track efficient hop trajectories in real-time. We present a robust motion planning framework for propulsive drones which tackles the aforementioned challenges. Our motion planning framework begins with a series of global waypoints, which are chosen using low-resolution existing DEMs of the moon. Our optimal trajectory planner then generates hops between these waypoints. Midway through each hop, we calculate the set of landing sites that are both reachable and obstacle-free. If the next global waypoint is not reachable or safe, we calculate an optimal trajectory to the nearest valid landing site. This motion planning process is illustrated in Fig. fig:main . We test our motion planning framework in a high-fidelity lunar simulation developed by the Stanford NAVLab vila_lupnt_2025 . Contributions Our main contributions are as follows: We design a motion planning architecture for fuel-efficient hop trajectories that are rapidly tracked using model predictive control. We propose a strategy for calculating the set of reachable landing sites under the drone's dynamics model in real-time. We develop a lightweight semantic segmentation model trained on aerial images of simulated lunar terrain to identify rocks and craters in real-time. Related Works Hopping Robots for Extraplanetary Exploration There are a number of existing works on hopping robots for extraplanetary exploration. Hopping robots are capable of exploring terrain that ground-constrained robots, like rovers, would struggle to reach. Unlike traditional rotorcraft or drones, hopping robots can traverse extraplanetary environments that do not have an atmosphere. Many works focus on hopping robots for exploration of small Solar System bodies hockman_stochastic_2020 jiang_path_2020 yoshimitsu_micro-hopping_2003 . We build off of some of the control strategies in these works, but we also incorporate vision and existing terrain models into our approach to deal with the complexity of the lunar surface. There are also a number of existing works on hopping robots for the Moon. kalita_dynamics_2020 proposes a multi-stage ballistic hopping control framework for a spherical robot to explore lunar pits. The spherical robot is designed to hop short distances and uses geometric analysis to identify obstacles. leitner_lunaroo_2016 also presents a hopping robot designed for short-distance traverses, though this robot is made to image the lunar surface rather than explore the lunar subsurface. kim_hopping_2016 presents a long-range, thruster-based Tensegrity robot for exploration of hilly terrain. However, this work uses fixed landing positions and thus does not consider the safety of a potential landing site in the path planning process. There are also a few existing works on the design and/or control of a propulsive drone for lunar exploration. In nothnagel_development_nodate , the author proposes a small, cold gas propulsion-based flying vehicle; this work primarily focuses on the design of the propulsion system and not optimal trajectory planning, utilizing a simple ballistic hop. tonasso_lunar_2024 presents the design of a larger lunar reconnaissance drone for mapping the lunar surface. For planning the hop, the authors combine a fuel-efficient ballistic trajectory with a constant-altitude hovering trajectory. Their work does not consider landing site safety or mid-flight diversions to new terrain. The closest existing work to ours is tanaka_linear_2021 , which proposes a linear quadratic tracking (LQT)-based optimal control strategy for lunar hoppers. The authors use reinforcement learning to dynamically plan an obstacle-avoidant reference trajectory that they track with LQT. This work uses a simplified lunar environment and directly queries the distance to the nearest obstacle, rather than solving for this distance from sensor information. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first vision-based optimal trajectory planning framework for lunar hoppers. Safe and Feasible Autonomous Landing Our approach to generating a safe and feasible landing trajectory is based on existing literature on lunar landers and autonomous extraplanetary aerocraft. There are a number of works on calculating reachable landing trajectories for lunar landers. eren_constrained_2015 proposes an algorithm for calculating the reachable and controllable states for a planetary landing vehicle; we directly build off of this work to calculate a reachable landing site. The real-time re-targeting policy used for the Chandrayaan-3 lunar landing mission is given in kumar_real-time_2026 . This work presents a data-driven re-targeting policy that uses the controllable set given by some baseline policy to find an optimal landing state. While this work is constrained to some base policy, our work uses a precomputed representation of the reachable set and thus does not require some base guidance policy. srinivas_lunar_2024 presents a guidance policy for a lunar lander to complete a feasible trajectory diversion in the event of hazard detection at a nominal landing site. Similar to this work, the authors of srinivas_lunar_2024 use eren_constrained_2015 to calculate a reachable set of landing sites; however, the authors use LiDAR to detect potential hazards. Our work purely uses vision for hazard detection, as future lunar propulsive drones will not necessarily have access to depth sensors like LiDAR. On the note of vision-guided hazard avoidance, the Mars Ingenuity Helicopter also used vision when planning its autonomous landings. Though its early landing sites were planned by human scientists, following a software update noauthor_flight_2022 , the helicopter was able to use its downward-facing camera to detect and avoid risky terrain before landing. Our work builds on this idea, detecting obstacles mid-flight and planning trajectories that touch down in the nearest safe region to the nominal landing site. Unlike the Ingenuity helicopter, it is not possible for our drone to hover in place while making decisions; instead, it quickly identifies safe sites and plans new trajectories while in motion. Methods sec:methods Dynamics The upcoming MoonFall propulsive drones will have a diameter of about 2.1 m, a height of about 1.2 m, and a weight of about 250 kg noauthor_moonfall_nodate . We use these specifications as a starting point for our simulated drone. title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
summary: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.

We present : Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6 in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer. Introduction sec:intro Humans, especially infants and children, develop dexterity from playing~ Needham2002APF . Play offers a task-agnostic source of interaction. Similarly, for robots, learning via playing holds tremendous potential for learning a rich physical understanding of the world required for dexterous manipulation without human supervision. In practice, however, play is a difficult behavior to engineer. Prior works model play by manually defining explicit heuristics as guidance~ ferguson2005guide, pathak2017curiosity, borja2022affordance and by engineering restrictive safety boundaries to prevent hardware damage~ Durr2026_Ace . However, play is inherently intuitive and difficult to formalize with hand-crafted rules, while manual safety constraints require excessive tuning that limits scalability. In this work, our core hypothesis is that play is a behavior that can be modeled as a `goal-agnostic' state-conditioned probabilistic model in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and therefore be learned through a standard behavior cloning pipeline. In other words, even though a safe play behavior is hard to be defined explicitly with heuristics, it can easily be learned implicitly through demonstration data. Therefore, we propose : Dexterity from Supervised Play, a framework that turns minutes of human play into a policy that can continue collecting robot interaction autonomously. An action-conditioned world model learns from these data, while the same play policy provides candidate action sequences for model-predictive control (MPC). As a preliminary acceleration study, we also explore distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. Our primary contribution is a framework for learning dexterous manipulation from data collected by an autonomous play policy. We evaluate how autonomous play supports world-model learning and goal-directed planning through four technical contributions: Supervised play. We formulate supervised play as a mechanism for turning a limited human interaction prior into autonomous contact-rich data collection. Scaling autonomous play data. We show that held-out world-model prediction improves monotonically as the real-robot autonomous-play dataset grows from 0.5 to 5 hours. Play policy as an action prior. We show that using play policy as an action-proposal model for MPC significantly improves manipulation performance. Self-play policy distillation. A method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through world-model self-play to accelerate inference. Experimental results show reaches within rad on 91.4 of trials and within rad on 72.7 , compared with 53.9 and 25.8 for hindsight BC. PPO reaches 86.7 at both thresholds after 344M counted frames, about 490 times the counted-frame budget. Real world experiment shows is able to transfer to real world with matched performance. We further validate on Push-T and visual in-hand manipulation, demonstrating that the framework generalizes across tasks and observation representations. We also provide detailed analysis to carefully examine the characteristics of the proposed algorithm and the impacts of the key design decisions. The code, data, and training details will be publicly available for reproducing our results. Related Work sec:related Play and interaction in RL RL agents can acquire sophisticated behavior via open-ended interaction and planning. Model-based agents such as MuZero~ schrittwieser2020mastering learn a latent dynamics model and plan within it to master board games and Atari without access to the rules. In multi-agent settings, emergent autocurricula produce complex strategies purely from self-play and environment interaction, as in the hide-and-seek tool-use environment~ baker2019emergent . Comparable interaction-driven pipelines now reach elite performance on physical systems such as competitive table tennis~ Durr2026_Ace . These results establish that interaction and planning are powerful, but they depend on well-specified rewards, simulators, or game rules. instead targets contact-rich manipulation, where reward engineering and designing safe exploration plans are difficult, and obtains its behavior from human play rather than from reward-driven search. Curiosity and intrinsic motivation To reduce dependence on hand-designed rewards, intrinsic-motivation methods reward the agent for reaching novel or hard-to-predict states. Prediction-error curiosity uses the error of a learned forward as an intrinsic signal~ pathak2017curiosity, pathak2019self , while Random Network Distillation measures novelty as the error of predicting a fixed random network's features~ burda2018exploration . While such signals drive broad exploration, they are still heuristics and they do not bias interactions toward safe, object-centric contact that dexterous manipulation requires. Learning from play Closest to our framing is robot learning from play: goal-free, human-generated interaction used as a task-agnostic source of supervision. Play-LMP learns latent plans from teleoperated play and reuses them for goal-conditioned control~ lynch2020play , and subsequent work distills affordances from play to improve sample efficiency~ borja2022affordance . These approaches largely treat play as a fixed dataset for imitation. In contrast, uses a human play data seed to train a policy that serves as a reusable, autonomous data-collection mechanism. Dexterous manipulation Dexterous, multi-fingered manipulation has been approached both by model-free reinforcement learning and by imitation. RL methods learn agile in-hand skills such as general object reorientation~ chen2022reorientation, qi2023general, chen2026ptld, qi2023hand and sim-to-real cube manipulation~ handa2023dextreme,andrychowicz2020learning, chen2023visual , but require carefully shaped task rewards and hundreds of millions of simulated interactions. differs from existing work and does not use simulation data: it learns contact-rich dynamics purely from autonomous play, without task-specific demonstrations or rewards, and plans for arbitrary goals by scoring play-policy proposals with the learned world model under MPC. Method sec:method Overview method:overview Given a dexterous manipulation task, our pipeline achieves it in 4 stages described in Fig.~ fig:method-pipeline . We first collect data through teleoperation to train a play policy (see Sec.~ method:supervised ). We then rollout this policy on the robot autonomously to collect a play dataset that contains observation--action transitions (see Sec.~ method:autonomous ). This play dataset is used to train an action-conditioned world model to model the dynamics of the interaction (see Sec.~ method:wm ). For inference, we could either directly perform online MPC to predict optimal action sequences (see Sec.~ method:mpc ) or optionally distill a goal-conditioned closed-loop policy from self-play to amortize the inference cost (see Sec.~ method:distillation ). Supervised Play method:supervised Play is difficult to engineer but intuitive for humans. We therefore train a diffusion-transformer~ peebles2023scalable play policy by behavior cloning on goal-free human teleoperation ( (a)). Let denote the observation of the robot and object and a recorded joint command. The policy samples action chunks conditioned on observation history: where is the action horizon. The demonstrations capture continued object interaction without prescribed goals or task-specific rewards. Safe behavior are not explicitly engineered but implicitly demonstrated in the data. Autonomous Play method:autonomous We then roll out the policy autonomously on the robot to collect a play dataset which achieves sufficient coverage in the state-transition space as described in~ b. This autonomous data collection process requires little human supervision and can be parallelized across mutliple robots and environments. We record sensory and proprioceptive observations as transitions . World Modeling method:wm With the play dataset collected from~ , we train a world model to predict future observations conditioned on recent observation history and an input action chunk: Here, and denote the context length and prediction horizon, respectively. The training objective has the generic form where denotes the parameters of . We train our action-conditioned world model using Diffusion Forcing~ chen2024diffusion , which assigns independent noise levels to observations at different time steps and learns to denoise them causally. This allows the model to condition on clean observed history while progressively denoising future observations, supporting autoregressive rollouts under candidate action sequences. Model Predictive Control method:mpc We combine the learned play policy and world model for MPC (Fig.~ fig:method-pipeline d). The play policy provides an action prior that focuses search on demonstrated interaction behaviors. At time , we sample candidate action chunks and predict their outcomes over steps: for . Given a target observation , we score each candidate by its best predicted goal reward and select Here, measures how well observation satisfies the goal . We execute the first actions ( ) of the selected chunk, receive a new observation, and replan. The goal thus enters through the reward, while the play policy and world model remain goal-agnostic. Policy Distillation method:distillation MPC incurs inference latency from repeated candidate evaluation. We therefore propose optional policy distillation through self-play in the learned world model. Starting from recorded observation histories and sampled goals , we run MPC within , advancing the history with model predictions after each selected action prefix. This produces a dataset of tuples , where is the current observation history and is the prefix selected by MPC. We train a goal-conditioned policy by behavior cloning: At deployment, directly predicts an action prefix from the actual observation history and goal. It executes the prefix and updates its prediction from new observations, yielding a closed-loop policy that amortizes MPC search. Experiments sec:experiments Our experiments evaluate whether can turn goal-free play into goal-directed manipulation across tasks and on real hardware, whether play-guided MPC is more interaction-efficient than direct policy learning and task-specific RL, and how play-policy design, autonomous-play scale, and world-model design affect prediction and control.
