title: Anvil: Scaling Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Knowledge Recirculation
summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We first evaluate against general-purpose and specialist models on public spatial benchmarks (RQ1: Performance). Controlled ablations and retention tests examine how supervision coverage and teacher allocation affect spatial learning and existing capabilities (RQ2: Learning mechanisms). We then measure the efficiency of source-based supervision construction and feedback-driven repair (RQ3: Production efficiency). Finally, task-structure and input controls test whether predictions depend on relevant scene evidence and task dependencies (RQ4: Evaluation validity). Complete comparisons appear in Appendix~ app:tradeoffs . Experimental Setup sec:setup Eight public benchmarks cover spatial understanding (CV-Bench~ tong2024cambrian , EmbSpatial~ liu2024embspatial , BLINK~ fu2024blink ), referring and placement (RefSpatial~ roborefer2025 , Where2Place~ yuan2024robopoint , RoboSpatial~ song2024robospatial ), and embodied reasoning and pointing (ERQA~ deepmind2025erqa , VABench~ yuan2026fsd ). The baselines span general-purpose VLMs, spatial specialists, and embodied models. We train from using native spatial supervision and multi-teacher distillation, and report the final checkpoint in the main table. Local comparisons share task-specific prompts, decoding settings, and scorers; published scores retain their source protocols. Ablations control training updates and record exposures for coverage, initialization, teachers, and maximum rollout budgets for routing, and candidate pools and per-candidate call counts for repair. Coverage and routing comparisons each use two seeds; full settings appear in Appendix~ app:training . The main-table mean covers seven public tasks; RoboSpatial supplies an additional coverage control. Earlier source-filtered checkpoints support the intervention analyses, while linked-source models support the routing study. These studies test individual mechanisms rather than provide additional scores for the final model. Published cross-protocol averages are descriptive; within-protocol comparisons provide the controlled evidence. Spatial Intelligence Assessment and Coverage sec:sota Observation 1: heterogeneous supervision transfers to spatial reasoning and pointing. We first ask whether improves both spatial understanding and interaction-relevant prediction (RQ1). Across the seven public benchmarks in Table~ tab:spatial_benchmark , the final checkpoint achieves a mean, exceeding by points. On EmbSpatial, it outperforms Qwen3-VL-8B and RynnBrain-8B by and points, respectively, showing gains over both general-purpose and embodied baselines. Excluding VABench-Point, the mean improvement over the base is points. The gains span spatial judgments and location prediction, with a regression on RefSpatial. In a preliminary control study with a source-filtered model, we test whether pointing gains rely on multiple predictions. Scoring only the first point on the common -item VABench subset retains a -point advantage over the base (Table~ tab:expanded-local ), supporting a localization benefit beyond additional guesses. Mechanism Ablations sec:distillation-ablation Observation 2: targeted coverage improves adaptation, while replay mitigates forgetting. sec:source-coverage We use preliminary controlled studies to isolate three decisions: which supervision to add, where to apply teacher correction, and how to repair rejected outputs (RQ2). Mixed training improves Where2Place over replay by points across two seeds and also benefits RoboSpatial context (Figure~ fig:mechanism-evidence a). Fixed updates and exposures separate these gains from simply training longer; increasing the decoding budget alone does not recover placement performance. Vacancy-only training favors placement, while replay better preserves pointing and depth. This trade-off motivates targeting at missing capabilities while retaining replay. Mixed training does not improve every task, and unique images and realized tokens remain unmatched (Appendix~ app:training ). Observation 3: selective teacher correction improves transfer with limited retention loss. We test where teachers should intervene. With common initialization and a matched maximum rollout budget, semantic-uniform routing improves strict Ground--Relation success over flat distillation by points (Figure~ fig:mechanism-evidence b). Semantic references expose incorrect but well-formed geometry that structural checks miss. Teacher supervision reaches of sampled responses, while reference learning covers all active stages, with general-VQA retention. The contrast supports selective correction over flat distillation. Observation 4: failure-specific feedback improves repair yield at comparable cost. sec:validity-evidence We test whether failure-specific information improves repair. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the repair model, both arms receive the same rejected candidates and one call per candidate. Named feedback recovers as many source-correct records as generic retry at comparable GPU cost (Figure~ fig:mechanism-evidence c). It identifies the failed category without reference coordinates or ranks, preserving the task while localizing correction. Recovery concentrates on depth ordering; grounding remains harder to repair. Together, these controls support organizing supervision around capability gaps, localizing teacher correction, and using explicit failure information to recover usable training targets. Qualitative Analysis and Production Efficiency sec:production-efficiency Figure~ fig:placement-showcase shows how the preceding mechanisms change individual outputs. In panel (a), adaptation moves placement predictions into the reference region; for the chair example, all three original predictions miss that region. In panel (b), feedback corrects the depth order of the coffee maker and sink while preserving their boxes. The latter case illustrates how an error can be localized to Relation while retaining the Ground output. These selected cases explain the form of the correction; the ablations measure its aggregate benefit, and Appendix~ app:scale-evidence includes a placement regression. Observation 5: source evidence amortizes supervision construction. We next examine where supervision production incurs computational cost (RQ3). From prepared RGB-D frames, eight CPU workers construct linked records in seconds without generative annotation. Registered depth and instance geometry provide the shared references needed to link Ground and Relation targets. A separate pass rechecks stored records in seconds, covering reading, parsing, hashing, and rule evaluation across four shards (Appendix~ app:scale-evidence ). These measurements show that available source evidence supports both target construction and large-scale structural checking with CPU computation. They are component timings: source preparation, image loading during rechecking, and semantic review remain outside the measured scope. For candidates requiring model-based repair, the relevant efficiency measure is source-correct output per unit of computation. Normalizing the repair comparison by allocated GPU time gives correct records per GPU-hour for named feedback and for generic retry, a advantage. The images, questions, and candidate pool are fixed, so this gain reflects the value of localized error information under the same repair workload. Thus, we reuse source geometry, apply inexpensive structural checks, and direct model calls to unresolved semantic errors. The practical implication is to allocate computation according to the evidence available for each record. Source-supported targets can be constructed and checked directly; unresolved candidates receive model-based adjudication or repair. This division makes heterogeneous sources useful for different parts of the production process, rather than requiring every annotation to pass through the same generative workflow. Task Structure and Evidence Dependence sec:dependency-evidence We ask whether linked-task gains survive format correction, whether predictions depend on visual and upstream evidence, and whether action judgments distinguish plans containing the same actions (RQ4). Figure~ fig:source-evidence addresses the question through composition, visual-input, and action-order controls. Observation 6: scene-linked supervision substantially improves spatial composition. We first test whether independently learned Ground and Relation outputs compose under a shared interface. On images from held-out physical scenes, linked supervision reaches strict Ground--Relation success, substantially exceeding the atomic mixture at matched updates (Figure~ fig:source-evidence a). To separate missing delimiters from errors in the predicted content, we close stage tags in the saved responses without changing their JSON outputs. This raises the atomic mixture to while leaving linked performance unchanged. The remaining gap indicates that output syntax is only part of the composition problem. A downstream stage must also receive the correct entities and geometry from its predecessor. Scene-linked supervision trains this dependency explicitly, making intermediate outputs useful inputs to subsequent reasoning rather than merely separately correct answers. Observation 7: spatial predictions depend on images and upstream geometry. We next examine dependence on the evidence supplied to these stages. With questions and targets fixed, blank images reduce the source-filtered model's accuracy on the 1,463-example grounding panel from 57.35 to 7.66 . Cross-scene shuffling also degrades grounding, while BLINK-depth approaches chance (Figure~ fig:source-evidence b). Keeping images and depth targets fixed but shifting upstream boxes reduces the Relation specialist's accuracy by points (Table~ tab:source-context ). In particular, errors in Ground can alter the context available to Relation even when the scene image remains fixed. These interventions establish sensitivity to both visual content and consumed geometry, motivating joint evaluation of stage accuracy and linked success. Observation 8: action rules support state-conditioned plan verification. We extend the evaluation to action order under state constraints. From ALFRED trajectories~ shridhar2020alfred across scenes, we construct balanced judgments, pairing each valid plan with an invalid permutation of the same actions. This fixes vocabulary and length, so action occurrence alone cannot distinguish the labels. Given the initial image, complete Boolean state, goal, and action rules, the Action specialist improves over the base by points (Figure~ fig:source-evidence c). Class-wise results remain uneven: accuracy is on invalid plans but only on valid ones (Table~ tab:alfred-plan-verification ). The improvement mainly comes from recognizing more valid plans, although many feasible sequences are still rejected. Summary and discussion. The experiments suggest that spatial learning depends on how supervision is organized, not only how much is available. Coverage controls favor task-relevant additions with replay; routing controls favor localized specialist correction; and repair controls show the value of actionable failure feedback. Source-based construction complements these mechanisms by reusing available geometric evidence. Beyond aggregate benchmark gains, the composition, input, and action-order controls test whether predictions remain useful when later decisions depend on their content. These findings motivate scaling spatial supervision through capability coverage, selective correction, and explicit task dependencies.

title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
comment: Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026); Project Website: https://libero-perm.github.io/
summary: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

Introduction Household manipulation has been a long-standing goal in robotics and embodied AI, with the promise of improving daily life by enabling robots to perform chores from natural language instructions (e.g., ``put an apple, bread, and milk on my plate''). Recent progress in generalist robotic manipulation has been driven in large part by Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ pi0black2024,amin2025pi,openvlakim2024,grootbjorck2025 , which show strong generalization across diverse multimodal inputs~ vlaszhao2025,pi05intelligence2025 and heterogeneous embodiments~ openxo2024,univlabu2025 . However, real-world deployment demands more than completing the nominal task: embodied agents must also execute tasks in ways that align with the preferences, habits, and constraints of individual users, a requirement we refer to as personalization. Preferences introduce diverse execution requirements for identical goals. For instance, placing a mug might require a specific handle orientation or a designated landing spot. Consequently, personalized manipulation must satisfy user-specific constraints on both what strategies are selected and how actions are performed. In this framework, preferences are treated as a learning dimension parallel to object-oriented task learning; the policy's objective is to maximize preference adherence within a single trajectory without compromising fundamental task success. Nevertheless, progress on personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) remains impeded by two major gaps. First, PeRM lacks a shared formulation and standardized evaluation protocol across prior work. Existing studies define personalization through diverse problem settings, including implicit preference alignment~ feastjenamani2025,personalizingRLHFpoddar2024 , multi-user style adaptation~ pecannemlekar2025 , user-specific object-receptacle pairing~ llmpersonalizedhan2025 , and helpful action prediction~ provox ; they also specify preferences through natural language~ provox,alignbotzhaxizhuoma2024 , few user examples~ feastjenamani2025 , explicit preference functions~ graspvladeng2025 , human speech~ vlaszhao2025 , or numerical preference vectors~ pecannemlekar2025 . Evaluation is similarly fragmented, spanning task success, user studies~ provox,feastjenamani2025,pecannemlekar2025,alignbotzhaxizhuoma2024 , and preference-based scoring functions~ pbarlwang2025,psharedliu2025 , making methods difficult to compare and failure modes hard to diagnose. Second, existing benchmarks typically emphasize high-level navigation or semantic selection over fine-grained manipulation preferences and multi-preference conflicts. The closest preference-based RL benchmark~ bpreflee2021 lacks robotic preference-learning datasets and multi-preference evaluation. Other personalization benchmarks focus on object navigation or high-level receptacle selection~ personalziliotto2025,tidybotwu2023 , while recent memory-based manipulation benchmarks~ sam2actfang2025,starchen2025 do not distinguish task-instance memorization from genuine user-preference-driven personalization. To address these gaps, we introduce a novel Personalized Robotic Manipulation Benchmark ( ), built using the popular LIBERO~ liberoliu2023 framework. We elevate user preferences to a fundamental building block alongside tasks and layouts. Following the taxonomy of human preferences~ surverypersonalizationzhang2024 , we define a controlled taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering (trajectory constraints), (task strategies), and (semantic biases). The benchmark is restricted to preferences that can be expressed in language, instantiated without changing the original task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Within this scope, we provide 37 single-preference instances and 18 two-preference combinations. features an extensible procedural generation pipeline that automatically instantiates tasks and their preference-conditioned variants within shared layouts. To support systematic training and evaluation, the pipeline simultaneously produces explicit preference satisfaction metrics and rich subtask-level metadata, including language instructions, goal images, and physical attributes. For benchmarking, we construct five task suites with preference-conditioned tasks and pipeline-generated, human-reviewed demonstrations, each targeting a core capability in personalized manipulation (Figure~ fig:teaser , top). evaluates single-preference learning; evaluates scaling across data sizes, tasks, and layouts; evaluates preference-preference and task-preference conflicts; evaluates multi-preference composition; and evaluates realistic preference-conditioned reasoning based on contextual language. In , we further provide no-preference data, unseen layouts, and different tasks to support in-domain evaluation, task/layout generalization, and preference-level generalization over different tasks in unseen layouts. We use to conduct an initial study of five key research topics in personalized manipulation (see bottom row of Figure~ fig:teaser ): 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how policies learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently policies acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose multiple preferences and behave under conflicts. These topics organize our experiments and highlight the core capabilities that robots must develop for reliable personalization. benchmarkcompare Our contributions and findings are as follows: [leftmargin=0.8em,labelsep=0.25em,itemsep=0.15em,topsep=0.25em] We introduce a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, together with an automated pipeline that produces preference-conditioned demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. We construct five task suites, , comprising preference-conditioned tasks with pipeline-generated, human-reviewed demonstrations and evaluation protocols for controlled personalization studies. Extensive experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training improves no-preference task success relative to sequential adaptation and contextual-prompt task success and preference satisfaction relative to preference-only LoRA, but weakens motion-preference learning; broader layout diversity and matched no-preference data also help, while preference generalization, decomposition, and execution under conflicts remain difficult. Related Work Robotic Manipulation Benchmark. Many benchmarks have been developed to evaluate different aspects of robotic manipulation, including cross-embodiment generalization~ openxo2024,interndata_a1tian2025,robomindwu2024 , generalized manipulation~ rlbenchjames2020,libero_prozhou2025,libero-para , long-horizon reasoning~ robocerebrahan2025,calvinmees2022,vlabenchzhang2025,internvla_m1chen2025 ~ zhang2025lamma,gupta2026scale , and sim-to-real transfer~ robocasanasiriany2024,robotwinchen2025,maniskill2gu2023 . Among them, LIBERO~ liberoliu2023 has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark due to its high-quality demonstrations and standardized data generation pipeline, primarily focusing on lifelong learning and task generalization. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on task completion, without explicitly modeling user-specific preferences. title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
summary: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.
full_text: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We instantiate this perspective in , a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5 to 73.5 and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD. Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as agents to operate professional software and complete long-horizon tasks~ achiam2023gpt,naveed2025comprehensive,guo2024large . Computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting for such agents~ willis2020fusion360gallery,wu2021deepcad . Unlike one-shot content generation, CAD modeling requires a sequence of state-dependent operations over a persistent design document. An agent must create and modify sketches, constraints, features, and geometric objects; inspect intermediate results; recover from execution failures; and maintain references across long interaction trajectories. In this process, the model outputs are interpreted as actions: each action changes the current CAD state, produces execution feedback, and conditions the next decision~ yao2022react,schick2023toolformer . The effectiveness of a CAD agent therefore depends not only on the underlying model and its reasoning strategy, but also on how CAD actions, states, and execution outcomes are represented to the model. Such a model--environment boundary is defined by an agent harness yang2024sweagent . In CAD, a harness determines which design operations the model can express, which parts of the evolving design state it can inspect, and how execution outcomes are returned for subsequent decisions. A general-purpose coding harness may expose the CAD system through programs, libraries, and runtime feedback, whereas a domain-native harness may expose structured CAD actions and object-level observations. Consequently, even when the model, task, and CAD backend remain fixed, different harnesses can present the model with substantially different decision spaces, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:harness-induced-decision-space . Existing work has studied CAD code generation, tool-using agents, execution repair, and interactive modeling~ mallis2024cadassistant,guan2025cadcoder,doris2025cadcoder, wang2025cadfusion,barkley2026cadsmith, gong-etal-2026-toolcad , but the harness itself is typically treated as implementation infrastructure rather than as a variable that shapes both agent execution and policy learning. This raises a central question: How should a CAD agent harness represent actions and states so that it preserves the decisions required for complex modeling while avoiding representation burden that is irrelevant to the task? This trade-off is important in CAD. A fine-grained coding interface gives the model broad control over the underlying software, but the same CAD operation can often be expressed through many programs, command sequences, variable names, temporary objects, and API combinations. These implementations may produce the same geometric state transition, but they appear as different generation and supervision targets. The model must then spend capacity on implementation choices that do not affect the intended state transition. A semantic interface can remove many of these choices by representing the intended operation directly. However, excessive compression can hide state differences that require different actions or remove operations needed for correct modeling and error recovery. A useful harness must therefore reduce irrelevant representation choices while preserving the actions and observations needed for correct decisions. To make this trade-off explicit, we formalize the model-facing interface as a Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space: a harness maps model outputs to executable operations, maps internal CAD states to model-visible observations, and returns execution results as feedback, thereby determining which operations the agent can perform, which state differences and failures it can identify, and which policies it can execute and learn. We then introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for this space: it compresses behaviorally equivalent implementations and removes state information that does not affect the next decision, while preserving the actions and observations needed to reach the target geometry and recover from errors. Following this principle, we develop , a domain-native harness for closed-loop CAD agents. represents task-relevant design transitions as semantic CAD actions, grounds these actions in a persistent CAD document, and returns structured execution feedback together with decision-oriented observations. We further develop a harness-grounded learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned action supervision from successful and recovered interaction trajectories, initializes CAD action policies through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and supports online reinforcement learning (RL) using policy-generated trajectories and geometry-grounded rewards. Figure~ fig:DeciCAD-overview summarizes this execution and learning loop. Across four CAD benchmarks, consistently produces more accurate final geometry than competitive CAD agents and a general-purpose coding harness, while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88 relative to the coding harness on text-to-CAD tasks. Observation ablations show that showing more CAD state does not always help: unfiltered state inflates the input context, and coarse feedback strips out what the agent needs in order to recover. With matched training settings, open-weight models trained in the decision space learn stronger long-horizon CAD action policies than the same models trained through code-level interaction. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We define the Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space and introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for CAD agent interfaces. We design , which combines semantic CAD actions, compact observations, structured feedback, and persistent object state. We develop a harness-grounded policy-learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned supervision from interaction trajectories, initializes policies through SFT, and supports geometry-grounded online RL. Experiments across four benchmarks verify improves geometric accuracy, token efficiency, error recovery, and long-horizon policy learnability significantly. Related Work Our work connects agent interaction interfaces, decision-preserving abstraction, and policy learning in interactive CAD environments. We review these directions through the common question of how an agent's operating representation affects execution and learning. Agent Interfaces and Decision Abstraction Tool-augmented language models connect generation to executable operations parisi2022talm,karpas2022mrkl,schick2023toolformer , while API-Bank, Gorilla, and ToolLLM extend tool learning to executable dialogues and large API ecosystems li2023apibank,patil2023gorilla,qin2023toolllm . ReAct interleaves reasoning, actions, and observations yao2022react ; SWE-agent, WebArena, and OSWorld further show that interaction design affects behavior in stateful coding, web, and computer environments yang2024sweagent,zhou2023webarena,xie2024osworld . They establish the empirical importance of interfaces, but generally treat them as tool provision or runtime infrastructure. We instead study the harness as the joint action--state representation that defines the policy space presented to the model. This view is related to abstraction in sequential decision-making. MDP homomorphisms and state-abstraction theory characterize when compressed representations preserve transition, reward, value, or policy structure ravindran2003smdp,li2006stateabstraction,abel2016nearoptimal, abel2020valuepreserving ; the Information Bottleneck similarly retains target-relevant information while suppressing irrelevant input dependence tishby2000informationbottleneck . Classical abstractions operate within an already specified decision process. An LLM harness instead jointly defines model actions, visible observations, execution bindings, and feedback semantics. Our Harness-Induced Decision Space describes this transformation, and the Semantic Decision Bottleneck constrains its compression by decision preservation. CAD Generation and Interactive Agents CAD generation has been studied through construction sequences, executable programs, and interactive actions. DeepCAD and Fusion 360 Gallery represent structured modeling histories wu2021deepcad,willis2020fusion360gallery , while Text2CAD and CADmium learn parametric command sequences from language khan2024text2cad,govindarajan2025cadmium . CAD-Coder systems generate executable CAD code guan2025cadcoder,doris2025cadcoder , and CADFusion, CADSmith, and CADDesigner incorporate rendering, execution repair, or multi-agent feedback wang2025cadfusion,barkley2026cadsmith,fan2025caddesigner . Code is expressive, but also makes program organization and API realization part of the model output. Interactive systems instead place decisions in evolving design state. CAD-Assistant combines a Python interpreter with FreeCAD operations mallis2024cadassistant ; ToolCAD trains tool-using CAD agents from demonstrations and online curriculum learning gong-etal-2026-toolcad ; CADMate learns sequential assembly actions using geometric and physical rewards chen2026cadmate . Our contribution is complementary: under fixed models, tasks, and terminal geometry, we compare the decision spaces induced by domain-semantic actions and a general-purpose coding harness. Policy Learning from Interaction Tool policies commonly acquire initial capability from generated or curated demonstrations schick2023toolformer,li2023apibank,qin2023toolllm . In a stateful environment, however, action validity depends on the preceding trajectory and feedback; imitation therefore encounters distribution shift when student-induced states depart from teacher trajectories ross2011reduction . Online methods address this gap using execution outcomes on states visited by the learned policy feng2025retool,qian2025toolrl , including curriculum reinforcement learning in CAD gong-etal-2026-toolcad . We align causal supervision, student rollouts, and environment feedback within the same Harness-Induced Decision Space, enabling a controlled study of how representation affects both imitation and online learning. Method The harness determines how the closed CAD loop is presented to the language model: whether the model writes general-purpose code or selects a semantic CAD action, which part of the current design is shown, and how execution failures are reported. We formalize this interaction, formulate the Semantic Decision Bottleneck, instantiate it in , and use the same representation for SFT and online RL. title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.

Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8 on MMSI and 13.0 on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks. 13 \ Project Page: Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong instruction-following and reasoning abilities, but they operate primarily over text. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) extend these capabilities to visual inputs, enabling multimodal understanding and reasoning. Recent VLMs such as Qwen3.8 qwen38 and Gemini 3.8 gemini38flash can effectively interpret images and analyze charts, and they are increasingly used in real-world multimodal applications. Beyond static image understanding, VLMs are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes. For example, a model may need to predict whether two objects would overlap if one were moved, reconstruct what happened between two observations, or infer what another viewpoint would reveal. Solving such problems requires going beyond observed visual evidence to reason about unobserved transitions and relations. One promising approach is visual imagination: explicitly generating task-relevant visual predictions of what is not observed and using them as additional evidence for reasoning. This raises a fundamental question: how can a VLM generate and exploit the right visual imagination for the reasoning problem at hand? Video World Models (VWMs), such as MiniMax H3 minimaxh3 and LTX-Video ltxvideo , provide a natural engine for visual imagination by modeling visual dynamics from large-scale video data. Given input images and an appropriate visual operation, they can generate video depicting unobserved views, intermediate states, future events, or intervention outcomes. Recent approaches, including MindJourney mindjourney and AVIC avic , use a VWM to generate additional visual evidence for spatial reasoning, including synthesized views for cross-view reasoning. However, these approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. This limits their applicability to diverse reasoning problems, which may require fundamentally different forms of visual imagination: changing viewpoints for perspective taking, interpolating between observations to reconstruct hidden transitions, continuing observed dynamics to anticipate future events, or intervening on the scene to reason about intervention outcomes, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:visual_operations . A visual reasoner should therefore actively determine what to imagine according to the reasoning problem and how to exploit the generated visual evidence to solve it. To enable task-dependent visual imagination, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Unlike an agent confined to a fixed workflow, it selects among VWM-driven tools to generate unseen views, intermediate states, continuations, or intervention outcomes according to the question. Skills guide when to invoke these tools, how to construct requests, and how to interpret the generated video; a verifier and execution code complete the harness. A predefined harness may fail to elicit the visual evidence required by different reasoning tasks or to guide its interpretation. Refinement must coordinate evidence generation and interpretation, because what the VLM can infer depends on what the VWM can reliably generate. We therefore introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which iteratively refines the interface between the VLM and VWM by jointly revising tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback. With both model weights fixed, co-evolution improves how the two models interact and use task-relevant visual evidence. We evaluated CoWorld Reasoner on seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence mmsi,sat,spin,spatialab , temporal and causal reasoning erqa,causalspatial , and perceptual reasoning perceptionbench . Across VLM/VWM variants, CoWorld Reasoner improves aggregate accuracy over direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant (GPT-5.6 and MiniMax H3) improves all seven benchmarks, with relative gains of 11.8 on MMSI and 13.0 on ERQA. It also outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone on five benchmarks. Further analysis highlights the contributions of generated visual evidence and co-evolved control of its request and interpretation. Our main contributions are summarized below: We leverage a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine for visual imagination, enabling the agent to generate task-relevant visual evidence through diverse visual operations. =-1 We design a Video World Model-Driven Harness that exposes diverse visual operations through standardized tools and encodes reusable reasoning workflows as skills, enabling the agent to decide whether visual imagination is needed, which operation to invoke, and how to interpret the generated visual evidence. =-1 We introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which iteratively refines the interface between the VLM and VWM by jointly revising tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback. We evaluate CoWorld Reasoner with multiple VLMs and VWMs across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, showing gains over direct reasoning and strong performance against evolving baselines, while analyzing the contributions of the harness and its co-evolution. Related Work Multimodal Reasoning Recent work uses visual evidence to support multimodal reasoning, particularly spatial tasks. MVoT mvot and ThinkMorph thinkmorph incorporate generated images into intermediate reasoning steps, while Omni-R1 omnir1generative uses image generation to unify diverse visual operations. Thinking with Video thinkingwithvideo uses video generation for visual reasoning. For spatial reasoning, SenseNova-SI sensenova and OpenSpatial openspatial use large-scale training datasets, while World2VLM world2vlm uses views generated by world models as supervision. At inference time, MindJourney mindjourney searches camera movements to explore a scene, and SpatialDreamer spatialdreamer uses a learned policy to explore generated views. AVIC avic controls world-model use and the amount of visual content generated. World Models World models capture the structure and dynamics of environments to support prediction and simulation. Video generation models such as Wan wan , Seedance 2.0 seedance2 , and MiniMax H3 minimaxh3 learn visual dynamics from video data, and Cosmos-Predict2.5 cosmospredict focuses on world simulation. Marble marbleworld generates explicit 3D environments that users can explore and edit. Interactive models such as RTFM rtfmworld generate video in real time in response to user actions. Our approach treats a VWM as a unified visual reasoning~engine and exposes it through multiple VWM-driven tools. Self-Evolving Agents =-1 Recent approaches improve agents by iteratively revising prompts, skills, and code. GEPA gepa optimizes prompts from execution traces, while SkillOpt skillopt refines reusable skills from execution feedback. DGM dgm revises the agent's own code, while Meta-Harness metaharness optimizes harness implementations. CoEvoSkills evoskills jointly evolves skills and a verifier that guides their refinement. title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
summary: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. full_text: We introduce , a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: , which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; , which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and , which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual--action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision–language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Introduction sec:introduction Dexterous manipulation requires more than mapping pixels directly to actions. An embodied model must answer three complementary questions: What happened in an observed interaction? What will happen under a specified action? What should be done to accomplish a desired goal? These questions correspond to three fundamental capabilities: perceiving the 3D motion underlying observed interactions, predicting action-conditioned world dynamics, and planning actions together with their anticipated consequences. Infants can use what they learn from observing adults' actions to guide their own behavior~ hauf2008actioneffect . Through their own interactions, they learn to predict action outcomes and use those expected outcomes to select actions~ verschoor2013outcome and organize movements toward a goal~ claxton2003motorplanning . Together, these findings suggest that perception, prediction, and planning are linked by knowledge of actions and their consequences. Despite these connections, prior work on egocentric manipulation has developed along three closely related but largely separate lines. Egocentric reconstruction methods recover structured 3D interaction information, such as hand motion and camera trajectories, from observed videos~ pavlakos2024hamer, yu2025dynhamr . Action-conditioned world models predict future observations under prescribed motion trajectories~ hao2026egosim, wang2026hand2world, sun2026handworld . World action models jointly generate actions and future observations for goal-directed control~ ye2026dreamzero . These capabilities, however, are still largely learned in isolation or coupled only in subsets. To close this loop, we introduce , a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates three complementary modes: 3D interaction reconstruction ( ), action-conditioned world prediction ( ), and joint action--future planning ( ). Reconstruction develops the model's capacity for 3D perception by recovering 3D motion from observed interactions. Prediction teaches the model to anticipate the visual consequences of prescribed actions. Together, these capabilities provide the foundation for world--action planning, in which the model learns to jointly generate goal-directed hand action trajectories and their anticipated visual futures. We learn all three modes through unified training. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates these three modes. We build on a pretrained video diffusion transformer~ wan2025video to draw on its rich visual and motion priors. We represent each action by the articulated poses of both hands and the camera pose, and encode these states as compact tokens alongside the video tokens. We integrate this representation into the video backbone through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with a dedicated action expert, which shares the backbone’s base weights while incorporating modality-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA)~ hu2022lora . To train this architecture across all three modes, we randomly vary the visibility of visual observations and actions: providing video while withholding actions supports perception, providing actions while withholding future video supports prediction, and withholding actions and video supports joint action--future planning, exposing the model to complete modes and partially observed interactions. Over long sequences, successive visual subgoals specify the target arrangement for each planning window. Unified training improves all three modes over single-mode training. Our model outperforms the evaluated baselines in and . Its videos receive higher VLM scores for action process and instruction adherence. Robot demonstrations illustrate how generated human-hand motion can be transferred to a dexterous robot. Our main contributions are: [nosep,leftmargin=*] A unified world action model, , for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates 3D interaction reconstruction, action-conditioned world prediction, and goal-guided world--action planning. We will release our code and model checkpoints. A unified training framework that connects pretrained video priors with structured 3D actions through a mixture-of-transformers architecture and randomized modality visibility, enabling complementary learning across perception, prediction, and planning. Extensive experiments indicating that perception, prediction, and planning reinforce one another through unified training, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across all three tasks. Robot demonstrations further illustrate the transfer of generated human-hand motion to a dexterous robot. Related Work sec:related_work Video World Models and World Action Models. Action-conditioned world models predict single images~ sudhakar2024controllingworldsleighthand or roll out videos~ akkerman2025interdyn,dreamx2026dreamxphi,gao2026lome . Wan~ wan2025video and Cosmos~3~ nvidia2026cosmos3 provide pretrained video priors. For action representation, Dexterous World Models~ kim2026dexterous uses rendered scenes and hand-mesh trajectories, while DreamDojo~ gao2026dreamdojo learns latent actions from human videos for robot-world rollouts. Explicit scene and camera geometry can also help maintain spatial consistency. EgoSim~ hao2026egosim combines video generation with an updatable 3D scene and shared human--robot keypoints, and EgoGenesis~ yan2026egogenesis uses camera-aware 3D action embeddings and online projective memory for autoregressive rollout. World action models generate actions alongside anticipated visual dynamics through causal video prediction and inverse dynamics, as in LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva , or joint video--action flow matching, as in DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero . Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam , Foresight Without Seeing~ huang2026forewam , and RIFT~ zhang2026rift study predictive visual information for control without a complete iterative visual rollout at deployment. Monocular Hand Reconstruction. Recovering 3D hand motion from video requires estimating hand articulation while accounting for a moving camera. Single-image methods provide hand pose and shape estimates: HaMeR~ pavlakos2024hamer scales transformer capacity and heterogeneous training data, while WiLoR~ potamias2025wilor integrates localization, handedness estimation, and image-aligned mesh refinement. For egocentric sequences, HaWoR~ zhang2025hawor and Dyn-HaMR~ yu2025dynhamr combine hand-motion estimation with SLAM to recover global trajectories, using temporal infilling or interacting-hand priors and optimization. Concurrent work MINT~ zhu2026mint jointly estimates camera and hand motion. Video generative models offer another source of information about hand motion. Concurrent works ViDiHand~ wang2026vidihand and ACE-Ego-Hand~ liu2026aceegohand use video diffusion features for hand motion recovery. We train reconstruction jointly with future prediction and planning, allowing the model to learn from how hand interactions unfold as well as from observed video. This joint training improves 3D hand reconstruction in our single-mode comparison (Sec.~ sec:ablations ). Unified Multimodal Models. A shared model can connect these tasks by changing which modalities are observed and which are generated. Unified World Models~ zhu2025unified couples video and action diffusion for forward, inverse, policy, and video inference. Language provides a further interface for world modeling and control: Motus~ bi2025motus combines language, video, and latent actions, while MotuBrain~ motubrain2026 jointly models text, video, and embodiment-specific actions. Geometric modalities extend this shared formulation to spatial reasoning. Flex- ~ yan2026flexpi includes pointmap and feature streams alongside RGB and actions, and Aether~ zhu2025aether unifies 4D reconstruction, camera-conditioned prediction, and goal-image-conditioned visual planning. applies joint reconstruction, prediction, and planning to articulated hand interaction. It plans hand and camera trajectories together with video and supports visual goals to preserve spatial targets across a task. Method sec:method Unified Task Formulation sec:problem_formulation We consider an egocentric video with aligned hand states and camera states , which encode rotation and translation relative to the first frame. We define the 3D action sequence as . Action tokens encode the aligned hand and camera observations. The text instruction and initial image are always given. For planning, the goal image specifies the desired terminal observation. Figure~ fig:unified-formulation defines the three modes through the information supplied to the same model. recovers hands and camera motion from a complete video. generates future video given hand and camera trajectories. generates video together with those trajectories guided by the text instruction and the optional visual goal. During training, we sample visibility patterns per clip and across temporal positions. We keep observed video latents clean, add noise to frames that the model must generate, and represent missing actions with learnable query embeddings. Joint Video--Action Modeling sec:unified_model We build the model on top of the pretrained Wan2.2-Fun-A14B-Control model~ alibabapai2025wan22fun . We retain its latent video representation, text and first-frame conditioning, skeleton-based control pathway, and high- and low-noise diffusion experts as the RGB generation backbone. Observed actions enter through two complementary paths: rendered hand skeletons and camera-ray maps provide spatially aligned controls for hand placement and viewpoint, while compact action tokens carry the corresponding states into joint attention. Specifically, the RGB sequence is encoded into a spatiotemporal latent using the Wan2.1 VAE~ wan2025video . The temporally aligned hand trajectory is rendered as a 2D skeleton video and encoded by the same VAE (Fig.~ fig:method-overview ). The resulting control latent is concatenated with the noisy RGB latent before DiT patch embedding. For camera conditioning, we express all camera-to-world poses in the first camera coordinate frame, making the first pose the identity, and construct per-pixel Pl\"ucker ray maps~ plucker1865geometry from the relative poses and camera intrinsics. After temporal packing to the video-latent frame rate, a lightweight convolutional adapter maps the Pl\"ucker representation into the DiT patch-feature space. Its output is then added to the joint RGB--hand patch embeddings. The same conditioning interfaces are used by both diffusion experts. represents RGB and action

title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
summary: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
full_text: Introduction By continuously processing an input video stream and responding to user queries, a streaming vision-language model (VLM) must reason over what has already happened, interpret what is happening now, and remain attentive to what may happen next. Such capabilities are central to key tasks ranging from streaming video understanding~ niu2025ovo to interactive AI assistants~ thinkingmachines2026interactionmodels and robotic planning~ li24simpler , where responses and decisions must be made online under latency and memory constraints. Streaming VLMs have thus emerged as an important research frontier. Recent work has shown that offline VLMs can be adapted to describe ongoing activities in streaming videos~ shen2026simple, lu2026aura , while instruction fine-tuning can further enable models to monitor future events~ li2026videochat3, wang2026moss . Despite these efforts, a fundamental open problem remains: how should a streaming VLM remember? As in the offline setting, an effective memory mechanism must preserve important visual information within a bounded memory footprint. The streaming setting, however, introduces additional challenges. First, memory must evolve incrementally as new observations arrive, rather than being repeatedly recomputed from the full history. Second, historical information must be incorporated without crowding out the current observation (see Fig. fig:teaser -2). Finally, a practical memory mechanism should introduce minimal inference overhead. To address these challenges, we propose (Memory as LoRA Weights), a framework that internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates of a streaming VLM, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser -1. incrementally consolidates incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing accumulated history to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. The base VLM architecture and parameters stay unchanged and only the lightweight LoRA memory evolves over time. More fundamentally, rather than placing memory and current observations in competition within the same context window, as in prior work~ guan2026video, liu2026thinking, zhang2026hermes , represents history as weights while keeping the current observation as input. At each step, the model takes the current observation and user query as input and performs inference using the updated LoRA weights that encode historical information. By separating historical memory from the input context, preserves the model's capacity to attend to current observations while retaining information from the past (Fig.~ fig:teaser -2), with only modest inference overhead. Specifically, employs a recurrent HyperNetwork~ hypernetwork to efficiently generate the LoRA weights that encode historical information. At each time step, the incoming video clip and its textual context are first compressed into a compact representation, which is then used to update a set of recurrent hidden states. To model the temporal dynamics of these hidden states, maintains two parallel branches: a state-space model~ yang2024parallelizing for modeling local temporal dependencies, and a gated summation branch for preserving global historical semantics. The resulting states are mapped through a linear projection to the LoRA weights used by the VLM. To facilitate training, we further construct -Instruct, a comprehensive streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer (QA) pairs over 56K videos, by adapting public offline video understanding datasets to the streaming setting. To evaluate our framework, we conduct extensive experiments across benchmarks and settings. demonstrates state-of-the-art results on streaming video benchmarks, including OVO-Bench~ niu2025ovo , StreamingBench~ lin2026streamingbench and StreamArena~ zhang2026streamarena . On the backward split of OVO-Bench, for example, outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9 --11.8 across different video backbones, while incurring modest latency overhead. Across base VLMs ranging from 0.8B to 11B parameters, yields consistent performance gains. Beyond streaming video understanding, we further extend to the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) setting, where incorporating historical observations and action trajectories improves the action success rate on Simpler~ li24simpler WidowX by 9.3 . Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=2em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt] We propose , a new streaming memory framework that internalizes historical context into evolving LoRA weights, introducing a distinct design in which history is represented as weights while current observations remain as input. We develop a recurrent HyperNetwork that incrementally updates LoRA memory from streaming video and other context. We also construct -Instruct, a large-scale training dataset for streaming video understanding, which we will release publicly. We demonstrate that achieves competitive results across streaming video benchmarks, attains consistent gains over diverse base VLMs, and generalizes to VLA settings. Related Work -Language Models. Vision-language models (VLMs)~ liu2023visual, alayrac2022flamingo, zhang2024llava, clark2026molmo2, qwen3.5 unify diverse visual understanding and reasoning tasks through a natural-language interface. Among these tasks, long-video understanding~ zhou2025mlvu, wang2025lvbench is particularly challenging because models must preserve and reason over information spanning extended temporal contexts. Prior works~ NEURIPS2024_d7ce06e9, he2024ma, song2024moviechat have explored various memory and context-management mechanisms for this offline long video understanding setting. Our work builds on pretrained VLMs and equips them with an evolving long-term memory that is needed in the streaming video setting and incrementally updated as new observations arrive. VLMs with Memory. Recent works on streaming VLMs~ xia2026streaming, chen2024videollm, li2026videochat3, wang2026moss explore several complementary directions, including constructing higher-quality instruction-tuning data, designing architectures tailored to streaming inputs, and incorporating stronger video encoders. More recent studies~ lu2026aura, shen2026simple show that strong VLMs with a small local video window yield surprisingly strong performance on real-time questions on existing streaming video benchmarks. Another line of work focuses on the memory mechanisms. Some methods compress historical visual observations into textual summaries or memories~ liu2026thinking, guan2026video, yao2026joyai , while others reduce the accumulated visual tokens through clustering or token merging~ zhang2024flash . Additional approaches organize historical information into hierarchical memory structures~ zeng2026streamforest, zhang2026hermes, xie2026fluxmem, liang2026oasis , or maintain a fixed-size memory buffer that selectively preserves useful historical observations~ qian2025dispider, yao2025timechat . Despite their differences, these methods generally address the growing streaming context by compressing historical information into a bounded token budget. In contrast, we represent long-term memory directly in model weights. Concurrent work~ chen2026streamttt similarly moves long-term memory outside the attention context. However, it stores historical information in a separate test-time-training (TTT) branch with online-updated fast weights. In contrast, our method directly internalizes history into the VLM itself by dynamically generating low-rank parameter adaptations, without introducing a separate memory branch. -Rank Adaptation and Context Internalization. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)~ hu2021lora has been widely adopted as a parameter-efficient approach for adapting pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) to downstream tasks or new domains~ dettmers2023qlora, chen2024longlora, liu2025pave . Recently, several works have explored using LoRA as a representation for encoding data-specific patterns~ shrestha2025finetuning, yin2026qwen or contextual information~ charakorn2026doc, charakorn2025text . These approaches demonstrate that model parameters can be a good representation for storing information beyond conventional token-based context. However, they typically require additional optimization when adapting to a new pattern, making it difficult to apply them directly to evolving inputs. -mem~ lei2026delta explores dynamically representing textual information through LoRA updates without test-time training. Nevertheless, it still relies on access to the historical context during inference. Different from these prior approaches, our work specifically handles the streaming setting, and introduces a context internalization mechanism that progressively incorporates incoming visual context into low-rank model representations.
