title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching
summary: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.
full_text: 0pt (a) Top scores on 7 of 12 spatial understanding benchmarks. (b) The highest mean score and lowest mean latency among eight evaluated models. (c) Direct option selection and coarse-to-fine numerical and point prediction. MJev-Spatial unifies these three spatial task types within a classification framework, enabling fast-thinking decisions with high accuracy and low inference latency. fig:teaser Introduction Spatial intelligence involves perceiving and reasoning about the geometry and spatial relationships of objects, which enables agents to navigate their surroundings and interact with the physical world~ spatialvlm,spatialrgpt . Many of these interactions require timely spatial judgments. Vision-language models (VLMs) support these capabilities by answering spatial questions grounded in visual observations. Such questions may require selecting an option that describes a spatial relation~ sat,cvbench,blink,mmsi , estimating a numerical quantity such as distance~ sensenova,cambrians,vst , or identifying a point for object placement~ refspatial,robopoint,robospatial,pointarena . To produce these spatial predictions, many existing VLMs retain their pretrained autoregressive text-generation capabilities~ spatialvlm,spatialrgpt,molmo,robopoint,refspatial . Each option, numerical value, or image location is therefore represented as a token sequence that the model is trained to reproduce. This couples learning the spatial answer with learning its textual form, including formatting and boilerplate when present, introducing supervision beyond the task-relevant prediction itself. At inference, the model must generate the answer tokens sequentially, after which the resulting text must be parsed to recover the spatial prediction, adding decoding and parsing overhead. This motivates a System~1 approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to make spatial judgments directly. Jev provides a precedent for this approach by returning probabilities over specified candidates without generating answer text~ jev . At the same time, we observe that all three common spatial output types can be represented as finite candidate sets: answer options are already finite, while numerical values and image locations can be discretized within a specified range and resolution. Building on these insights, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a multimodal decision model specifically tailored to spatial understanding. MJev-Spatial unifies the three output types by casting prediction as classification over finite candidate sets. Each class represents a supplied answer option, a numerical bin, or an image region, depending on the task. Selecting a class gives the chosen option, predicts which bin contains the target value, or predicts which region contains the target point. To choose among these classes, MJev-Spatial encodes their descriptions together with the observation and question, then reuses the final attention layer's pretrained query and key projections to compute class scores. A softmax over these scores gives the class probabilities, without additional prediction heads or trainable parameters. At inference, each classification decision scores all its candidates in one forward pass. Furthermore, to obtain fine-grained values and coordinates without evaluating a large number of classes at once, we subdivide the selected numerical bin or image region and classify again. Numerical prediction uses up to two stages; single-point prediction uses three stages, re-encoding the selected image crop before each later decision to recover local visual detail. The final selection is decoded to a numerical value or image coordinates. Conditional tree expansion evaluates multiple region paths to extend the same trained point predictor to multiple points without additional training. Numerical and point prediction can require multiple supervised stages, with new image crops introduced between point decisions. Ground-truth answers determine the target classes and crops, allowing all stages to be jointly supervised in one teacher-forced causal forward pass. We average the stage cross-entropy losses per question so that a multi-stage example does not receive greater weight than a one-stage choice. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing address the padding and workload imbalance caused by different sequence lengths and crop counts while preserving optimizer-batch membership. An audited conversion pipeline supplies 12.3M QA from existing spatial annotations for full-parameter training of the retained language backbone. Built on Qwen3.5-4B~ qwen35 , MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score among eight evaluated models, leads on seven benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve. Across all twelve benchmarks, it achieves 2.5 and 5.6 speedups over the fastest autoregressive baseline and the base model, respectively. Separate studies examine candidate scoring, visual refinement, numerical discretization, and training execution. The readout and refinement studies assess how candidate scoring with pretrained projections and crop re-encoding contribute to prediction quality and computational cost; the numerical study shows that coarser length discretization can reduce prediction error despite its lower resolution. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing further improve training throughput by 30.8 over the original batching strategy. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,label=( )] We propose a novel System~1 paradigm for spatial intelligence, unifying option selection, numerical estimation, and image pointing through direct classification over finite candidate sets. Building on this paradigm, we develop MJev-Spatial and a unified training recipe, using pretrained attention projections for candidate scoring and joint supervision across spatial tasks and refinement stages. Across twelve spatial benchmarks, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest mean score among eight evaluated models and a 5.6 speedup over its autoregressive base model, Qwen3.5-4B. Related Work System 1 decision model. Jev motivates predicting over declared answer spaces instead of generating unrestricted answer text~ jev . Jev-Omni extends this interface to multimodal inputs~ jevomni , while KEV implements candidate scoring with learned query and key projections~ kev . visualjev and jevvisual study direct decisions and shared-context execution; embodiedjev applies decision interfaces to skill and action selection. Concurrent work, VideoJev, uses a shared candidate scorer for temporal grounding and video question answering, with cached and joint inference for queries about the same video~ zhu2026videojevmodelvideounderstanding . Visual Jev reads candidate-token probabilities from the existing language-model head and finds no consistent accuracy advantage from an added typed head in its matched control. MJev-Spatial instead scores contextual candidate content with the backbone's final-layer query and key projections and trains all output types with the same candidate-classification objective. Our matched readout experiments show competitive quality and lower training cost for this design, with task-dependent tradeoffs ( ). The earlier Molmo2-ER-based MJev-Spatial prototype used LoRA and an added decision head~ molmo2er,lora . The present model uses Qwen3.5-4B and trains all retained language parameters. Backbone efficiency is also studied through pruning and quantization, joint low-rank and sparsity optimization, and adaptive execution~ zhou2026buddy,zhou2026deputy,zhou2025qpruner, zhou2025largecompression . Class-aware adaptation provides a complementary route to efficient vision-language classification. AWT enriches class descriptions and combines augmented views through entropy-based weighting and optimal transport~ zhu2024awt . Self-TPT uses self-supervised prompt adaptation for new classes to avoid costly per-image optimization at inference~ zhu2026efficient . Spatial understanding with VLMs. Broader multimodal research covers visual reasoning~ qin2025unicot , retrieval~ qin2024bvrcc , and multimodal generation~ zhang2024musetalk,qin2026univigu,zhong2025anytalker . Video understanding further requires temporal localization~ zhu2024dual,zhu2026timelens2 and efficient processing of long or streaming observations~ li2026videochat3,zeng2026onestreamer . SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT learn spatial relations and numerical answers from spatial supervision~ spatialvlm,spatialrgpt , while Molmo, RoboPoint, and RoboRefer support pointing through coordinate text~ molmo,robopoint,refspatial . Alternative interfaces can ground predictions more directly. MolmoPoint selects visual patches and refines locations through a sequence of specialized grounding tokens~ molmopoint . MJev-Spatial uses one candidate-classification mechanism for options, numerical values, and points, with task-specific candidates supplying the output structure. Its multi-point extension expands conditional classification paths rather than generating a variable-length coordinate string. Representing continuous predictions with discrete classes is established in computer vision. DORN formulates monocular depth estimation as ordinal regression over logarithmically spaced depth intervals~ dorn . Our length representation also uses logarithmically spaced coarse intervals, followed by linear refinement, but its intervals are candidate descriptions scored by a shared language backbone. Counts and angles retain their own ranges and discretization schemes. Visual search methods such as V refine image regions to recover details needed for answering~ vstar . Video-o3 similarly acquires evidence iteratively in long videos, interleaving clue seeking with inspection of relevant segments~ zeng2026video . In MJev-Spatial, region selection itself is supervised as classification, and re-encoded crops provide the evidence for subsequent decisions. Method sec:method MJev-Spatial takes visual observations, a spatial question, and task-specific candidates as input. Following Jev~ jev , it predicts by selecting candidates rather than generating text. We first explain how one classification framework handles answer options, numerical values, and image locations, including coarse-to-fine refinement and multi-point prediction. We then describe the shared model architecture and the training recipe. Unified Classification Framework for Spatial Intelligence sec:transitions Given ordered images and a spatial question , the model predicts an option, a number with a declared unit, or a point in normalized image coordinates. Each candidate is a possible answer for the current decision. For a choice question, it is one of the supplied options; for a numerical or point question, it identifies an interval or region in which the target is predicted to lie. This lets all three output types use the same candidate-classification rule. At stage , a deterministic task controller constructs candidates from the question and preceding selections and visual refinements . The shared scorer assigns a logit to each candidate, and prediction selects the highest-scoring class: Only the current legal candidates enter the softmax; padded slots receive . A choice question ends after this decision. For numerical and point prediction, the selected class determines the next candidate set and any new image crop. The final class is decoded to an exact value or interval midpoint for numerical tasks, or a region center for pointing. illustrates these prediction paths, and summarizes the output contracts. Each classification decision scores all current candidates in one forward pass, with no answer-token generation or text parsing. A complete prediction can require several such decisions: numerical tasks use up to two stages and single-point prediction uses three. Multi-point prediction evaluates additional branches of the same spatial hierarchy. The common score

title: Velox: Spatial Memory Makes World Models Efficient
summary: Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by $4.36\times$ and denoising by $2.43\times$. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.

Introduction sec:introduction Video world models are emerging as a practical interface for interactive simulation. A user specifies an action trajectory or camera motion, and the model rolls the world forward by generating future video frames. This direction builds on rapid progress in video diffusion transformers and large video foundation models~ ho2020denoising,rombach2022high,peebles2023scalable,blattmann2023stable,chen2024videocrafter2,yang2024cogvideox,kong2024hunyuanvideo,wan2025wan,ma2025step . Recent works increasingly target controllable long video worlds rather than isolated short clips~ alonso2024diffusion,valevski2024diffusion,bruce2024genie,parkerholder2024genie2,teng2025magi,gao2026advancing,cao2026hyworld . For these models, context management is a central methodological challenge. Past frames carry the appearance, geometry, and object state that future frames must respect. Without access to the right history, long rollouts drift, forget revisited regions, or re-synthesize the same scene inconsistently. The most direct way to preserve this history is to retain an ever-growing visual context. Chunked or causal video diffusion models let each new chunk attend to historical frame tokens through a KV cache. Dense FlashAttention makes this practical at moderate lengths~ dao2022flashattention,dao2023flashattention , and causal diffusion or self-forcing training makes long rollouts natural~ chen2024diffusion,huang2025self . The cost, however, grows with the number of generated chunks. Later chunks inherit larger context even when the current camera overlaps only a small part of the past scene. As a result, chunk-wise generation becomes progressively slower exactly when long-horizon consistency matters most. This motivates context selection rather than naive context accumulation. Frame- and view-memory methods select a smaller set of relevant past observations. Context-as-Memory retrieves historical views by camera field-of-view overlap, and VMem stores surfel-indexed views for consistent revisits~ yu2025context,li2025vmem . AnchorWeave and related works~ xiao2025worldmem,wu2025spatialmemory,wang2026anchorweave further inject warped renderings from persistent memory through ControlNet~ zhang2023adding to stabilize camera-controlled generation. These methods show that not all past frames are equally useful, and summarizes this progression from dense history to view-level retrieval. Yet frame-level selection remains coarse for transformer attention. It provides the same selected context to all regions in the active chunk, although dynamic scenes often need local temporal continuity and different regions in the same noisy chunk can depend on different parts of the past. Methods that inject warped point renderings into the model input can also require architectural adaptation or fine-tuning, which limits direct reuse of a pretrained video generator. Inspired by inverse rendering works~ kerbl20233d,mildenhall2021nerf , we observe that regions whose geometry has already been observed should primarily attend to their corresponding past regions. Newly revealed or uncertain regions, in contrast, may require model-derived semantic context and local temporal neighbors. A road block, a facade block, and newly revealed sky in the same noisy chunk should therefore not necessarily attend to the same past views. The question, then, is no longer only which frames to retrieve, but whether long-context video generation can assign each region its own relevant history while preserving local motion continuity and leaving the pretrained generator unchanged. We consider this question at the token-block level in the block-wise execution model of FlashAttention~ dao2023flashattention . Our key insight is that camera frustum slabs with depth intervals can provide region-specific routing signals at the same granularity used by tiled attention. Instead of adding a new conditioning branch or fine-tuning the video generator, summarizes generated history as per-block frustum slabs and uses their overlap to guide which historical KV token blocks each current region should see. For each target chunk, obtains query-side depth through recency-priority multiwarp and scores query and historical blocks by world-space OBB frustum slab overlap. In well-covered regions, this score softly reweights each layer's model-derived block importance before selection. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. Previous-chunk retention and global-aligned Gilbert neighborhoods preserve local motion continuity without a separate cross-chunk seam table. Across 48-chunk timing traces and the 158-case WBench navigation split~ ying2026wbench , reduces the growing long-context attention cost while preserving aggregate quality near dense attention. Its advantage grows with the number of generated chunks. At chunk 48, attention latency decreases from approximately ms with dense FlashAttention to ms, a speedup. Denoising time decreases from approximately s to s under the same single-H200 asynchronous setting. Built on LingBot-Fast-Cam~ gao2026advancing , remains within points of dense attention on the WBench API-free average and improves the 19-metric overall average from to . These results support the scoped claim that soft frustum slab routing can alleviate the late-chunk attention bottleneck without materially degrading benchmark quality. Our contributions can be summarized as: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt] We introduce , a training-free framework that uses frustum slab correspondences to reduce growing KV attention cost in chunked video world models. We devise a soft geometric fusion rule that uses OBB frustum slab overlap to modulate each layer's model-derived block importance while preserving an unbiased fallback for uncovered regions. We implement with global-aligned Gilbert KV storage, an optimized sparse attention kernel, and asynchronous frustum slab construction on the same H200 as denoising, reaching a attention speedup and a denoising speedup at chunk 48. Related Work Video World Models and Spatial Memory Video generation has progressed from latent diffusion to scalable diffusion transformers and rectified flow~ ho2020denoising,rombach2022high,blattmann2023stable,peebles2023scalable,esser2024scaling , with foundation models supplying strong visual priors~ yang2024cogvideox,kong2024hunyuanvideo,wan2025wan,hacohen2024ltx,ma2025step,gao2025seedance,team2025longcat . These directions make history management central: more context supports consistency but makes dense attention increasingly expensive. Spatial-memory methods address this tension by retrieving views, preserving revisits, or expanding reconstructed worlds~ yu2025context,li2025vmem,xiao2025worldmem,wu2025spatialmemory,huang2025voyager,chen2025flexworld,yu2024wonderjourney,yu2024wonderworld,engstler2024invisible . title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.
full_text: Method sec:method Speculative Forcing allows individual tokens to stop denoising at different steps. Accepted drafts are fixed as output, while their cached keys and values provide context for tokens that continue denoising (Section~ sec:framework ). To determine when to accept each draft, we introduce two verifiers that predict convergence from latent estimates or the generator's intermediate features (Section~ sec:verification ). Preliminaries sec:prelim Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate a video as a sequence of latent chunks , each containing one or more consecutive frames. The joint distribution is factorized as where each conditional distribution is modeled through a diffusion process. At inference, the model generates each chunk by progressively denoising Gaussian noise conditioned on previously generated chunks. We consider generators that use clean history as conditioning and cache its keys and values to avoid recomputing history features during subsequent generation. Distilled AR video generators~ causvid, selfforcing, longlive reduce the denoising process to steps, enabling real-time streaming. Each chunk contains spatiotemporal latent tokens indexed by . At step , the generator takes the current noisy latent and the clean history as input and predicts a clean estimate . For , this estimate is re-noised to the next noise level for further denoising, and the final estimate is returned as the generated chunk. These generators can be trained with distribution matching distillation~ dmd, dmd2 , which aligns their output distribution with a target distribution represented by a pretrained teacher. In particular, Self Forcing~ selfforcing trains on autoregressive rollouts conditioned on self-generated history and randomly selects a denoising exit step at which to evaluate the distribution-matching objective. Intermediate clean estimates thus receive supervision as generated samples, although the standard inference procedure runs every token through all steps. Token-wise Commitment sec:framework Figure~ fig:diff_map shows that tokens approach the full-step output at different rates: some intermediate estimates already closely match their final values, while others continue to change. This motivates committing converged tokens while continuing to refine the rest. Speculative Forcing treats each intermediate token estimate as a draft and uses a verifier to predict whether further denoising would substantially change it (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). Accepted drafts are committed as final outputs and removed from further denoising, while the remaining tokens continue to be refined. Every token starts active, and the first step produces a draft for every token. At each step , the verifier evaluates the active tokens. An accepted token has its output fixed to and is excluded from all subsequent denoising forwards. Its layer-wise keys and values computed at commitment remain cached, allowing active tokens to continue attending to it. Rejected tokens are re-noised to the next noise level and continue denoising. Any tokens still active at step are committed at that step. Let denote the commit step of token . The completed chunk combines estimates accepted at potentially different steps, The base generator's clean pass over then refreshes the KV cache for subsequent chunks. Commitment reduces the number of denoising token evaluations from to , with mean denoising depth . Both methods additionally perform token evaluations for the clean pass. To decide which drafts can be accepted, we measure how closely an intermediate estimate agrees with the generator's full-step output. Here, denotes the output of the original generator with every token evaluated at all steps, using the same initial noise and conditioning. This reference measures the change that remains under the original denoising schedule. We normalize the distance by , the median token norm in the full-step output of chunk , and define the convergence gap as A draft meets the convergence criterion when . Since the full-step output is unavailable during early commitment, this gap serves as an oracle and is used as the ground truth in . Convergence Verification sec:verification To make acceptance decisions before the full-step output is available, we seek evidence of convergence in the current draft and the features used to produce it. The draft can be compared with clean content or its own previous estimate, motivating a training-free verifier. The generator's intermediate features provide additional contextual information, which a learned verifier uses to predict the convergence gap. Since latent tokens encode content across multiple output frames, isolated acceptance decisions can affect both spatial and temporal coherence. We therefore apply a spatiotemporal smoothing operator to each verifier's scores before thresholding, encouraging coherent decisions across neighboring tokens. Training-Free Verifier sec:tf At the first step, only one draft exists, so a token's own change cannot be observed. We therefore rely on its redundancy with content that is already clean. From the second step on, we judge convergence by how much the token's consecutive drafts differ. We observe that drafts resembling previously generated or reference content often have smaller remaining changes (Figure~ fig:diff_map ). This motivates similarity to clean content as a proxy for convergence. At the first step, we score each token by the distance from its draft to the most similar clean latent token, where contains clean latent tokens from previous chunks within the generator's attention window and any reference frames, including those retained as attention sinks. The search covers all spatial positions within this bank to accommodate camera and object motion. Tokens with are accepted. From the second step on, two consecutive drafts of the same active token are available. Their difference measures how much the token's estimate has changed over the latest denoising step, Active tokens with are accepted. Both thresholds are calibrated on held-out data. Tokens whose drafts closely match clean content can thus be committed at the first step, while tokens with sufficiently small changes between consecutive drafts can be committed at later steps. Tokens that satisfy neither condition run the full schedule. Learned Verifier sec:head Redundancy and stability are proxies for convergence rather than convergence itself. A token can match the history and still need refinement, or change little between two steps and yet remain far from its final value. The learned verifier instead predicts the convergence gap directly from the generator's own features. A shallow convolutional head suffices for this prediction, indicating that the intermediate features contain information about each token's remaining discrepancy to the full-step output. The head takes the hidden state of a selected backbone layer at step and outputs a predicted gap for each token. It consists of layer normalization followed by three 3D convolutions and is shared across all steps. We run the frozen generator for the full steps and collect intermediate hidden states together with their oracle convergence gaps. Only the head is trained, using a Huber loss, where denotes the head parameters. At inference, we retain the last hidden states of committed tokens and update those of active tokens, preserving the token grid for the convolutional head. At each step , the head predicts , and active tokens with are accepted. Because the head predicts the convergence gap itself, sets a tolerance on the predicted discrepancy to the full-step output. Local smoothing encourages spatially and temporally coherent decisions. Adjusting controls the speed-quality trade-off at inference without retraining or fine-tuning.
